01 · CCR Start-Up & Power

20 of 20 topics published
CCR-001 CCR Not Starting

Symptom — CCR does not enter run state when a start command is issued (local or remote/ALCMS). Front panel remains in standby/OFF; no output current is generated at the series circuit.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator (CCR) — series circuit lighting control unit, thyristor or IGBT-regulated, rated 4–100 kW, 6.6A (or 20A/30A legacy) constant-current output, 5-step or stepless intensity control.

Possible Causes
HighEmergency stop or door interlock active — cabinet door open, E-stop latched, or interlock switch misaligned
HighStart command not received — faulty local start switch, broken control wiring, or ALCMS/PLC output not energized
HighInput supply fault — upstream MCB/breaker tripped, phase loss, or input voltage below undervoltage threshold
MediumControl circuit fuse blown — F1/F2 control fuse open, isolating the 24VDC or 230VAC control rail
MediumMain contactor not energizing — failed coil, mechanically stuck contactor, or auxiliary contact feedback mismatch
Medium24VDC control power supply failure — internal SMPS module has failed or is out of regulation
LowerPLC/controller fault or firmware lock-up — controller unresponsive, requires power-cycle or firmware reset
LowerProtection relay latched from a prior trip — earth fault, overcurrent, or overtemperature trip not yet reset
LowerMechanical/key interlock misaligned — key switch not in RUN/REMOTE position, or MCB handle interlock not engaged
Required Tools
True-RMS digital multimeter (CAT III)Clamp meterInsulation resistance tester (500V/1000V)CCR wiring diagram / O&M manualInsulated torque screwdriver setContinuity/probe test leads
Safety Precautions
  • CCR output can reach several kV under load depending on circuit length — never work on output terminals while the CCR is running or capacitors are charged.
  • Apply lock-out/tag-out (LOTO) on the CCR input isolator before any internal inspection. Treat all terminals as live until proven de-energized with a tested meter.
  • Follow site electrical safety procedure and the two-person rule for HV isolation. Use appropriate PPE.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCheck CCR front panel/HMI: is the power-on lamp lit? Is a fault/alarm indicator active? Note the exact displayed status and any alarm code before touching anything.
  2. ObservationInspect the E-stop button and cabinet door interlock switch. Confirm E-stop is released and the door is fully closed and latched.
  3. MeasurementWith power isolated and verified dead, or per LOTO procedure, measure incoming 3-phase supply voltage at CCR input terminals L1-L2-L3.
  4. MeasurementCheck continuity of control circuit fuses (F1/F2).
  5. MeasurementMeasure the 24VDC control supply output terminals.
  6. MeasurementMeasure contactor coil terminals A1-A2 for correct coil voltage when a start command is issued.
  7. MeasurementVerify the start command signal at the PLC/ALCMS digital input terminal, toggling the local start switch and confirming the state change.
  8. ObservationReview the CCR controller's alarm/event log for any latched fault blocking a fresh start.
  9. DecisionBranch based on findings: no input supply → upstream distribution. Supply present but no 24VDC → control power supply fault. 24VDC present but no start signal → control wiring/ALCMS fault. Start signal present but contactor doesn't pull in → contactor/coil fault. Contactor pulls in but CCR still doesn't run → controller/PLC fault or latched alarm.
  10. Fault LocationIsolate the fault to one subsystem: incoming supply, control circuit, contactor, PLC/controller, or interlock chain.
  11. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component within the isolated subsystem rather than stopping at the subsystem level.
Test Points
Input terminals L1/L2/L3 (3-phase supply)
Control fuse F1/F2 continuity
24VDC control supply output
Contactor coil terminals A1-A2
Start command digital input (PLC/ALCMS)
E-stop loop continuity
Door interlock switch continuity
Controller alarm/event log
Root Cause Verification

Confirm the identified root cause by isolating the suspect component and re-testing in isolation before reassembly. Do not close out on a single successful start — verify stability across at least one full intensity-step cycle.

Corrective Action
  • Reset E-stop and confirm door interlock is fully latched before re-attempting start.
  • Restore upstream input supply / reset tripped distribution breaker after confirming no downstream fault caused the trip.
  • Replace blown control fuse with correct rating and type — do not upsize.
  • Repair or replace faulty start-command wiring, terminal, or ALCMS/PLC output card.
  • Replace failed contactor coil or contactor assembly if mechanically seized.
  • Replace the 24VDC control power supply module if out of regulation.
  • Power-cycle and, if required, reflash/reset the PLC controller per manufacturer procedure.
  • Clear the latched protection alarm only after the underlying trip cause has been independently confirmed resolved.
Preventive Action
  • Include monthly functional testing of E-stop and door interlock circuits in the CCR PM schedule.
  • Perform periodic insulation/megger testing of control wiring during scheduled maintenance windows.
  • Track contactor duty cycles and replace preventively based on manufacturer MTBF data.
  • Maintain a current firmware/configuration backup for each CCR controller.
  • Document the CCR start sequence and interlock chain in the site SOP.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist), SOP-CCR-04 (CCR Isolation & LOTO Procedure)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-002 CCR Completely Dead

Symptom — No response at all from the CCR — no display, no indicator lights, no contactor activity, completely unresponsive to any command.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator, all ratings — total loss-of-function condition at the unit level.

Possible Causes
HighTotal loss of input supply — upstream breaker fully open/tripped
HighMain input isolator open or contact-failed
MediumBlown main incoming fuse on all phases
MediumCatastrophic failure of internal control power supply
LowerRodent/insect damage to control wiring
LowerWater ingress causing an internal short that has tripped upstream protection
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meterInsulation resistance testerInspection torchMain isolator key
Safety Precautions
  • Verify zero energy state with a proven meter before opening the cabinet.
  • Assume possible internal short or water ingress — inspect visually before re-energizing to avoid re-faulting the circuit.
  • If water ingress is suspected, do not re-energize until the cabinet is dried and inspected by qualified personnel.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the complete absence of all indications — display, LEDs, and cooling fan noise.
  2. MeasurementCheck the upstream distribution panel: is the dedicated CCR breaker/isolator ON and supply present at the panel?
  3. MeasurementTest at the CCR main input terminals — if the upstream breaker is on but no voltage reaches the CCR, suspect an open link or isolator fault in between.
  4. ObservationVisually inspect the CCR cabinet interior (after LOTO and a verified-dead check) for water ingress, burning, rodent damage, or loose main terminal connections.
  5. MeasurementCheck the main incoming fuses on all phases for continuity.
  6. DecisionNo supply at the panel → escalate to upstream distribution fault (see CCR-003). Supply present at panel but not at CCR → isolator/cabling fault. Supply present at CCR terminals but CCR still dead → internal catastrophic failure.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to upstream distribution, the interconnecting cable/isolator, or an internal CCR failure.
  8. Root CauseIdentify the specific failed link — isolator contact, blown fuse element, corroded terminal, or internal component.
Test Points
Upstream distribution panel output
CCR main isolator, both sides
Main incoming fuses
CCR main input terminals
Root Cause Verification

After repair, re-energize under supervision starting from the isolator and confirm a normal power-up sequence before restoring the connected load.

Corrective Action
  • Restore or repair the upstream supply.
  • Replace the failed isolator or fuse.
  • Repair or replace the damaged interconnecting cable.
  • Dry and inspect the cabinet after water ingress before re-energizing.
  • Engage qualified repair support for a confirmed internal catastrophic failure.
Preventive Action
  • Verify upstream breaker/isolator condition during scheduled PM.
  • Seal cable entries and cabinet gaskets against water ingress.
  • Rodent-proof cabinet cable entries.
  • Include periodic thermal imaging of main terminals in the PM programme.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01, SOP-CCR-04

Standards: ICAO Annex 14, FAA AC 150/5345-10, IEC 61439

Diagram: CCR Single Line Diagram, Cabinet Layout Drawing

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-003 CCR Main Power Not Available

Symptom — The upstream feeder to the CCR shows no voltage — the CCR itself is not at fault, the source supply is de-energized.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator and its dedicated upstream feeder/distribution path.

Possible Causes
HighUpstream substation/transformer outage
HighMain LV panel breaker for this feeder tripped or left open
MediumGenerator/UPS failure on standby supply
MediumCable fault between substation and the CCR feeder panel
LowerScheduled maintenance isolation not restored
LowerFuse blown at the upstream distribution board
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meterDistribution panel keys and PPEAirport electrical single line diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Coordinate with the airport electrical control room before working on main distribution.
  • Verify correct feeder identification before any isolation work, to avoid affecting other live circuits.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCheck the main distribution board/substation status — alarms and breaker position indicators.
  2. MeasurementMeasure voltage at the LV panel busbar feeding the CCR circuit.
  3. MeasurementTrace the dedicated feeder breaker for this CCR and confirm its position and load-side voltage.
  4. DecisionBusbar itself dead → upstream supply/generator issue, escalate to the power engineering team. Busbar live but feeder breaker open/tripped → breaker-specific fault.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the substation/transformer, the main busbar, or the dedicated feeder breaker.
  6. Root CauseConfirm the exact failure — breaker trip cause (overload/fault), cable fault, or a genuine supply outage.
Test Points
Substation output
Main LV busbar
Dedicated CCR feeder breaker, load side
Feeder cable at the CCR end
Root Cause Verification

Confirm stable voltage over a minimum monitoring period before reconnecting the CCR load, and check for no repeat trip once load is restored.

Corrective Action
  • Restore upstream supply per the utility/generator procedure.
  • Reset the feeder breaker only after confirming there is no downstream fault.
  • Repair the faulty feeder cable.
  • Switch to standby/generator supply per the site contingency plan if required.
Preventive Action
  • Maintain the standby generator/UPS testing schedule.
  • Include periodic thermal imaging of main distribution.
  • Keep the single line diagram current and feeder labelling accurate.
Related References

SOP: SOP-ELEC-02 (Main Distribution Isolation Procedure)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 (secondary power supply requirements), IEC 60364

Diagram: Airport Electrical Single Line Diagram

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-004 CCR Input Voltage Low

Symptom — CCR input terminals show voltage below rated tolerance (commonly below −10% of nominal); the CCR may run with reduced output, raise an undervoltage alarm, or fail to start depending on the configured threshold.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator input supply and its feeder cable path.

Possible Causes
HighLong feeder cable run with excessive voltage drop
HighUndersized feeder cable for the connected load
MediumOverloaded upstream transformer or distribution circuit
MediumLoose or high-resistance connection upstream
LowerIncorrect transformer tap-changer setting
LowerSimultaneous heavy load on a shared feeder (e.g., coincident lighting start-up surge)
Required Tools
Multimeter with min/max holdClamp meterPower quality analyzer / voltage loggerCable sizing/voltage-drop calculation reference
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV measurement precautions apply.
  • Be cautious of fluctuating readings, which may indicate an active fault condition rather than a steady-state drop.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementLog input voltage at the CCR terminals over a representative period, including at load switch-on, using a power quality analyzer or logging multimeter.
  2. MeasurementCompare against upstream distribution panel voltage at the same time to isolate whether the drop originates at source or along the feeder.
  3. ObservationCheck the feeder cable size and length against the original design/voltage-drop calculation.
  4. MeasurementInspect and torque-check all connections along the feeder path — terminals, joints, isolator contacts — looking for discoloration indicating overheating.
  5. DecisionDrop present at the panel too → upstream supply/transformer issue. Panel voltage normal but CCR terminal voltage low → feeder cable/connection issue.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific cable section or connection point using sequential voltage-drop measurement.
Test Points
Upstream panel busbar
Mid-run feeder junction (if accessible)
CCR input terminals
All load-side connections, for thermal/visual check
Root Cause Verification

After remedial work, re-log voltage under full load, including the peak intensity step, to confirm it stays within tolerance.

Corrective Action
  • Rectify loose or high-resistance connections.
  • Upgrade an undersized cable.
  • Rebalance loads across feeders where the drop originates from shared loading.
  • Coordinate with the utility on transformer tap setting if the drop originates upstream.
Preventive Action
  • Include a periodic voltage-drop survey in the PM programme.
  • Perform annual thermal imaging of feeder connections.
  • Review load management as airport lighting load grows over time.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (Periodic Electrical Testing)

Standards: IEC 60364 (voltage drop limits), FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: Feeder Cable Route Drawing, Voltage Drop Calculation Sheet

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-005 CCR Input Voltage High

Symptom — Input voltage exceeds rated tolerance (commonly above +10%); this may trigger overvoltage protection or accelerate component wear even if no alarm is raised.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator input supply.

Possible Causes
HighTransformer tap setting too high for actual site loading
HighLight loading on the distribution transformer causing voltage rise
MediumFaulty automatic voltage regulator (AVR) upstream
MediumIncorrect generator output voltage during standby operation
LowerCapacitor bank over-compensation on the network
Required Tools
Multimeter with min/max holdPower quality analyzerGenerator/AVR manual
Safety Precautions
  • Sustained overvoltage can stress and damage CCR components — do not repeatedly force-start against an active overvoltage alarm.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementLog input voltage over a representative period, noting peak values and their time of occurrence.
  2. ObservationCorrelate high-voltage periods with system loading — for example, overnight low-load periods — or with generator/standby operation.
  3. MeasurementCheck the upstream transformer tap position against the design record.
  4. DecisionOvervoltage correlates with light network loading → transformer tap/AVR issue. Overvoltage correlates with generator operation → generator AVR fault.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the transformer tap setting, the network AVR, or generator regulation.
Test Points
Transformer secondary
Upstream distribution panel
CCR input terminals
Generator output (if applicable)
Root Cause Verification

Re-log voltage after correction across varying load conditions, including a generator changeover test if standby power is involved.

Corrective Action
  • Adjust the transformer tap setting.
  • Repair or recalibrate the AVR.
  • Adjust the generator voltage regulator setting.
Preventive Action
  • Perform a periodic voltage survey across the full day/night load cycle.
  • Include an overvoltage check in the generator test schedule.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-GEN-01 (Generator Test Procedure)

Standards: IEC 60364, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: Airport Electrical Single Line Diagram

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-006 CCR Input Phase Failure

Symptom — One or more input phases are missing or significantly unbalanced; the CCR protection trips on a phase-failure/unbalance alarm, or the CCR fails to start.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator 3-phase input supply.

Possible Causes
HighBlown fuse on one phase upstream
HighSingle-pole breaker trip where a common-trip 3-phase breaker should be used
MediumLoose or burnt phase connection at a terminal
MediumBroken conductor in one phase of the feeder cable
LowerUpstream isolator contact failure on one pole
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meterPhase rotation/sequence meterThermal camera (optional)
Safety Precautions
  • A missing-phase fault can leave equipment partially live while appearing mechanically off — verify all three phases are individually dead before working on the circuit.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementMeasure phase-to-neutral (or phase-to-phase) voltage on all three phases at the CCR input terminals individually.
  2. ObservationNote which specific phase or phases show zero or abnormal voltage.
  3. MeasurementTrace the affected phase back through the isolator, fuse, and feeder to locate the break point using sequential voltage checks.
  4. ObservationInspect the affected phase's fuse, breaker pole, and terminal connections for visible damage or burning.
  5. DecisionThe fault lies between the two consecutive test points where voltage transitions from present to absent.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific fuse, breaker pole, terminal, or cable conductor.
Test Points
Upstream panel, all 3 phases
Isolator load side, all 3 phases
Fuse output, all 3 phases
CCR input terminals, all 3 phases
Root Cause Verification

Confirm balanced 3-phase voltage under load after repair; check phase sequence is correct if any conductor was reterminated.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the blown fuse.
  • Repair or replace the faulty breaker pole.
  • Repair the broken conductor or terminal connection.
  • Retorque all phase terminals.
Preventive Action
  • Include a 3-phase balance check in routine PM.
  • Use thermal imaging to catch developing high-resistance phase connections before failure.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02

Standards: FAA AC 150/5345-10, IEC 60364

Diagram: CCR Single Line Diagram

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-007 CCR Control Supply Failure

Symptom — Main 3-phase power is present at the CCR input, but the internal control circuit (24VDC or 230VAC control rail) has no power, so the CCR cannot process a start command even though it is electrically live.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator internal control power circuit.

Possible Causes
HighFailed control transformer
HighBlown control circuit fuse
MediumFailed internal SMPS/24VDC power supply module
MediumLoose control transformer wiring
LowerInternal control PCB fault
Required Tools
MultimeterSpare control fuse of correct ratingSpare SMPS module, if available
Safety Precautions
  • Control circuit failure does not mean the CCR is de-energized — main input remains live. Follow full LOTO before internal inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm main input voltage is present (per CCR-004/005/006) while display and control functions remain unresponsive.
  2. MeasurementCheck control transformer primary and secondary voltage.
  3. MeasurementCheck control circuit fuse continuity.
  4. MeasurementCheck the 24VDC (or applicable) output of the internal control power supply module.
  5. DecisionControl transformer output absent → transformer or its fuse. Transformer output present but 24VDC absent → SMPS module fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the control transformer, control fuse, or SMPS module.
Test Points
Control transformer primary
Control transformer secondary
Control fuse output
SMPS 24VDC output
Root Cause Verification

Confirm stable 24VDC (within ±5%) under full control load — all relays and indicators active — before returning to service.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the blown control fuse.
  • Replace the failed control transformer.
  • Replace the SMPS/control power supply module.
  • Re-terminate loose control wiring.
Preventive Action
  • Include a control supply voltage check in routine PM.
  • Keep critical spares — fuse, SMPS module — in site stores.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-CCR-05 (Spares Management)

Standards: FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-008 CCR Auxiliary Supply Failure

Symptom — Auxiliary supply feeding non-critical CCR accessories — cabinet heater, cabinet lighting, socket outlet, auxiliary cooling fan — has failed while main CCR control and output functions remain normal.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator auxiliary/accessory supply circuit.

Possible Causes
HighBlown auxiliary circuit fuse/MCB
MediumFailed auxiliary supply transformer
MediumTripped RCD on the auxiliary socket circuit
LowerFailed heater element causing circuit protection to trip
LowerMoisture ingress at auxiliary wiring
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meterSpare fuse/MCB
Safety Precautions
  • Auxiliary circuits are often on separate protective devices — confirm which specific circuit is isolated before working, as the main CCR circuit may remain live.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationIdentify which auxiliary function has failed — heater, lighting, socket, aux fan — and confirm main CCR operation is otherwise normal.
  2. MeasurementCheck the dedicated auxiliary fuse/MCB/RCD for trip status and continuity.
  3. MeasurementMeasure voltage at the auxiliary supply transformer output, if a separate transformer is used.
  4. ObservationInspect auxiliary wiring and the heater element for signs of moisture ingress or insulation damage that may have caused an RCD trip.
  5. DecisionProtective device trips again on reset → downstream fault (heater/wiring). Device holds after reset → likely a transient cause.
Test Points
Auxiliary fuse/MCB/RCD
Auxiliary transformer output
Heater element resistance
Auxiliary wiring insulation resistance
Root Cause Verification

Confirm the auxiliary circuit holds under load for an extended period, particularly through a heater cycling test, before closing out.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the blown fuse/MCB.
  • Reset the RCD only after the fault has been cleared and confirmed.
  • Replace the failed heater element.
  • Repair moisture-damaged wiring.
Preventive Action
  • Include the auxiliary circuit in routine PM checks.
  • Verify cabinet heater operation before onset of the monsoon/humid season.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02

Standards: FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-009 CCR Fuse Failure

Symptom — A specific fuse within the CCR — main input, control, or output-side — has blown, isolating its associated circuit; the failure mode depends on which fuse is affected.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator internal fuse protection, any position.

Possible Causes
HighGenuine overcurrent/short-circuit fault downstream of the fuse
MediumFuse rating too low for the circuit's normal transient (e.g., inrush)
MediumAged or degraded fuse element
LowerIncorrect fuse type/rating installed at a previous replacement
LowerMoisture-induced fuse holder corrosion causing nuisance opening
Required Tools
MultimeterInsulation resistance testerSpare fuses of correct rating/typeFuse puller
Safety Precautions
  • Never replace a blown fuse without first checking for a downstream short circuit. Always test insulation resistance of the protected circuit before re-energizing. Never substitute a higher-rated fuse.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationIdentify exactly which fuse has blown — main, control, or output — from its position and visual inspection/indicator.
  2. MeasurementBefore replacing, test insulation resistance and continuity of the circuit downstream of the blown fuse to check for a genuine short circuit.
  3. DecisionInsulation resistance low or a short found → locate and repair the downstream fault before replacing the fuse. Downstream circuit tests healthy → likely a nuisance blow (age, transient, or incorrect rating).
  4. Root CauseConfirm fuse rating and type match the CCR manufacturer's specification for that position.
Test Points
Fuse holder, both sides
Downstream circuit insulation resistance
Downstream circuit continuity
Root Cause Verification

After fitting a correctly rated fuse, monitor the circuit under normal load for repeat failure before closing out.

Corrective Action
  • Repair the downstream short/overload fault first.
  • Replace the fuse with the correct type and rating.
  • Replace a corroded fuse holder if applicable.
Preventive Action
  • Standardize fuse rating/type per manufacturer specification across all CCRs.
  • Maintain adequate correctly-rated spares.
  • Inspect fuse holders for corrosion during PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-CCR-05

Standards: FAA AC 150/5345-10, IEC 60269

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-010 CCR MCB/Breaker Tripping

Symptom — An internal or dedicated feeder MCB/breaker trips, either on attempted start or during operation, cutting supply to the CCR or a CCR subsystem.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator internal or dedicated feeder circuit breaker.

Possible Causes
HighGenuine overload on the protected circuit
HighShort-circuit fault downstream
MediumEarth leakage tripping an RCBO
MediumBreaker itself degraded and nuisance tripping
LowerAmbient temperature affecting the thermal-magnetic trip curve
LowerInrush current at start exceeding the breaker's instantaneous trip setting
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meter (for load current)Insulation resistance testerBreaker curve reference/datasheet
Safety Precautions
  • Do not repeatedly reset a tripping breaker without investigation — repeated fault-current interruption can degrade the breaker and pose an arc-flash/fire risk.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationNote whether the trip occurs immediately on closing (suggests short circuit/instantaneous trip) or after a delay under load (suggests thermal/overload trip).
  2. MeasurementMeasure load current on the protected circuit and compare against the breaker rating.
  3. MeasurementTest insulation resistance and continuity of the downstream circuit to rule out a short or earth fault.
  4. DecisionImmediate trip on closing with healthy downstream insulation → possible breaker fault or inrush exceeding the instantaneous setting. Delayed trip under a measured overload → genuine overload, review circuit sizing.
  5. Root CauseConfirm whether the breaker's trip curve/rating matches the circuit's design load and inrush characteristics.
Test Points
Breaker load-side current under normal operation
Downstream insulation resistance
Downstream continuity/earth fault loop
Root Cause Verification

After remedial action, monitor the circuit through several start/stop cycles, including the peak intensity step, before closing out.

Corrective Action
  • Repair the downstream short/earth fault.
  • Replace a degraded breaker.
  • Resize the breaker/circuit if genuinely overloaded.
  • Adjust breaker curve type if inrush-related and permitted by the manufacturer.
Preventive Action
  • Verify breaker selection against actual load/inrush data during design review.
  • Include breaker trip testing in periodic maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02

Standards: IEC 60947-2, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-011 CCR Contactor Not Energizing

Symptom — Start command and control supply are both confirmed present, but the main contactor fails to pull in, so the CCR does not proceed to the output stage.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator main contactor and its coil circuit.

Possible Causes
HighFailed contactor coil — open circuit
HighCoil voltage present but the contactor is mechanically seized
MediumIncorrect or mismatched coil voltage rating
MediumLoose coil wiring connection
LowerAn interlocking auxiliary contact (from a protection relay) preventing energization
LowerContactor coil overheated or damaged
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meterReplacement contactor/coilMechanical operation check tool
Safety Precautions
  • The contactor may control a high-current output circuit — fully isolate before mechanical inspection or replacement.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementConfirm coil voltage is present at the contactor coil terminals (A1-A2) when start is commanded.
  2. ObservationIf voltage is present but the contactor doesn't pull in, with power isolated, gently attempt to move the contactor armature to check for mechanical seizure.
  3. MeasurementIf no coil voltage is present despite a confirmed start command, check for an open interlock — a protection relay auxiliary contact — in series with the coil circuit.
  4. DecisionVoltage present, mechanically free, but no pull-in → failed coil. Voltage present and seized → mechanical fault. No voltage → upstream interlock or wiring fault.
  5. Root CauseConfirm the exact cause via coil resistance measurement (open circuit = infinite resistance), or identify which interlock contact is open.
Test Points
Contactor coil terminals A1-A2
Coil circuit interlock contacts
Coil resistance, with power isolated
Root Cause Verification

After correction, cycle the contactor several times under no-load, then confirm normal pull-in and drop-out under load.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed coil/contactor.
  • Free and lubricate a mechanically seized contactor per manufacturer guidance, or replace it.
  • Clear the interlocking protection condition.
  • Retighten loose coil wiring.
Preventive Action
  • Include contactor mechanical/electrical checks in PM.
  • Track contactor operation count against rated mechanical life.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02

Standards: IEC 60947-4-1

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-012 CCR Emergency Stop Active

Symptom — CCR will not start because the emergency stop circuit is in a tripped/latched state, shown by an E-stop or safety circuit fault indication.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator emergency stop / safety circuit.

Possible Causes
HighE-stop pushbutton physically latched, not released after a previous activation
MediumE-stop circuit wiring fault — an open loop
MediumSafety relay in the E-stop chain not reset
LowerA second E-stop station elsewhere in the loop (e.g., a remote panel) still latched
LowerDamaged E-stop button/contact block
Required Tools
MultimeterSafety relay reset procedure/manual
Safety Precautions
  • Never bypass or defeat an E-stop circuit to force a start. Always investigate and resolve the actual condition, and confirm no personnel are at risk before resetting.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationPhysically inspect all E-stop stations in the circuit — CCR local, remote panel, associated equipment — for a latched/pressed button.
  2. MeasurementIf all buttons appear released, measure continuity across the full E-stop loop to identify an open section.
  3. ObservationCheck the safety relay/monitoring module status indicator for a fault or not-reset condition.
  4. DecisionLatched button found → release and reset. Loop open with all buttons released → wiring fault between stations. Safety relay shows a fault → relay or its wiring.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific E-stop station, wiring segment, or safety relay.
Test Points
Each E-stop station individually
E-stop loop continuity end-to-end
Safety relay status/reset input
Root Cause Verification

After reset, functionally test the E-stop circuit by deliberately activating and releasing it to confirm correct trip/reset behaviour before returning to service.

Corrective Action
  • Release the latched button.
  • Repair open wiring in the E-stop loop.
  • Replace a damaged E-stop button/contact block.
  • Reset or replace a faulty safety relay.
Preventive Action
  • Include an E-stop functional test in monthly PM.
  • Label all E-stop stations clearly.
  • Protect wiring runs from mechanical damage.

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-013 CCR Start Command Not Received

Symptom — All internal CCR conditions are healthy — supply, control power, and interlocks are clear — but the CCR does not start because no start signal arrives at its command input.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator start-command interface, local switch through to ALCMS/PLC.

Possible Causes
HighFaulty local start pushbutton/selector switch
HighBroken or disconnected control wiring between the command source and the CCR
MediumALCMS/PLC output card fault, or the output not configured/energized
MediumIncorrect wiring at the terminal — wrong terminal number
LowerRemote/local selector switch in the wrong position
Required Tools
MultimeterALCMS/PLC diagnostic accessWiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV control circuit precautions apply. Coordinate with the control room before testing ALCMS outputs, to avoid unintended commands to other circuits.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the local/remote selector switch position matches the source from which the start command is being issued.
  2. MeasurementToggle the start command and measure at the CCR's command input terminal for a state change.
  3. MeasurementIf no change is seen at the CCR terminal, trace back toward the source, checking at intermediate terminals/junction boxes.
  4. ObservationAt the ALCMS/PLC end, confirm the relevant output point is being commanded and is physically energized — check the status LED on the output card, if available.
  5. DecisionSignal confirmed present at the source but not at the CCR → wiring fault in between. Signal absent even at the source output → ALCMS/PLC configuration or output card fault. Selector switch in the wrong position → operator/configuration error.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific wiring segment, terminal, selector switch, or ALCMS output point.
Test Points
Local start switch
Remote/local selector switch
Intermediate junction box terminals
CCR command input terminal
ALCMS/PLC output card status
Root Cause Verification

Confirm a clean, repeatable state change at the CCR terminal correlating exactly with the operator's command before closing out.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the faulty pushbutton/selector switch.
  • Repair the broken wiring.
  • Correct the ALCMS/PLC output configuration.
  • Replace a faulty output card.
  • Correct the terminal wiring error.
Preventive Action
  • Include start-command path verification in commissioning and periodic PM.
  • Maintain accurate as-built wiring/IO schedule documentation.

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-014 CCR Start Command Received but CCR Not Starting

Symptom — The start command is confirmed present at the CCR's input terminal by direct measurement, yet the CCR does not proceed to run — the fault lies internal to the CCR beyond the command interface.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator internal controller and command-processing path.

Possible Causes
HighInternal controller/PLC fault preventing command processing
HighA latched internal alarm blocking start despite a valid command
MediumContactor circuit fault downstream of the confirmed command (see CCR-011)
MediumFirmware/logic requiring a specific command sequence — e.g., stop-then-start — that isn't being met
LowerInternal command relay/opto-isolator failure
Required Tools
MultimeterCCR controller diagnostic/service toolWiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV control circuit precautions apply. Internal diagnostics may require accessing live control circuitry — follow safe working practice.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRe-confirm, independently of the earlier check, that the start signal reaches the correct internal terminal with correct polarity/logic level.
  2. ObservationCheck the controller's alarm/status log for any latched condition blocking the start.
  3. MeasurementTrace the command signal internally from the input terminal through any interposing relay or opto-isolator to the controller's logic input.
  4. DecisionCommand confirmed reaching the controller cleanly with no latched alarm → controller/firmware fault. Command lost internally → interposing relay/isolator fault. Latched alarm present → resolve the specific alarm first via its own topic.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the controller itself, an internal interposing component, or a latched protection condition.
Test Points
CCR command input terminal
Interposing relay/opto-isolator, input and output
Controller logic input
Controller alarm/status log
Root Cause Verification

After correction, confirm the CCR starts reliably across multiple consecutive start commands, including after a controlled stop.

Corrective Action
  • Clear the specific latched alarm per its own topic.
  • Repair or replace the faulty interposing relay or opto-isolator.
  • Reset or update controller firmware per manufacturer guidance.
  • Replace the controller if a core fault is confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Keep controller firmware version documented and current.
  • Include internal command-path verification in commissioning tests.

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-015 CCR Repeated Start Failure

Symptom — The CCR fails to start on multiple consecutive attempts, whether from a specific recurring cause or an unresolved intermittent condition, rather than a single isolated no-start event.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator, all subsystems — investigation spans the full start-up chain.

Possible Causes
HighAn underlying cause from CCR-001 through CCR-014 that has only been symptomatically reset, not resolved
HighA genuinely intermittent fault — loose connection or marginal component — that passes isolated testing
MediumProtection system re-latching immediately after each reset due to a persistent downstream fault
MediumControl power supply marginal/degrading under load
LowerOperator repeatedly attempting a start against an unresolved safety interlock
Required Tools
MultimeterData logger for repeated-attempt trendingCCR event log export tool
Safety Precautions
  • Repeated forced start attempts against an unresolved fault can cause component damage or a safety risk. Do not simply keep resetting and retrying without investigation.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationExport and review the CCR event/alarm log across all recent failed start attempts to identify whether the same fault code recurs each time.
  2. DecisionSame specific fault code repeats → treat as that specific topic's fault not yet fully resolved; re-open the relevant investigation with more rigorous root cause verification. Fault codes vary or none is logged → treat as an intermittent fault per Division 22 methodology.
  3. MeasurementWhere an intermittent connection is suspected, perform a wiggle test — with power isolated — on suspect connectors/terminals while monitoring continuity.
  4. Root CauseConfirm root cause with a sustained multi-cycle test rather than a single successful start.
Test Points
As per the specific recurring fault code identified in the event log
Root Cause Verification

Require a minimum of five consecutive successful start/stop cycles, including under realistic field conditions (e.g., after an overnight cold soak), before closing out.

Corrective Action
  • Apply the specific recurring fault's corrective action, with emphasis on thorough root cause verification rather than a quick reset.
Preventive Action
  • Make event log review a standing part of any repeated-failure investigation.
  • Track recurring fault codes in the site failure database to catch developing problems early.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Repeated Fault Investigation Procedure)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-016 CCR Unexpected Shutdown

Symptom — CCR was running normally and then shuts down without an operator-issued stop command, output current dropping to zero.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator, running state — protection, supply, and command systems all in scope.

Possible Causes
HighA protection trip — overcurrent, earth fault, overtemperature (see the Protection & Alarms subsection)
HighA genuine loss of input supply
MediumAn unintended stop command from ALCMS/PLC
MediumControl power supply momentary failure/brownout
LowerInternal controller watchdog reset
Required Tools
MultimeterCCR event log export toolPower quality logger
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV precautions apply. Treat an unexpected shutdown as a potential protection event until proven otherwise — do not force a restart without reviewing the cause.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationImmediately review the CCR event/alarm log for the exact timestamp and logged cause of the shutdown.
  2. DecisionSpecific protection alarm logged → proceed to that alarm's specific topic in the Protection & Alarms subsection. No alarm logged → investigate the supply/command path.
  3. MeasurementIf no protection alarm, check for a logged loss of input supply at the shutdown timestamp, cross-referenced against site power monitoring if available.
  4. ObservationCheck the ALCMS/PLC command history for an unintended or scheduled stop command issued at that time.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the protection system, a supply interruption, the command system, or control power stability.
Test Points
CCR event/alarm log
Input supply logger
ALCMS/PLC command history
Control power supply stability
Root Cause Verification

Monitor the CCR through a full operating cycle, including peak-load periods, to confirm the shutdown does not recur.

Corrective Action
  • Address the specific protection cause identified.
  • Restore or stabilize input supply.
  • Correct ALCMS/PLC command logic.
  • Replace an unstable control power supply component.
Preventive Action
  • Ensure event logging is active and reviewed regularly.
  • Ensure ALCMS command logic includes safeguards against unintended stop commands.

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-017 CCR Restarting Automatically

Symptom — CCR restarts on its own after a stop/trip without an operator command — this may be an auto-restart function operating as designed, or a fault causing unintended cycling.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator restart logic — internal configuration and/or ALCMS/PLC command sequencing.

Possible Causes
HighAuto-restart/auto-reclose function intentionally configured, operating after a transient trip — verify against design intent
MediumALCMS/PLC sending a repeated/looping start command due to a logic fault
MediumA marginal protection setting causing rapid trip-reset-trip cycling
LowerControl relay contact bouncing/chattering
Required Tools
MultimeterCCR configuration/parameter accessALCMS/PLC logic review access
Safety Precautions
  • Uncommanded restart of high-voltage output equipment poses a risk to personnel working nearby. Treat any circuit with unexplained auto-restart as potentially live at all times and apply LOTO before any physical work, regardless of its apparent OFF state.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCheck CCR configuration parameters for an enabled auto-restart/auto-reclose function and its configured delay/attempt count.
  2. DecisionAuto-restart intentionally configured → confirm this matches the design intent and site operating philosophy; if not, treat as a configuration error to correct. Auto-restart not configured in the CCR → review ALCMS/PLC command logic for a repeating or looping start command.
  3. MeasurementIf relay chattering/bouncing is suspected, physically inspect and test the specific control relay.
Test Points
CCR auto-restart configuration parameter
ALCMS/PLC command sequence log
Suspect control relay contacts
Root Cause Verification

Confirm the CCR behaves per the intended design — either staying off after a manual stop, or auto-restarting only per documented design logic — across several test cycles.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the auto-restart configuration to match design intent.
  • Fix the ALCMS/PLC repeating command logic.
  • Replace a chattering relay.
Preventive Action
  • Document the intended auto-restart philosophy clearly in the O&M manual and site SOP.
  • Review ALCMS logic changes through a formal change control process.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01, SOP-ALCMS-02

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-018 CCR Power-On Self-Test Failure

Symptom — CCR controller runs an internal power-on self-test (POST) at start-up and reports a failure, halting the start sequence before reaching run state.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator controller and its monitored internal subsystems.

Possible Causes
HighInternal memory/firmware checksum failure
MediumA monitored internal sensor — current, voltage, or temperature — reading out of expected range at power-on
MediumAn internal communication bus fault between controller sub-modules
LowerA genuine internal hardware fault detected by the self-test
Required Tools
CCR controller diagnostic/service toolMultimeterManufacturer POST fault code reference
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV/control circuit precautions apply. Do not attempt to bypass a POST failure — it exists specifically to prevent starting with a detected fault.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the exact POST fault code or message displayed.
  2. ObservationCross-reference the fault code against the manufacturer's service manual to identify the specific flagged subsystem.
  3. MeasurementTest the specific flagged subsystem — sensor, module, or bus — per the manufacturer's guidance.
  4. DecisionConfirmed hardware fault in the flagged subsystem → component-level repair/replacement. Fault clears after a power cycle and does not recur → likely a transient condition; monitor closely.
Test Points
As specified by the manufacturer's POST fault code reference for the flagged subsystem
Root Cause Verification

After remedial action, power-cycle the CCR and confirm POST completes successfully across at least three consecutive power-up cycles.

Corrective Action
  • Replace or repair the specific faulty sensor/module identified.
  • Reflash/restore controller firmware if a checksum fault is confirmed.
  • Replace the controller if a core hardware fault is confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Keep firmware backups current.
  • Avoid uncontrolled power interruptions during firmware updates.
  • Include POST result review in commissioning records.

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-019 CCR Internal Fault at Start-Up

Symptom — CCR displays a generic internal fault indication specifically during the start-up sequence — after POST, before reaching stable run state — distinct from a POST failure or a specific named protection alarm.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator power electronics and start-sequence control logic.

Possible Causes
HighA transient internal fault detected during the soft-start/ramp-up sequence, e.g. a current spike beyond the expected start-up profile
MediumA control logic fault in the start sequencing itself
MediumAn internal component — thyristor/IGBT module, driver board — failing specifically under start-up electrical stress rather than at steady state
LowerA marginal internal connection that only fails under the inrush condition of starting
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meter with inrush/peak captureCCR controller diagnostic toolManufacturer internal fault code reference
Safety Precautions
  • Internal fault conditions during start-up may indicate a partially failed power semiconductor. Treat with caution and fully isolate before any internal inspection — damaged components can retain unexpected charge or present a short-circuit hazard.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the exact internal fault code/message and the precise point in the start sequence at which it occurs.
  2. MeasurementWhere possible, capture the current/voltage waveform during a start attempt to observe the fault's electrical signature.
  3. ObservationCross-reference the fault code against the manufacturer's internal fault code reference to identify the flagged internal subsystem.
  4. DecisionFault consistently occurs at the same point in the sequence → likely a specific component or logic fault at that stage. Fault occurs inconsistently → intermittent internal connection or marginal component, refer to Division 22 methodology.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific internal module/board flagged by the fault code.
Test Points
Thyristor/IGBT module gate signals
Driver board supply
Internal current sensor output during ramp-up (plus manufacturer-specific test points per fault code)
Root Cause Verification

After component-level repair, perform multiple start cycles under representative load, including at the highest intensity step used on site, to confirm the fault does not recur.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the specific faulty internal component/module identified.
  • Repair the marginal internal connection.
  • Update start-sequence control logic if a genuine logic fault is confirmed by the manufacturer.
Preventive Action
  • Schedule periodic internal inspection and connection torque-checks per the manufacturer PM schedule.
  • Monitor start-up current signature trends over time to catch developing component degradation.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-CCR-05

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-020 CCR Display Not Initializing

Symptom — CCR powers up — contactor energizes, output may even be present — but the front panel display/HMI remains blank or does not complete its initialization sequence, leaving the operator without local status indication.

Equipment / System

Constant Current Regulator front panel display/HMI module.

Possible Causes
HighDisplay module power supply fault
HighDamaged or loose display ribbon/data cable
MediumDisplay module itself has failed
MediumController not sending display initialization data due to a communication fault
LowerDisplay firmware corruption
Required Tools
MultimeterCCR controller diagnostic toolSpare display module, if available
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV/control circuit precautions apply. A blank display does not confirm the CCR is off — verify actual run/output status independently, e.g. via clamp meter on the output, before assuming a safe state.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm whether the CCR is otherwise operating normally — contactor energized, output present — despite the blank display, to distinguish a display-only fault from a broader control fault.
  2. MeasurementCheck the display module's power supply voltage.
  3. ObservationInspect the display ribbon/data cable connection at both the display and controller ends for looseness or damage.
  4. MeasurementIf accessible, check for communication activity between the controller and display module, e.g. via diagnostic tool or activity LED.
  5. DecisionDisplay power absent → power supply/wiring fault. Display power present but no initialization → data cable or communication fault. Both confirmed healthy → the display module itself has failed.
Test Points
Display module power supply
Display ribbon/data cable connections
Controller-to-display communication link
Root Cause Verification

After remedial action, power-cycle the CCR and confirm the display completes full initialization and shows correct live status.

Corrective Action
  • Reseat or replace the display ribbon/data cable.
  • Replace the display module power supply.
  • Replace the display module.
  • Reflash display firmware if corruption is confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Include display initialization check in routine PM start-up verification.
  • Keep a spare display module in site stores given its role in local diagnostics.

02 · CCR Output

20 of 20 topics published
CCR-021 CCR Output Current Zero

Symptom — CCR is in RUN with a commanded intensity step above 0% and no active alarm is displayed, but the output current feedback reads zero and the series circuit is completely dark.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage — thyristor/IGBT firing bridge, output (step-up) transformer, output current feedback sensor, and the series circuit loop to the isolating transformers.

Possible Causes
HighFiring/gate drive circuit not triggering the thyristor or IGBT bridge despite a valid run command
HighOutput-side fuse or output circuit breaker open
MediumOutput transformer primary or secondary winding open-circuited
MediumCurrent feedback sensor (shunt/CT) failed or its signal wiring to the controller broken, causing the controller to hold firing at a null point
LowerController firmware/logic fault holding the firing angle at zero despite a valid step command
LowerSeries circuit loop broken (open isolating transformer primary or damaged L-823 connector) — usually accompanied by an open-circuit alarm, but not always on older controllers
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meter (loop-rated)Oscilloscope (for gate drive pulses)Insulation resistance tester (5kV)MultimeterCCR power stage schematicLoop continuity tester
Safety Precautions
  • Do not open the series circuit loop while the CCR is energized — an open loop under load can develop several kV at the break point.
  • Apply LOTO on the CCR input isolator before any internal inspection of the bridge or output transformer.
  • Confirm zero energy with a proven meter before handling output transformer or fuse terminals.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the CCR is in RUN with a commanded step above 0% and check specifically whether an open-circuit/no-load alarm is present — its absence points toward an internal firing or transformer fault rather than a loop break.
  2. MeasurementWith the unit isolated and LOTO applied, inspect the output fuse/breaker for continuity.
  3. MeasurementUsing an oscilloscope, check for gate drive pulses at the thyristor/IGBT bridge during a commanded run.
  4. MeasurementCheck output transformer primary and secondary winding continuity and insulation resistance.
  5. MeasurementVerify the current feedback sensor output and its wiring back to the controller.
  6. DecisionNo gate pulses → firing circuit fault. Gate pulses present but no output → bridge device or transformer failure. Output present internally but zero at the loop → loop break, escalate to circuit isolation resistance testing.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the firing circuit, the bridge device, the output transformer, the output fuse, or the series circuit loop.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component by substitution or isolated component testing.
Test Points
Thyristor/IGBT gate drive signals
Output transformer primary terminals
Output transformer secondary/series circuit terminals
Output fuse/breaker continuity
Current feedback sensor signal
Root Cause Verification

After repair, run the CCR through its full intensity step range and confirm the clamp-meter reading at the output terminals matches each commanded step within tolerance, with no open-circuit alarm.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the failed firing/gate drive circuit board.
  • Replace the failed thyristor or IGBT module.
  • Replace the blown output fuse or reset the output breaker after confirming no downstream fault.
  • Replace the failed output transformer.
  • Repair or replace the current feedback sensor and its wiring.
Preventive Action
  • Include a gate drive pulse check and output transformer megger test in scheduled PM.
  • Keep spare thyristor/IGBT modules and output fuses in site stores.
  • Verify current feedback sensor calibration during annual photometric testing.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-022 CCR Output Current Too Low

Symptom — CCR output current reads consistently below the value required for the commanded intensity step — lights are dim across the series circuit rather than fully off.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage and closed-loop current regulation circuit, series circuit with isolating transformers and lamps/LED fixtures.

Possible Causes
HighThyristor/IGBT bridge partially firing — one or more devices in the bridge degraded, reducing effective conduction angle
HighInput supply voltage below nominal, limiting the maximum current the regulator can develop
MediumCurrent feedback sensor reading high (over-reporting), causing the closed loop to under-drive the output
MediumExcessive series circuit loop resistance/impedance — corroded L-823 connectors, degraded cable, or a partially failed isolating transformer increasing loop losses
MediumOutput transformer tap set incorrectly or transformer partially shorted turns reducing available output
LowerCooling fan/thermal derate active, limiting maximum firing angle to protect the bridge
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterInsulation resistance tester (5kV)MultimeterInput power quality analyzerCCR wiring diagramThermal imaging camera
Safety Precautions
  • Treat series circuit terminals as live and potentially at several kV while the CCR is running — do not probe the loop directly; use a clamp meter externally.
  • Apply LOTO before accessing the bridge, transformer taps, or fuses.
  • Use insulated tools when working near the output stage even when isolated, in case of stored capacitor charge.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementClamp-meter the actual output current at each commanded step and compare against the rated value for that step.
  2. MeasurementCheck the incoming 3-phase supply voltage for undervoltage or single-phasing.
  3. ObservationCheck the CCR HMI for any active thermal derate or power-limiting indication.
  4. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, verify the output transformer tap setting against the O&M manual for the installed circuit length/load.
  5. MeasurementMegger the series circuit loop and compare against baseline commissioning values to check for elevated loop resistance.
  6. DecisionLow current with normal input voltage and correct tap → bridge device degradation or feedback sensor drift. Low current with confirmed undervoltage → escalate to upstream supply quality. Elevated loop resistance → circuit-side fault, not a CCR fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the CCR bridge/feedback loop, the input supply, or the external series circuit.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed or degraded component through targeted testing.
Test Points
CCR output terminals (clamp meter)
3-phase input supply voltage
Output transformer tap terminals
Current feedback sensor output
Series circuit loop resistance
Root Cause Verification

Confirm output current matches the rated value within tolerance at every intensity step after correction, and that the reading remains stable over a sustained run period.

Corrective Action
  • Replace degraded thyristor/IGBT devices in the bridge.
  • Correct the output transformer tap setting for the actual circuit length.
  • Recalibrate or replace the current feedback sensor.
  • Repair or replace corroded connectors/damaged cable sections in the series circuit.
  • Report and escalate a confirmed upstream undervoltage condition.
Preventive Action
  • Verify transformer tap setting whenever the series circuit length or fixture count changes.
  • Include loop resistance trending in the annual megger test record.
  • Schedule periodic thermal imaging of the bridge to catch device degradation early.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 12290, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic, Series Circuit Single Line Diagram

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-023 CCR Output Current Too High

Symptom — CCR output current reads above the value required for the commanded intensity step, with lamps running brighter than expected or premature lamp/LED driver failures occurring on the circuit.

Equipment / System

CCR closed-loop current regulation circuit, output transformer, current feedback sensor.

Possible Causes
HighCurrent feedback sensor under-reporting (drifted low), causing the closed loop to over-drive the bridge to compensate
HighFeedback signal wiring open or intermittent, with the controller defaulting toward maximum firing to seek the setpoint
MediumController regulation loop parameters (gain) incorrectly configured after a firmware update or parameter reset
MediumOutput transformer tap set for a shorter circuit than actually installed, over-driving the loop
LowerBridge firing circuit fault causing an uncontrolled higher conduction angle regardless of feedback
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterOscilloscopeCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • An overcurrent condition can overheat isolating transformers and lamp bases — do not leave the circuit running unattended once overcurrent is confirmed.
  • Apply LOTO before accessing the feedback sensor wiring or transformer taps.
  • Verify zero energy state before disconnecting the current feedback sensor for testing.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementClamp-meter the actual output current at each commanded step and compare against the rated value.
  2. ObservationCheck the CCR HMI displayed current against the independently clamp-metered value — a mismatch points to a feedback sensor fault rather than a true overcurrent.
  3. MeasurementInspect the current feedback sensor wiring for looseness, corrosion, or an open connection.
  4. MeasurementVerify the output transformer tap setting against the documented circuit length.
  5. ObservationReview the controller's regulation loop configuration/parameters against the commissioned baseline.
  6. DecisionHMI and clamp-meter agree and both read high → true overcurrent, check transformer tap and loop configuration. HMI reads normal but clamp-meter reads high → feedback sensor/wiring fault causing the loop to over-correct.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the feedback sensor/wiring, the transformer tap setting, or the controller regulation parameters.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through sensor substitution or parameter comparison against baseline.
Test Points
CCR output terminals (independent clamp meter)
Current feedback sensor output
Output transformer tap terminals
Controller regulation loop parameters
Root Cause Verification

Confirm the HMI-displayed current and an independent clamp-meter reading agree and both track the rated value at every step, sustained over a full run cycle.

Corrective Action
  • Replace or recalibrate the current feedback sensor.
  • Repair the feedback sensor wiring.
  • Correct the output transformer tap setting.
  • Restore regulation loop parameters to the commissioned baseline.
  • Repair the firing circuit if confirmed as the root cause.
Preventive Action
  • Cross-check HMI current display against an independent clamp-meter reading during routine PM.
  • Lock configuration parameters after commissioning and log any authorized changes.
  • Include feedback sensor calibration in the annual photometric test cycle.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 12290
