Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-024 CCR Output Current Unstable

Symptom — Output current reading jumps erratically between values rather than settling on the commanded setpoint, with no clear periodic pattern — distinct from a steady hunting oscillation.

Equipment / System

Current feedback sensor and its signal path, controller ADC input, firing circuit.

Possible Causes
HighLoose or corroded current feedback sensor wiring/terminal introducing an intermittent signal
HighElectrical noise/interference coupling into the feedback signal wiring, e.g. routed alongside power cabling without shielding
MediumPoor or corroded connection at an L-823 connector in the series circuit causing an intermittent high-resistance point
MediumDegraded thyristor/IGBT device with intermittent firing failure on individual half-cycles
LowerController ADC or feedback conditioning circuit fault
Required Tools
OscilloscopeTrue-RMS clamp meter (with data logging if available)Insulation resistance testerContact cleaner and torque screwdriverCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Do not assume an intermittent reading is a display artifact — treat it as a genuine electrical fault until proven otherwise.
  • Apply LOTO before tightening or cleaning any current-carrying terminal.
  • Be alert for arcing/heat discoloration at loose connections, which indicates an active fire risk.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationLog the CCR output current over a sustained period (or review controller trend/event log) to characterise the pattern — random spikes versus a steady periodic oscillation (see CCR-035 for hunting).
  2. MeasurementInspect and re-torque the current feedback sensor wiring and terminal block.
  3. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, inspect all series circuit L-823 connectors accessible without excavation for corrosion or looseness.
  4. MeasurementCheck feedback signal cable routing for proximity to power cabling without adequate separation or shielding.
  5. ObservationUse an oscilloscope on the feedback signal to identify noise spikes correlating with the instability.
  6. DecisionInstability correlates with cable routing/noise → shielding/routing fix. Instability traced to a specific loose terminal → mechanical repair. Neither found → suspect a degraded bridge device or controller feedback circuit.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the feedback wiring, a series circuit connector, or an internal bridge/controller fault.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by reproducing and then eliminating the instability after each corrective step.
Test Points
Current feedback sensor terminal block
Feedback signal cable at controller input
Accessible series circuit L-823 connectors
Controller ADC input signal
Root Cause Verification

Log output current over a minimum 30-minute sustained run after repair and confirm the reading remains within normal tolerance with no unexplained excursions.

Corrective Action
  • Clean, re-terminate, and torque the feedback sensor connection.
  • Repair or reroute the feedback signal cable with proper shielding and separation from power cabling.
  • Repair or replace the affected L-823 connector.
  • Replace the degraded bridge device or controller feedback conditioning circuit.
Preventive Action
  • Include torque-check of feedback wiring terminals in the PM schedule.
  • Verify signal cable segregation from power cabling during any circuit rework.
  • Trend output current data where the controller/ALCMS supports logging, to catch intermittent faults early.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic, Series Circuit Single Line Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-025 CCR Output Current Fluctuating

Symptom — Output current shows a slow, repeating rise-and-fall pattern over several seconds to minutes, distinct from rapid random noise — a gradual periodic drift rather than a sharp oscillation.

Equipment / System

Closed-loop current regulation circuit, input supply, cooling/thermal management system.

Possible Causes
HighInput supply voltage fluctuating (e.g. from a generator or a heavily loaded distribution feeder), with the regulation loop tracking the disturbance
MediumThermal cycling of the bridge causing gain drift as component temperature varies with cooling fan cycling
MediumRegulation loop gain set too low, causing sluggish correction that manifests as a slow drift rather than tight regulation
LowerA partially loose series circuit connection heating and cooling under load, changing loop resistance cyclically
Required Tools
Power quality analyzerTrue-RMS clamp meter with data loggingThermal imaging cameraCCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before any internal inspection.
  • If a cyclically heating connection is suspected, treat it as a potential fire risk and inspect promptly rather than deferring to the next scheduled PM.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementLog input supply voltage over the same period as the observed output fluctuation to check for correlation.
  2. ObservationCheck whether the fluctuation period correlates with cooling fan on/off cycling.
  3. MeasurementThermal-image the bridge and series circuit connectors during a sustained run to identify any point with cyclical heating.
  4. ObservationReview the controller's regulation loop gain setting against the commissioned baseline.
  5. DecisionFluctuation correlates with input supply → upstream power quality issue, not a CCR fault. Fluctuation correlates with fan cycling/thermal drift → bridge thermal stability issue. A hot spot found on a connector → mechanical/connection fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the upstream supply, the bridge thermal behaviour, the regulation loop tuning, or a specific series circuit connection.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by eliminating each candidate through targeted correction and retest.
Test Points
Input supply voltage (logged)
Bridge heatsink temperature
Series circuit connector temperature (thermal image)
Regulation loop gain parameter
Root Cause Verification

Log output current over a sustained run after correction and confirm the fluctuation amplitude is within normal tolerance with no correlation to fan cycling or supply variation.

Corrective Action
  • Report and address the upstream supply quality issue where confirmed.
  • Improve bridge cooling/ventilation to reduce thermal-driven gain drift.
  • Re-tune the regulation loop gain per manufacturer guidance.
  • Repair the cyclically heating series circuit connection.
Preventive Action
  • Include a power quality check in commissioning and periodic audits for sites on generator or weak feeders.
  • Trend bridge temperature alongside output current where data logging is available.
  • Include thermal imaging of series circuit connectors in the annual PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-026 CCR Output Current Not Matching Selected Step

Symptom — The commanded intensity step (local, remote, or ALCMS-selected) does not correspond to the actual measured output current — e.g. Step 3 commanded but Step 5 current delivered, or the step changes but current does not follow.

Equipment / System

Controller intensity-step logic, step-selection input (local switch, remote/ALCMS command), step reference table/configuration.

Possible Causes
HighStep reference table/configuration incorrectly programmed — commanded step mapped to the wrong current setpoint
HighLocal/remote selector switch in the wrong position, or local override active without operator awareness
MediumCommand signal from ALCMS/PLC to the CCR corrupted or mismatched (e.g. wrong step code on a serial/analog interface)
MediumController stuck on a previous step due to a communication or logic fault, not updating on new commands
LowerStep relay/contactor (on non-digital step-relay-type CCRs) failed to switch to the commanded tap
Required Tools
MultimeterCCR configuration/parameter toolProtocol analyzer or serial monitor (for ALCMS link)CCR wiring diagramTrue-RMS clamp meter
Safety Precautions
  • Confirm actual delivered current independently with a clamp meter before relying on the HMI display, since the fault may be a display/logic mismatch rather than a true output fault.
  • Apply LOTO before accessing step relay contacts on step-relay-type CCRs.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the exact command issued (local switch position, or the specific step code sent by ALCMS/PLC) and compare it to what the CCR HMI displays as the received command.
  2. MeasurementClamp-meter the actual output current and compare it against both the commanded step and the step the HMI claims to be running.
  3. ObservationCheck the local/remote selector switch position and any local override status.
  4. MeasurementVerify the step reference table/configuration in the controller against the design intensity schedule.
  5. ObservationIf ALCMS-commanded, monitor the communication link for the actual step code being transmitted and received.
  6. DecisionHMI-received command matches operator intent but output current doesn't match → step table misconfiguration or step relay fault. HMI-received command differs from what was sent → communication/wiring fault on the command path.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the step configuration table, the local/remote selection path, the ALCMS communication link, or a step relay.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific misconfiguration or failed component.
Test Points
Local/remote selector switch
ALCMS/PLC command signal at CCR input
Controller step reference table
Step relay contacts (if applicable)
CCR output terminals (clamp meter)
Root Cause Verification

Command each intensity step in turn from the intended control source and confirm the clamp-metered output current matches the design value for that step every time.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the step reference table/configuration.
  • Correct the local/remote selector position and clarify override procedures with operations staff.
  • Repair the ALCMS/PLC communication wiring or resolve the protocol mismatch.
  • Replace the failed step relay/contactor.
Preventive Action
  • Verify the step reference table against the design intensity schedule at every commissioning and after any firmware update.
  • Include an end-to-end step command verification (ALCMS to measured output) in periodic PM.
  • Label and periodically audit local/remote selector switch positions.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, ALCMS Interface Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-027 CCR Output Voltage Abnormally High

Symptom — Output (series circuit loop) voltage reads significantly above the expected value for the connected load and commanded step, with no corresponding increase in current — the regulator is working harder than the circuit should require.

Equipment / System

CCR output transformer, series circuit loop and isolating transformers, insulation condition of the loop.

Possible Causes
HighElevated series circuit loop impedance — degraded cable insulation-to-earth is not the driver here, but increased conductor/joint resistance or a partially open isolating transformer primary increases the voltage the CCR must develop to maintain rated current
HighOne or more isolating transformers open-circuited (primary winding failed), forcing the CCR to raise voltage trying to maintain current through the remaining loop resistance
MediumOutput transformer tap set for a longer circuit than actually connected
LowerVoltage sensing/feedback circuit fault causing a false high reading rather than a true condition
Required Tools
High-voltage-rated multimeter/meggerInsulation resistance tester (5kV)True-RMS clamp meterCCR wiring diagramSeries circuit as-built drawing
Safety Precautions
  • An abnormally high loop voltage significantly increases shock and flashover risk at every isolating transformer and connector along the circuit — treat the entire loop as elevated-hazard until the cause is resolved.
  • Apply LOTO on the CCR before any loop testing.
  • Do not attempt to trace an open isolating transformer by working on live fixtures.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the CCR is delivering rated current at the commanded step despite the high voltage reading — this indicates the loop, not the CCR, is the primary driver.
  2. MeasurementWith the CCR isolated, megger the series circuit loop insulation and measure loop resistance, comparing against baseline commissioning values.
  3. MeasurementSystematically segment-test the loop (if pull boxes/junctions allow) to localise a section with abnormally high resistance.
  4. ObservationVerify the output transformer tap setting against the actual documented circuit length.
  5. DecisionLoop resistance significantly above baseline → open or degraded isolating transformer/connector somewhere in the loop, proceed to segment isolation. Loop resistance normal but voltage still reads high → feedback/sensing circuit fault or transformer tap mismatch.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to a specific loop segment, a specific isolating transformer, or the CCR's own voltage sensing/tap configuration.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed isolating transformer or connector by direct inspection once the segment is localised.
Test Points
Series circuit loop insulation resistance
Series circuit loop resistance (segment by segment)
Output transformer tap terminals
CCR output voltage sensing circuit
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm output voltage returns to the expected range for rated current at each step, and re-megger the loop to confirm insulation and resistance are within baseline.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed isolating transformer identified during segment testing.
  • Repair or replace the degraded cable section or L-823 connector.
  • Correct the output transformer tap setting.
  • Repair the voltage sensing circuit if confirmed faulty.
Preventive Action
  • Maintain a baseline loop resistance and insulation record from commissioning for future comparison.
  • Include periodic segment-wise loop testing in the PM programme for long circuits.
  • Track isolating transformer replacement history to identify circuits prone to repeat failures.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 12290, IS 7785

Diagram: Series Circuit Single Line Diagram, Isolating Transformer Layout

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-028 CCR Output Voltage Abnormally Low

Symptom — Output (series circuit loop) voltage reads well below the expected value for the connected load and commanded step, while current remains close to normal.

Equipment / System

CCR output transformer, series circuit loop, voltage sensing/feedback circuit.

Possible Causes
HighOutput transformer tap set for a much shorter circuit than actually connected, understating available voltage headroom
MediumA section of the series circuit has been shortened or bypassed (e.g. temporary jumper left in place after fixture removal) reducing loop impedance and therefore required voltage
MediumVoltage sensing/feedback circuit fault causing a false low reading
LowerPartial short or reduced insulation resistance to earth on the loop, reducing the effective circuit impedance the CCR sees
Required Tools
Insulation resistance tester (5kV)True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterSeries circuit as-built drawingCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • A low measured voltage with normal current can mask a partial insulation fault or an unauthorised bypass — do not assume it is benign.
  • Apply LOTO before loop testing.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm output current is at or near the rated value for the commanded step — if current is also low, redirect to CCR-022.
  2. MeasurementVerify the output transformer tap setting against the documented, as-built circuit length and fixture count.
  3. ObservationCheck as-built records against current field configuration for any fixtures added or removed, or temporary jumpers installed.
  4. MeasurementMegger the loop insulation resistance to earth and compare against baseline.
  5. DecisionTap mismatch found → correct tap. As-built discrepancy found → investigate and formalise or remove the unauthorised change. Reduced insulation resistance found → escalate as a developing insulation fault even though current appears normal.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the transformer tap setting, an unrecorded circuit modification, or a developing insulation fault.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through physical circuit verification against as-built records.
Test Points
Output transformer tap terminals
Series circuit loop insulation resistance
Voltage sensing/feedback circuit
Root Cause Verification

After correction, confirm output voltage is consistent with the documented circuit length at rated current, and update as-built records if a physical change is confirmed as the cause.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the output transformer tap setting.
  • Remove unauthorised jumpers/bypasses and restore the circuit to its designed configuration, or formally update records if the change is intentional.
  • Repair the voltage sensing circuit if confirmed faulty.
  • Investigate and repair any confirmed reduction in insulation resistance.
Preventive Action
  • Enforce as-built record updates for any series circuit modification.
  • Include tap setting verification whenever fixture counts change.
  • Trend loop insulation resistance over successive PM cycles to catch gradual degradation.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 7785

Diagram: Series Circuit Single Line Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-029 CCR Output Voltage Unstable

Symptom — Output voltage reading swings noticeably while current remains comparatively steady — the regulation loop is not settling on a stable voltage operating point even though current control appears to be holding.

Equipment / System

Voltage sensing/feedback circuit, series circuit loop connections, regulation loop control logic.

Possible Causes
HighIntermittent high-resistance connection somewhere in the series circuit loop, with contact resistance varying as the connection heats and cools
MediumVoltage sensing circuit wiring loose or subject to electrical noise
MediumRegulation loop attempting to maintain constant current against a marginal/borderline loop impedance near the transformer's tap limit, causing voltage to hunt around the ceiling
LowerPartial intermittent insulation fault to earth on the loop
Required Tools
OscilloscopeTrue-RMS clamp meter with loggingInsulation resistance testerThermal imaging cameraCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Treat an intermittent high-resistance connection as a fire and flashover risk — do not defer investigation.
  • Apply LOTO before loop inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementLog output voltage and current together over a sustained period to confirm current is stable while voltage varies.
  2. MeasurementThermal-image accessible series circuit connectors during a sustained run to identify a cyclically heating joint.
  3. MeasurementInspect and re-torque the voltage sensing circuit wiring at the controller.
  4. ObservationCompare the operating voltage against the transformer tap's rated ceiling to check whether the loop is near the tap limit.
  5. DecisionA hot, cyclically-varying connector found → intermittent connection fault. Voltage instability with no thermal anomaly and near the tap ceiling → tap undersized for the actual loop impedance, consider re-tapping. Neither found → sensing circuit fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to a specific series circuit connection, the transformer tap margin, or the voltage sensing circuit.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by physical repair and retest.
Test Points
Series circuit connectors (thermal imaging)
Voltage sensing circuit wiring at controller
Output transformer tap setting versus loop impedance
Root Cause Verification

Log output voltage and current over a sustained run after repair and confirm both remain stable within normal tolerance.

Corrective Action
  • Repair the intermittent high-resistance connection.
  • Re-terminate and secure the voltage sensing circuit wiring.
  • Re-tap the output transformer to provide adequate voltage margin for the loop impedance.
  • Repair any confirmed intermittent insulation fault.
Preventive Action
  • Include thermal imaging of series circuit connectors in the annual PM.
  • Verify tap margin against loop impedance whenever the circuit configuration changes.
  • Torque-check sensing circuit terminals during scheduled maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 7785

Diagram: Series Circuit Single Line Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-030 CCR No Output Despite Healthy Input

Symptom — Input supply and internal control power are confirmed healthy, and the CCR appears to accept the start/run command, but no output current is delivered and no fault alarm is raised — the unit appears to be running normally on the HMI while producing nothing.

Equipment / System

CCR controller run-logic and firing enable path, output contactor (where fitted between the bridge and the output transformer), bridge firing circuit.

Possible Causes
HighOutput enable contactor/relay (separate from the main input contactor) not energizing, physically disconnecting the bridge from the output transformer despite the controller believing it is running
HighController run-state logic satisfied internally but the firing enable signal to the bridge gate driver not actually asserted — a software/logic fault
MediumA latched soft-alarm that is suppressing firing internally without surfacing as a visible fault code (e.g. a self-test failure not mapped to a display message)
MediumOutput contactor auxiliary contact feedback mismatch — controller reads a false 'closed' status from a stuck-open auxiliary contact
LowerFirmware fault causing the run state and the firing subroutine to become desynchronised
Required Tools
MultimeterTrue-RMS clamp meterOscilloscopeCCR event/alarm log toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Confirm zero energy at the output stage with a proven meter before assuming the unit is safe to touch, even though it is 'not producing output' — a partially engaged contactor can still present a hazard.
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm input supply, control power, and run-state indication are all genuinely healthy (cross-check with independent meters, not just the HMI).
  2. ObservationPull the full controller event/alarm log, including suppressed or low-priority events, not just the currently displayed status.
  3. MeasurementCheck the output enable contactor/relay coil voltage and its mechanical state directly.
  4. MeasurementVerify the auxiliary contact feedback from the output contactor against its actual physical position.
  5. MeasurementUsing an oscilloscope, confirm whether a firing enable signal is actually present at the gate driver during the run state.
  6. DecisionOutput contactor not energizing despite a valid command → contactor/coil/wiring fault. Contactor confirmed closed but no firing enable signal present → controller logic/firmware fault. Auxiliary contact mismatch found → feedback wiring fault masking the true contactor position.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the output contactor circuit, the firing enable logic, or the auxiliary feedback wiring.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific fault by direct measurement at each stage of the run/firing chain.
Test Points
Output enable contactor coil terminals
Output contactor auxiliary contact
Firing enable signal at gate driver
Controller full event/alarm log
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm output current is delivered immediately on a run command and that the auxiliary contact feedback matches the true physical contactor state across several start/stop cycles.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the failed output contactor/relay.
  • Correct the auxiliary contact wiring or replace the failed contact.
  • Reflash/reset controller firmware if a logic desynchronisation is confirmed.
  • Escalate to the manufacturer for a suppressed self-test fault not visible on the standard display.
Preventive Action
  • Include a full output verification (not just run-state confirmation) as a mandatory step after every start-up in the PM checklist.
  • Periodically review the complete event/alarm log, not only currently active alarms, during PM.
  • Keep firmware documentation and revision history for each controller.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-031 CCR Output Present but Lights Not Operating

Symptom — CCR confirms it is delivering rated current at the output terminals, but some or all fixtures on the series circuit are not illuminated.

Equipment / System

Series circuit isolating transformers, lamp/LED fixtures and their internal drivers, secondary circuit wiring within each fixture.

Possible Causes
HighOne or more isolating transformer secondaries open-circuited or the fixture's internal wiring/lamp base connection failed
HighLamp filament failed (incandescent fixtures) or LED driver failed (LED fixtures) at the affected location(s)
MediumIsolating transformer primary-to-secondary insulation failure causing the transformer to pass current in the loop without delivering usable secondary voltage
MediumPhotometric/optical issue mistaken for an electrical fault — lens heavily contaminated or physically obstructed
LowerFixture-level surge protection device failed in a mode that opens the secondary circuit
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterInsulation resistance tester (5kV)MultimeterFixture-specific test set/lamp testerTorque screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Do not open or work on isolating transformers or fixtures while the CCR is running — isolate the CCR and apply LOTO first, since the series loop can induce hazardous secondary voltage.
  • Follow airside work permit and NOTAM procedures before accessing runway/taxiway fixtures.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationIdentify exactly which fixture(s) on the circuit are affected — a single fixture points to a local fault, multiple scattered fixtures suggest a batch lamp/driver failure, and a contiguous group suggests a shared cable/transformer issue.
  2. MeasurementWith the CCR isolated, check the affected isolating transformer's secondary output using an appropriate low-voltage test method or fixture tester.
  3. MeasurementCheck the isolating transformer primary-to-secondary insulation resistance.
  4. ObservationInspect the fixture for lamp/LED driver condition, secondary wiring integrity, and lens contamination.
  5. DecisionTransformer secondary confirmed dead with healthy primary loop current → transformer or secondary wiring fault. Transformer secondary healthy but fixture still dark → lamp/LED driver failure at the fixture. Lens heavily contaminated → not an electrical fault, redirect to cleaning/maintenance.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the isolating transformer, the fixture wiring, or the lamp/LED driver.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component by direct replacement/substitution testing.
Test Points
Isolating transformer secondary output
Isolating transformer primary-to-secondary insulation
Fixture lamp base/driver input terminals
Root Cause Verification

After replacement, re-energize the circuit and visually confirm the repaired fixture(s) illuminate correctly at each commanded intensity step alongside the rest of the circuit.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed lamp or LED driver.
  • Replace the failed isolating transformer.
  • Repair the fixture secondary wiring or connector.
  • Clean the fixture lens if contamination was the actual cause of perceived non-operation.
Preventive Action
  • Track lamp/LED driver and isolating transformer replacement history per fixture to identify recurring failure points.
  • Include lens cleaning in the routine airfield lighting maintenance schedule.
  • Batch-test isolating transformers periodically rather than only on failure.
Related References

SOP: SOP-AGL-03 (Fixture Isolation Transformer Testing), SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 7785

Diagram: Series Circuit Single Line Diagram, Fixture Wiring Diagram

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-032 CCR Output Present but Circuit Current Abnormal

Symptom — CCR confirms it is producing an output at the commanded step, but the current actually flowing in the series circuit loop (measured with an independent clamp meter at a point downstream of the CCR) does not match the CCR's own displayed/regulated value.

Equipment / System

CCR current feedback sensor location relative to the actual load path, series circuit loop.

Possible Causes
HighA parallel leakage path to earth on the loop is diverting a portion of the current before it reaches the CCR's feedback sensor location, if the sensor is positioned such that this is possible
HighCurrent feedback sensor sensing a different point in the circuit than the actual load path due to an internal wiring or CT-orientation fault
MediumA partial short between the series circuit loop and an adjacent circuit or structure, providing an unintended alternate current path
LowerInstrument/clamp meter measurement error — miscounted turns through the clamp, wrong meter range, or interference
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meter (verify against a second reference meter)Insulation resistance tester (5kV)MultimeterCCR wiring diagramSeries circuit as-built drawing
Safety Precautions
  • A leakage or partial short to earth is a serious safety hazard — treat this as high priority and do not leave the circuit energized pending investigation once confirmed.
  • Apply LOTO before any loop segment testing.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementRe-verify the discrepancy using a second, calibrated clamp meter at the same measurement point to rule out an instrument error.
  2. MeasurementWith the CCR isolated, megger the full loop insulation resistance to earth and to any adjacent circuits.
  3. MeasurementIf insulation resistance is low, segment-test the loop to localise the leakage/short.
  4. ObservationVerify the current feedback sensor's physical installation and CT orientation against the wiring diagram.
  5. DecisionDiscrepancy confirmed with a second meter and low insulation resistance found → genuine leakage/short fault, proceed to segment isolation. Discrepancy not reproducible with a second meter → original measurement error. Insulation resistance normal but discrepancy persists → feedback sensor installation/wiring fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to a specific loop segment with a confirmed leakage/short, or to the CCR's own feedback sensor installation.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cable, connector, or transformer responsible for the leakage path.
Test Points
Series circuit loop insulation resistance to earth
Series circuit loop insulation resistance to adjacent circuits
Current feedback sensor installation/orientation
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm the CCR's regulated current and an independent downstream clamp-meter reading agree, and re-megger the loop to confirm insulation resistance is within baseline.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the cable/connector/transformer responsible for the leakage or short path.
  • Correct the current feedback sensor installation/orientation.
  • Recalibrate or replace the field clamp meter if an instrument error was confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Maintain a baseline insulation resistance record and re-test after any circuit disturbance.
  • Cross-check CCR displayed current against an independent clamp meter during routine PM as standard practice.
  • Verify feedback sensor installation whenever the controller or sensor is replaced.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IS 7785

Diagram: Series Circuit Single Line Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-033 CCR Output Drops Under Load

Symptom — Output current is correct immediately after start-up or at light load, but sags below the commanded value once the full series circuit load (all fixtures) is drawing current, or after the circuit has been running for some time.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage thermal capacity, output transformer, bridge current rating margin.

Possible Causes
HighBridge thermal derate/foldback engaging as internal temperature rises under sustained full load, due to a cooling fault or undersized cooling for the actual ambient conditions
HighOutput transformer thermally derating or saturating under sustained full load due to a cooling or sizing issue
MediumMarginal supply voltage that sags further under the CCR's own full-load input current draw, reducing available headroom for the regulator
MediumA loose high-current connection within the CCR (bus bar, output terminal) heating and increasing resistance under load, which the regulator cannot fully compensate for once it reaches its voltage ceiling
LowerRegulation loop response too slow to correctly track the load transition from light to full
Required Tools
Thermal imaging cameraTrue-RMS clamp meter with loggingPower quality analyzerTorque screwdriver setCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Do not touch internal bus bars or terminals to check for heat by hand — use a thermal imaging camera or a non-contact method with the unit running, or isolate first.
  • Apply LOTO before tightening any internal high-current connection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementLog output current from start-up through to full sustained load to characterise the drop's timing and magnitude.
  2. MeasurementThermal-image the bridge heatsink and output transformer during the load period when the drop occurs.
  3. ObservationCheck cooling fan operation and airflow/filter condition.
  4. MeasurementLog input supply voltage through the same period to check for supply sag correlating with the CCR's own load.
  5. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, torque-check internal high-current bus bar and terminal connections.
  6. DecisionThermal derate confirmed via imaging correlating with the drop → cooling deficiency, address ventilation/fan first. Loose internal connection found hot under load → mechanical repair. Supply sag confirmed independent of CCR load → upstream supply issue.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the CCR's internal thermal management, a loose internal connection, or the upstream supply.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and verify the drop no longer occurs once corrected.
Test Points
Bridge heatsink temperature under sustained load
Output transformer temperature under sustained load
Internal high-current bus bar/terminal connections
Input supply voltage under CCR full load
Root Cause Verification

Run the CCR at full commanded step for a minimum of one hour and confirm output current remains stable within tolerance throughout, with no thermal derate triggered.

Corrective Action
  • Clean/repair the cooling fan and ventilation path, or upgrade cooling if undersized for site ambient conditions.
  • Re-torque or replace the loose internal high-current connection.
  • Report and address the upstream supply sag.
  • Adjust regulation loop response tuning if a slow tracking response is confirmed as contributory.
Preventive Action
  • Include a sustained full-load thermal check in the annual PM, not just a spot-check at start-up.
  • Keep cooling fans and filters on a defined cleaning/replacement schedule.
  • Torque-check internal high-current connections at each major PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-034 CCR Output Rises Without Load

Symptom — Output voltage climbs toward the transformer's maximum limit and/or an open-circuit alarm threatens to trip when the series circuit load is reduced or removed (e.g. during isolation testing), even though the commanded current step has not changed.

Equipment / System

Closed-loop constant-current regulation behaviour, output transformer voltage limit/protection.

Possible Causes
HighExpected constant-current behaviour — as load (loop impedance) decreases, a true constant-current source naturally increases voltage to maintain current; this is normal operation being misread as a fault, unless the rise is uncontrolled
HighOne or more fixtures/transformers genuinely disconnected from the loop (e.g. during maintenance) without first reducing the CCR to a lower step or isolating it, causing the regulator to chase full open-circuit voltage
MediumOpen-circuit/no-load protection threshold set incorrectly, tripping prematurely on a load reduction that should be within normal tolerance
LowerVoltage limit protection circuit fault failing to cap the rise at the designed ceiling
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterInsulation resistance tester (5kV)CCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Never reduce or remove series circuit load without first reducing the CCR to a low step or isolating it — an unloaded constant-current regulator will attempt to develop full open-circuit voltage, which is a serious shock/flashover hazard.
  • Apply LOTO before working on any part of the loop, including for planned load reduction during maintenance.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm whether the load reduction was planned (e.g. maintenance disconnecting fixtures) or unplanned, and whether the CCR was correctly stepped down or isolated beforehand per procedure.
  2. MeasurementIf the rise is unplanned, verify actual loop continuity to identify which section is now open-circuit or under-loaded, per CCR-027/030 procedures as applicable.
  3. ObservationReview the open-circuit/no-load protection threshold configuration against the manufacturer's recommended setting.
  4. DecisionRise correlates with a known, planned load change and stays within the transformer's designed ceiling → normal constant-current behaviour, procedural reminder only. Rise is unplanned or protection fails to limit it → genuine protection or loop fault requiring correction.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to a procedural gap (load changed without stepping down the CCR), a genuine loop disconnection, or a protection threshold/circuit fault.
  6. Root CauseConfirm whether the event was a procedural violation or an equipment fault.
Test Points
Series circuit loop continuity
Open-circuit/no-load protection threshold setting
Output voltage limit circuit
Root Cause Verification

Confirm the open-circuit/no-load protection reliably trips within its designed threshold and time when the loop is genuinely opened during a controlled test, and that operations staff correctly step down the CCR before any planned disconnection.

Corrective Action
  • Reinforce the procedure requiring the CCR to be stepped down or isolated before any planned load disconnection.
  • Correct the open-circuit/no-load protection threshold configuration.
  • Repair the voltage limit protection circuit if confirmed faulty.
  • Restore the loop continuity if an unplanned disconnection is found.
Preventive Action
  • Include a mandatory 'step down before disconnect' step in every maintenance work instruction touching the series circuit.
  • Verify open-circuit protection function as part of the annual protection test (see Division 04).
  • Brief operations and maintenance staff on constant-current source behaviour during induction/refresher training.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-04 (CCR Isolation & LOTO Procedure), SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-035 CCR Output Hunting

Symptom — Output current oscillates in a regular, repeating pattern around the setpoint — rising and falling in a consistent cycle rather than settling, often visible as a rhythmic flicker in lamp brightness.

Equipment / System

Closed-loop current regulation control algorithm — proportional/integral/derivative (PID) or equivalent gain settings, feedback sensor response time.

Possible Causes
HighRegulation loop gain (proportional/integral) set too high for the actual loop dynamics, causing the control loop to overcorrect each cycle
HighFeedback sensor or signal path introducing a delay or lag that the control loop's tuning does not account for
MediumLoop tuning parameters left at generic factory defaults rather than tuned for the specific installed circuit length/impedance
MediumA firmware update changed default control parameters without re-verification against the site's circuit characteristics
LowerMechanical/relay-based step switching (on step-relay-type CCRs) chattering due to a marginal relay/contactor
Required Tools
OscilloscopeTrue-RMS clamp meter with loggingCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Sustained hunting can cause repeated thermal cycling stress on the bridge and output transformer — do not leave a hunting condition unaddressed for extended periods.
  • Apply LOTO before any internal parameter or wiring changes; parameter changes via the configuration tool can typically be made with the unit running under supervision per manufacturer procedure.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementLog/oscilloscope the output current to characterise the hunting period and amplitude precisely.
  2. ObservationReview the current regulation loop gain (P/I/D or equivalent) settings against the manufacturer's recommended range and the commissioned baseline.
  3. MeasurementCheck the feedback sensor signal for excessive lag or filtering delay relative to actual current changes.
  4. ObservationIf step-relay-type, inspect the step relay/contactor for chatter or marginal pull-in during a step-hold condition.
  5. DecisionGain settings found outside the recommended range or altered from baseline → re-tune. Feedback lag confirmed as the dominant factor → address sensor/signal path first before re-tuning gain. Relay chatter confirmed → mechanical relay fault, not a control loop issue.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the control loop gain tuning, the feedback sensor response, or a step relay.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific tuning or component correction that eliminates the oscillation.
Test Points
Output current waveform (oscilloscope/logger)
Regulation loop gain parameters
Feedback sensor signal timing
Step relay/contactor condition
Root Cause Verification

After adjustment, run the CCR at each intensity step for a minimum of 15 minutes and confirm output current settles within normal tolerance with no repeating oscillation.

Corrective Action
  • Re-tune the regulation loop gain per manufacturer guidance for the actual installed circuit characteristics.
  • Correct or replace the feedback sensor/signal path causing excessive lag.
  • Replace the marginal step relay/contactor.
  • Revert to previously verified firmware/parameter settings if a recent update introduced the issue.
Preventive Action
  • Document and preserve the tuned regulation loop parameters at commissioning as the site baseline.
  • Re-verify loop tuning after any firmware update or controller replacement.
  • Include a hunting check (visual and measured) as a standard PM test.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-036 CCR Current Overshoot

Symptom — On a step change (start-up or intensity step increase), output current briefly spikes above the new commanded setpoint before settling — a transient excursion rather than a sustained overcurrent (see CCR-023 for sustained high current).

Equipment / System

Closed-loop regulation transient response, step-change ramp/soft-start logic.

Possible Causes
HighRegulation loop gain tuned too aggressively for a fast transient response, trading overshoot for speed
MediumStep-change ramp/soft-start function disabled or configured with too short a ramp time
MediumFeedback sensor response lag causing the loop to overdrive briefly before the true current value is registered
LowerLoad impedance changing abruptly at the step transition (e.g. a large fixture count) exceeding the loop's designed transient handling range
Required Tools
OscilloscopeTrue-RMS clamp meter with logging (fast sample rate)CCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Repeated current overshoot stresses lamp filaments and LED driver components — do not dismiss as cosmetic if it is causing premature fixture failures.
  • Apply LOTO before any wiring-level intervention; parameter/ramp adjustments are typically made via the configuration tool under manufacturer procedure.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementCapture the output current transient on an oscilloscope or fast-sampling logger during a deliberate step change, measuring overshoot magnitude and duration.
  2. ObservationCheck whether a step-change ramp/soft-start function exists on this controller model and whether it is enabled and correctly configured.
  3. ObservationReview regulation loop gain settings against the manufacturer's recommended range.
  4. DecisionRamp function disabled or too aggressive → enable/lengthen the ramp first, as the simplest correction. Ramp already correctly configured but overshoot persists → loop gain re-tuning required.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the step-change ramp configuration or the underlying regulation loop gain tuning.
  6. Root CauseConfirm the specific parameter correction that brings overshoot within acceptable limits.
Test Points
Output current transient waveform at step change
Step-change ramp/soft-start configuration
Regulation loop gain parameters
Root Cause Verification

Repeat a deliberate step change after adjustment and confirm the overshoot magnitude is within the manufacturer's specified tolerance and settles promptly.

Corrective Action
  • Enable or lengthen the step-change ramp/soft-start function.
  • Re-tune the regulation loop gain to reduce transient overshoot within an acceptable settling time.
  • Address feedback sensor lag if confirmed as a contributing factor.
Preventive Action
  • Verify step-change ramp configuration at commissioning and after any parameter reset.
  • Include a step-change transient check in periodic PM for circuits with a history of premature fixture failure.
  • Document the tuned transient response parameters as part of the site baseline.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-037 CCR Current Undershoot

Symptom — On a step change, output current briefly dips below the new commanded setpoint before settling, or momentarily drops noticeably below setpoint after a step decrease — a transient dip rather than a sustained low current (see CCR-022 for sustained low current).

Equipment / System

Closed-loop regulation transient response, step-change ramp/soft-start logic.

Possible Causes
HighRegulation loop response too slow (excessively conservative gain/ramp) causing a lag before the loop catches up to the new setpoint
MediumFeedback sensor or signal filtering introducing excessive smoothing/delay
MediumStep-change ramp/soft-start function configured with too long a ramp time for the operational requirement, perceived as an undershoot/slow response by pilots or ATC
LowerBridge thermal foldback momentarily engaging at the step transition, briefly limiting available current
Required Tools
OscilloscopeTrue-RMS clamp meter with logging (fast sample rate)CCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • A significant, operationally noticeable dip in runway/approach lighting intensity during a step change can affect pilot visual reference during critical phases — treat reports of a perceptible dip as an operational priority, not just a technical curiosity.
  • Apply LOTO before any wiring-level intervention.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementCapture the output current transient on an oscilloscope or fast-sampling logger during a deliberate step change, measuring undershoot magnitude and duration.
  2. ObservationReview the step-change ramp/soft-start configuration — an overly long ramp on a step decrease can present as a slow, undershoot-like response.
  3. ObservationReview regulation loop gain settings against the manufacturer's recommended range for responsiveness.
  4. DecisionRamp configured too long for the operational need → shorten within manufacturer limits. Ramp already appropriate but undershoot persists → loop gain or feedback lag issue requiring further tuning.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the step-change ramp configuration or the underlying regulation loop response tuning.
  6. Root CauseConfirm the specific parameter correction that brings the transient response within acceptable limits.
Test Points
Output current transient waveform at step change
Step-change ramp/soft-start configuration
Regulation loop gain parameters
Root Cause Verification

Repeat a deliberate step change after adjustment and confirm the undershoot magnitude and settling time are within the manufacturer's specified tolerance.

Corrective Action
  • Shorten the step-change ramp time within manufacturer-permitted limits.
  • Re-tune the regulation loop gain for a faster, still-stable transient response.
  • Address feedback sensor filtering/lag if confirmed as a contributing factor.
Preventive Action
  • Balance ramp/soft-start settings against operational responsiveness requirements at commissioning, not just equipment protection.
  • Include a step-change transient check in periodic PM.
  • Document the tuned transient response parameters as part of the site baseline.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-038 CCR Current Regulation Failure

Symptom — The CCR no longer maintains a constant current regardless of load or supply variation — output current tracks changes in loop impedance or input voltage directly, as if the unit were operating open-loop rather than closed-loop.

Equipment / System

Complete closed-loop current regulation chain — feedback sensor, controller control algorithm, and firing circuit acting on that feedback.

Possible Causes
HighCurrent feedback signal path completely broken (sensor failed open or wiring severed), with the controller unable to close the loop and defaulting to a fixed or uncontrolled firing angle
HighController regulation algorithm fault/crash — the control task is not executing even though the unit otherwise appears to be running
MediumFeedback sensor calibration grossly out of range, effectively removing meaningful control authority even though a signal is present
LowerA configuration error has placed the controller in an open-loop/manual firing test mode and it was not returned to closed-loop automatic operation
Required Tools
OscilloscopeTrue-RMS clamp meterCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagramManufacturer diagnostic software (if available)
Safety Precautions
  • A regulation failure means the CCR is no longer providing its core safety function of limiting current — treat this as a priority fault and reduce risk by not leaving the circuit running unattended until the cause is identified.
  • Apply LOTO before internal wiring inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationVary the load or input condition in a controlled way (e.g. compare readings across two different commanded steps, or note input voltage change) and confirm output current does not respond to closed-loop correction as expected.
  2. MeasurementCheck for a valid, in-range current feedback signal reaching the controller.
  3. ObservationCheck the controller's operating mode configuration to confirm it is set to closed-loop/automatic rather than an open-loop or manual test mode.
  4. MeasurementIf the manufacturer provides diagnostic software, check for a control algorithm fault/exception logged internally.
  5. DecisionNo valid feedback signal reaching the controller → sensor/wiring fault, proceed as CCR-021/030. Valid feedback present but no closed-loop correction happening → controller algorithm fault or mode misconfiguration.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the feedback sensor/wiring, the controller's operating mode setting, or the control algorithm itself.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and verify closed-loop regulation is restored.
Test Points
Current feedback signal at controller input
Controller operating mode configuration
Controller diagnostic/exception log
Root Cause Verification

After correction, deliberately vary loop impedance or input voltage within a safe test procedure and confirm output current is actively held constant, demonstrating genuine closed-loop regulation rather than coincidental stability.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the failed feedback sensor and wiring.
  • Return the controller to closed-loop/automatic operating mode.
  • Reset, reflash, or replace the controller if a persistent algorithm fault is confirmed.
  • Recalibrate the feedback sensor if grossly out of range.
Preventive Action
  • Verify and lock the controller's operating mode after any diagnostic/test session before returning it to service.
  • Include a genuine closed-loop response check — not just a static current reading — in periodic PM.
  • Maintain manufacturer diagnostic software access for controller-level fault investigation.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-039 CCR Output Transformer Overheating

Symptom — Output transformer runs at an abnormally high temperature (by thermal imaging, thermal sensor alarm, or a burning smell) during normal or sustained operation, distinct from an internal cabinet-wide overtemperature (see Division 05 for cabinet cooling).

Equipment / System

CCR output (step-up) transformer, its cooling path, and its loading condition.

Possible Causes
HighSustained overcurrent or a marginal overvoltage condition on the loop causing the transformer to operate beyond its rated duty (see CCR-023/027)
HighBlocked or degraded transformer cooling — dust accumulation, blocked ventilation, or a failed dedicated cooling fan if fitted
MediumTransformer winding insulation degrading with age, increasing losses and heat generation at a given load
MediumTransformer tap set incorrectly for the circuit, causing it to operate consistently near or beyond its rated voltage/current combination
LowerLoose internal transformer connection increasing localized resistive heating
Required Tools
Thermal imaging cameraTrue-RMS clamp meterInsulation resistance tester (5kV)Torque screwdriver setCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • An overheating transformer is a fire risk — if temperature is significantly above normal or a burning smell is present, de-energize immediately rather than continuing to monitor.
  • Allow the transformer to cool before physical inspection; apply LOTO throughout.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementThermal-image the transformer during sustained operation and compare against the manufacturer's normal operating temperature range.
  2. MeasurementClamp-meter the actual output current and voltage to check for a sustained overcurrent/overvoltage condition (cross-reference CCR-023/CCR-027).
  3. ObservationInspect the transformer's ventilation path and any dedicated cooling fan for blockage or failure.
  4. MeasurementWith the unit isolated and cooled, megger the transformer winding insulation resistance and compare against baseline.
  5. ObservationVerify the tap setting against the documented circuit length and load.
  6. DecisionConfirmed sustained overcurrent/overvoltage → address the root loop or configuration cause first, per CCR-023/027. Cooling path blocked → clean/repair ventilation. Insulation resistance degraded from baseline with load/tap confirmed normal → ageing transformer, plan replacement.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to a loop-side overcurrent/overvoltage condition, a blocked cooling path, an incorrect tap setting, or transformer winding degradation.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and verify operating temperature returns to normal after correction.
Test Points
Transformer surface/winding temperature (thermal imaging)
Output current and voltage under sustained load
Transformer ventilation path/cooling fan
Transformer winding insulation resistance
Root Cause Verification

After correction, run the CCR at the normal commanded step for a minimum of one hour and confirm transformer temperature stabilises within the manufacturer's normal range.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the sustained overcurrent/overvoltage root cause per CCR-023/027.
  • Clean or repair the transformer's ventilation path or cooling fan.
  • Correct the transformer tap setting.
  • Replace the transformer if winding insulation is confirmed degraded beyond acceptable limits.
  • Re-torque any loose internal transformer connection.
Preventive Action
  • Include transformer thermal imaging under sustained load in the annual PM.
  • Keep transformer ventilation paths and filters on a defined cleaning schedule.
  • Trend transformer insulation resistance year over year to plan replacement proactively.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-040 CCR Internal Output Connection Failure

Symptom — Intermittent or total loss of output traced to a specific internal wiring, bus bar, or terminal connection within the CCR cabinet between the bridge, output transformer, output fuse, and output terminal block — rather than an external loop or component fault.

Equipment / System

Internal high-current wiring, bus bars, and terminal connections within the CCR power stage.

Possible Causes
HighLoose high-current terminal or bus bar connection due to inadequate original torque or vibration-induced loosening over time
HighCorroded or oxidised connection, particularly in coastal or high-humidity airport environments
MediumConnector or lug damaged during a previous maintenance intervention (e.g. over-torqued, cross-threaded, or a crimp lug improperly applied)
MediumThermal cycling fatigue at a connection carrying high current over an extended service life
LowerManufacturing defect at a factory-made internal connection, surfacing after a period of service
Required Tools
Thermal imaging cameraTorque screwdriver/wrench set (calibrated)True-RMS clamp meterInsulation resistance tester (5kV)Contact cleanerCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Internal high-current connections can carry lethal voltage/current — apply LOTO and verify zero energy state with a proven meter before touching any internal terminal.
  • A connection showing heat discoloration or arcing damage should be treated as an active fire risk; do not re-energize until repaired.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationThermal-image the full internal power path (bridge to output transformer to output terminal block) during sustained operation to localise any abnormally hot connection.
  2. MeasurementWith the unit isolated and LOTO applied, visually inspect the identified connection for looseness, corrosion, discoloration, or physical damage.
  3. MeasurementCheck the connection's resistance/continuity and compare against an equivalent healthy connection elsewhere in the same unit.
  4. DecisionA specific hot, loose, or corroded connection identified → direct mechanical repair. No single hot spot found despite a confirmed intermittent fault → widen the thermal survey and consider a load-cycling test to reproduce the fault under controlled conditions.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific bus bar, terminal, or connector responsible.
  6. Root CauseConfirm the connection is the true root cause by repairing it and verifying the fault does not recur under sustained load.
Test Points
Bridge output terminals
Output transformer primary and secondary terminals
Output fuse/breaker terminals
Output terminal block connections
Root Cause Verification

After repair, thermal-image the same connection points during a sustained full-load run and confirm no abnormal temperature rise, with output current stable throughout.

Corrective Action
  • Clean, re-terminate, and torque the affected connection to the manufacturer's specified value using a calibrated tool.
  • Replace a damaged lug, connector, or bus bar section.
  • Apply approved anti-oxidant compound on connections in corrosive environments per manufacturer guidance.
Preventive Action
  • Include torque-verification of internal high-current connections in the periodic PM schedule, using a calibrated torque tool rather than by feel.
  • Include internal thermal imaging under load as a standard PM test, not only during fault investigation.
  • Use anti-oxidant compound on internal connections as standard practice in coastal/high-humidity installations.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61439

Rev 0 — Initial issue

03 · CCR Intensity Control

15 of 15 topics published
CCR-041 Brightness Step 1 Not Working

Symptom — Commanding intensity Step 1 (locally, remotely, or via ALCMS) does not produce the expected brightness level on the series circuit — either no current change occurs, or the delivered current does not match the value defined for Step 1.

Equipment / System

CCR intensity-step control path — step relay/contactor or digital step reference, controller step configuration table, output transformer tap (on step-relay-type CCRs) or current setpoint table (on digital/thyristor CCRs).

Possible Causes
HighStep relay/contactor for Step 1 failed to pull in — coil open, mechanically stuck, or contact worn
HighStep 1 reference/tap wiring open or disconnected between the controller and the output transformer tap or step relay
MediumController's Step 1 configuration parameter corrupted or set to zero/disabled
MediumStep 1 selection signal (local switch position or ALCMS command code) not reaching the controller
LowerStep 1 indication only is faulty while the actual current step is correct — a display/feedback fault rather than a true step failure
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagramInsulated torque screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Confirm actual output current independently with a clamp meter before concluding the step itself has failed — the fault may be indication-only.
  • Apply LOTO before accessing step relay contacts or transformer tap terminals.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCommand Step 1 from the intended control source and note both the HMI-displayed step and the actual clamp-metered output current.
  2. MeasurementOn step-relay-type CCRs, check the Step 1 relay/contactor coil voltage and contact continuity when commanded.
  3. MeasurementOn digital/thyristor CCRs, verify the Step 1 current setpoint value in the controller configuration table against the design intensity schedule.
  4. MeasurementCheck the Step 1 selection signal path — local switch contact or the specific ALCMS/PLC command code — reaches the controller correctly.
  5. DecisionHMI shows Step 1 accepted but current does not change → relay/tap/setpoint fault, isolate within the step hardware or configuration. Step 1 command itself not reaching the controller → upstream selection/communication fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the Step 1 relay/contactor, its tap wiring, the controller's Step 1 configuration entry, or the step selection signal path.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed relay, wiring point, or configuration entry through direct testing.
Test Points
Step 1 relay/contactor coil and contacts
Step 1 tap wiring at output transformer (if applicable)
Step 1 setpoint value in controller configuration
Step selection signal at controller input
Root Cause Verification

Command Step 1 repeatedly from each control source and confirm the clamp-metered output current matches the design value every time, with the HMI indication agreeing.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed Step 1 relay/contactor.
  • Repair the Step 1 tap wiring or connection.
  • Correct the Step 1 setpoint value in the controller configuration.
  • Repair the step selection signal wiring or resolve the command code mismatch.
Preventive Action
  • Include a full 5-step verification (not just the commonly used steps) in every routine PM.
  • Track step relay duty cycles/switching counts and replace preventively per manufacturer MTBF data.
  • Lock configuration parameters after commissioning and log any authorized changes.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, Intensity Step Reference Table

Step 3 tap wiring at output transformer (if applicable)

Step selection signal at controller input
Root Cause Verification

Command Step 3 repeatedly from each control source and confirm the clamp-metered output current matches the design value every time, with the HMI indication agreeing.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed Step 3 relay/contactor.
  • Repair the Step 3 tap wiring or connection.
  • Correct the Step 3 setpoint value in the controller configuration.
  • Repair the step selection signal wiring or resolve the command code mismatch.
Preventive Action
  • Include a full 5-step verification (not just the commonly used steps) in every routine PM.
  • Track step relay duty cycles/switching counts and replace preventively per manufacturer MTBF data.
  • Lock configuration parameters after commissioning and log any authorized changes.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-044 Brightness Step 4 Not Working

Symptom — Commanding intensity Step 4 (locally, remotely, or via ALCMS) does not produce the expected brightness level on the series circuit — either no current change occurs, or the delivered current does not match the value defined for Step 4.

Equipment / System

CCR intensity-step control path — step relay/contactor or digital step reference, controller step configuration table, output transformer tap (on step-relay-type CCRs) or current setpoint table (on digital/thyristor CCRs).

Possible Causes
HighStep relay/contactor for Step 4 failed to pull in — coil open, mechanically stuck, or contact worn
HighStep 4 reference/tap wiring open or disconnected between the controller and the output transformer tap or step relay
MediumController's Step 4 configuration parameter corrupted or set to zero/disabled
MediumStep 4 selection signal (local switch position or ALCMS command code) not reaching the controller
LowerStep 4 indication only is faulty while the actual current step is correct — a display/feedback fault rather than a true step failure
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagramInsulated torque screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Confirm actual output current independently with a clamp meter before concluding the step itself has failed — the fault may be indication-only.
  • Apply LOTO before accessing step relay contacts or transformer tap terminals.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCommand Step 4 from the intended control source and note both the HMI-displayed step and the actual clamp-metered output current.
  2. MeasurementOn step-relay-type CCRs, check the Step 4 relay/contactor coil voltage and contact continuity when commanded.
  3. MeasurementOn digital/thyristor CCRs, verify the Step 4 current setpoint value in the controller configuration table against the design intensity schedule.
  4. MeasurementCheck the Step 4 selection signal path — local switch contact or the specific ALCMS/PLC command code — reaches the controller correctly.
  5. DecisionHMI shows Step 4 accepted but current does not change → relay/tap/setpoint fault, isolate within the step hardware or configuration. Step 4 command itself not reaching the controller → upstream selection/communication fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the Step 4 relay/contactor, its tap wiring, the controller's Step 4 configuration entry, or the step selection signal path.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed relay, wiring point, or configuration entry through direct testing.
Test Points
Step 4 relay/contactor coil and contacts
Step 4 tap wiring at output transformer (if applicable)
Step 4 setpoint value in controller configuration
Step selection signal at controller input
Root Cause Verification

Command Step 4 repeatedly from each control source and confirm the clamp-metered output current matches the design value every time, with the HMI indication agreeing.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed Step 4 relay/contactor.
  • Repair the Step 4 tap wiring or connection.
  • Correct the Step 4 setpoint value in the controller configuration.
  • Repair the step selection signal wiring or resolve the command code mismatch.
Preventive Action
  • Include a full 5-step verification (not just the commonly used steps) in every routine PM.
  • Track step relay duty cycles/switching counts and replace preventively per manufacturer MTBF data.
  • Lock configuration parameters after commissioning and log any authorized changes.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification)
