Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-046 One Intensity Step Missing

Symptom — Exactly one intensity step in the 5-step (or configured) schedule is unavailable or produces no change from the adjacent step, while all other steps operate correctly.

Equipment / System

Single step relay/tap or a single controller step configuration entry, isolated from the rest of the step schedule.

Possible Causes
HighThe specific step relay/contactor for the affected step has failed (see CCR-041 through CCR-045 for step-specific diagnostics)
HighThe controller configuration entry for that one step was altered, disabled, or set equal to an adjacent step's value
MediumA single tap connection on the output transformer for that step is loose or broken
LowerThe physical local selector switch has a worn or missing detent/contact position for that one step only
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before inspecting relay contacts or transformer tap connections.
  • Verify zero energy state before handling any internal tap or relay terminal.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationIdentify precisely which single step is affected and confirm all other steps operate correctly, to rule out a general controller or feedback fault.
  2. MeasurementCommand the affected step and clamp-meter the actual output current against its design value.
  3. MeasurementCheck that specific step's relay/contactor and tap wiring per the single-step diagnostic procedure (CCR-041 to CCR-045).
  4. ObservationReview the controller's configuration table entry for that specific step against the commissioned baseline.
  5. DecisionConfiguration entry found altered/duplicated → correct the configuration. Physical relay/tap fault confirmed → proceed with mechanical repair.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the single affected step's relay, tap connection, or configuration entry.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through direct testing of the isolated step.
Test Points
Affected step relay/contactor
Affected step transformer tap connection
Affected step's configuration table entry
Root Cause Verification

Command all steps in sequence, including the previously affected one, and confirm every step delivers its design current value.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed step relay/contactor.
  • Correct the controller configuration entry for the affected step.
  • Repair the loose or broken tap connection.
  • Replace a worn local selector switch position/detent.
Preventive Action
  • Verify all steps individually — not just spot-checking the commonly used ones — during every PM.
  • Lock and periodically audit the step configuration table against the commissioned baseline.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, Intensity Step Reference Table

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-047 Multiple Intensity Steps Missing

Symptom — Two or more intensity steps are unavailable or produce incorrect current, while at least one step (commonly the lowest or highest) still operates — distinct from a total loss of step control.

Equipment / System

Controller step configuration table as a whole, shared step-relay control wiring/bus, or a shared portion of the tap winding.

Possible Causes
HighA shared control wiring fault (e.g. a common bus feeding several step relay coils) affecting a contiguous group of steps
HighA controller firmware update or configuration reset partially overwrote the step schedule, leaving some entries correct and others reset to default/zero
MediumA section of the output transformer's multi-tap winding failed, affecting every step that depends on that winding section
MediumA shared step-selection relay/multiplexer upstream of the individual step relays has failed
LowerProgressive relay/contactor wear affecting several of the more frequently used steps first
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagramInsulation resistance tester (5kV)
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection of shared wiring, tap windings, or relay assemblies.
  • Treat a partial configuration overwrite as a signal to verify the entire step schedule, not just the reported steps, before returning the unit to service.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCommand every step in sequence and record which specific steps are affected, looking for a pattern (contiguous steps, alternating steps, or steps sharing a common relay/wiring group).
  2. ObservationReview the complete controller step configuration table against the commissioned baseline for all steps, not only the reported ones.
  3. MeasurementTrace the shared control wiring/bus feeding the affected group of step relays for a common fault point.
  4. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, check the output transformer's multi-tap winding continuity and insulation resistance section by section.
  5. DecisionConfiguration table shows multiple altered/reset entries → configuration corruption, restore from backup. A shared wiring fault traced to a common point → repair that shared connection. Winding section fault confirmed → transformer replacement required.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the controller configuration table, a shared wiring/bus fault, or a specific transformer winding section.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and verify all previously affected steps are restored.
Test Points
Full controller step configuration table
Shared step relay control wiring/bus
Output transformer multi-tap winding sections
Root Cause Verification

Command every step in sequence and confirm all steps, including the previously affected group, deliver their design current values consistently.

Corrective Action
  • Restore the controller configuration from a verified backup or re-enter the correct step schedule.
  • Repair the shared control wiring/bus fault.
  • Replace the failed shared step-selection relay/multiplexer.
  • Replace the output transformer if a winding section is confirmed failed.
Preventive Action
  • Maintain a current, verified configuration backup for every controller and restore from it after any firmware update.
  • Verify the complete step schedule after any configuration or firmware change, not just the steps that were reportedly modified.
  • Include multi-tap winding insulation testing in the annual PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management), SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, Intensity Step Reference Table

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-048 Incorrect Intensity Selection

Symptom — The CCR delivers a valid, stable current output, but it does not correspond to the step that was actually commanded — the unit runs a step other than the one requested, without an error being flagged.

Equipment / System

Controller step command interpretation logic, local/remote selector, ALCMS/PLC command mapping.

Possible Causes
HighStep command mapping table incorrectly configured — e.g. the ALCMS sends a code intended for Step 3 but the controller has that code mapped to Step 4
HighLocal/remote selector switch left in the wrong position, causing local commands to be ignored while a stale remote step remains active, or vice versa
MediumA prior local override was never cleared, so new remote commands are being accepted but not acted upon
MediumALCMS-side configuration error sending the wrong step code for the intended runway/taxiway lighting circuit
LowerController display bug showing the previous step while actually running the new one, or the reverse (see CCR-053 for indication-only faults)
Required Tools
MultimeterTrue-RMS clamp meterCCR configuration/parameter toolProtocol analyzer or serial monitor (for ALCMS link)CCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • An incorrect intensity level on approach/runway lighting has direct flight-safety implications — treat any confirmed mismatch as an operational priority and notify air traffic services per local procedure while it is being resolved.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the exact step actually commanded (by the pilot-controller, tower, or ALCMS schedule) versus the step the CCR is actually running, verified by clamp meter, not just the HMI.
  2. ObservationCheck the local/remote selector switch position and whether a local override is active.
  3. MeasurementIf ALCMS-commanded, monitor the communication link to confirm the exact step code transmitted by the ALCMS and received by the CCR.
  4. ObservationReview the controller's step command mapping table against the design intent.
  5. DecisionMapping table found incorrect → correct the mapping. Selector switch in the wrong position or an uncleared override found → correct switch position and clear override, and review operating procedure with staff. Correct code confirmed sent and received but wrong step still runs → controller logic fault, escalate to manufacturer.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the step command mapping table, the local/remote selection state, or the ALCMS communication link.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific misconfiguration or procedural gap responsible.
Test Points
Local/remote selector switch position
ALCMS/PLC command code at CCR input
Controller step command mapping table
CCR output terminals (clamp meter)
Root Cause Verification

Command each step from the intended control source in turn and confirm the clamp-metered output current matches the intended step exactly, every time, across both local and remote control paths.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the controller's step command mapping table.
  • Correct the local/remote selector switch position and clear any stale override.
  • Correct the ALCMS-side step code configuration.
  • Escalate a confirmed controller logic fault to the manufacturer.
Preventive Action
  • Verify the step command mapping table against the design intensity schedule at commissioning and after any configuration change.
  • Brief operations staff on correctly clearing local overrides before returning control to ALCMS.
  • Include an end-to-end step verification (ALCMS command to measured output) in periodic PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-ALCMS-02 (Lighting Command Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, ALCMS Interface Diagram

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-049 Intensity Changes Automatically

Symptom — The CCR's output intensity step changes on its own, without a corresponding operator, ALCMS, or scheduled command — an unexplained step-up, step-down, or repeated cycling between steps.

Equipment / System

Controller command input monitoring, ALCMS scheduling/automation logic, local control wiring.

Possible Causes
HighAn unintended ALCMS automation rule or schedule (e.g. an astronomical/time-based dimming schedule) is active and changing the step as designed, but was not communicated to site staff
HighElectrical noise or a faulty contact on the local step-selection wiring intermittently simulating a step-change command
MediumA protection function (e.g. thermal derate) automatically reducing the step, which is a designed safety response rather than a fault (cross-reference CCR-033/039)
MediumALCMS communication link fault causing spurious/corrupted step commands to be received and acted upon
LowerController firmware fault causing an internal, unintended step change
Required Tools
MultimeterProtocol analyzer or serial monitor (for ALCMS link)CCR event/alarm log toolCCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • An unexplained automatic intensity change during active operations should be reported to air traffic services immediately, since it directly affects visual reference for pilots.
  • Do not disable a protection-driven automatic step reduction (e.g. thermal derate) without first understanding and addressing its underlying cause.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationPull the controller's full event/alarm log and the ALCMS command history for the time window of the unexplained change, to determine whether a legitimate automated command (e.g. a dimming schedule) or protection trip actually caused it.
  2. DecisionA legitimate scheduled/automated command found → not an equipment fault; align site procedures and staff awareness with the automation schedule.
  3. MeasurementIf no legitimate command is found in the logs, inspect the local step-selection wiring for a noise source or intermittent contact.
  4. MeasurementCheck the ALCMS communication link for error rates or corrupted message events around the time of each unexplained change.
  5. DecisionIntermittent local wiring fault confirmed → repair wiring. Communication link errors correlate with each event → address the communication link. Neither found → escalate as a possible controller firmware fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to an ALCMS automation/scheduling configuration, the local control wiring, the ALCMS communication link, or controller firmware.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by correlating each occurrence against logged events.
Test Points
Controller full event/alarm log
ALCMS command history
Local step-selection wiring
ALCMS communication link error log
Root Cause Verification

Monitor the CCR over a period spanning at least one full operational cycle after correction and confirm the intensity step changes only in response to legitimate, logged commands.

Corrective Action
  • Align site procedures and staff awareness with a confirmed legitimate ALCMS automation schedule.
  • Repair the intermittent local step-selection wiring fault.
  • Repair or replace the faulty ALCMS communication link hardware.
  • Reflash/reset controller firmware if a confirmed internal fault.
Preventive Action
  • Document all active ALCMS automation/dimming schedules and brief maintenance and ATC staff.
  • Include a communication link error-rate check in periodic PM.
  • Log and review all automatic step changes as part of routine system health monitoring.
Related References

SOP: SOP-ALCMS-02 (Lighting Command Verification), SOP-CCR-07 (Controller Parameter Management)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, ALCMS Interface Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-050 Intensity Command Not Accepted

Symptom — A step-change command issued locally, remotely, or via ALCMS is not acted upon at all — the CCR continues running its previous step and does not respond, though it remains otherwise healthy with no active alarm.

Equipment / System

Controller command input path — local switch, remote/ALCMS communication interface, command validation logic.

Possible Causes
HighController is in local mode while the command was sent remotely, or vice versa, with the selector position not matching the command source
HighA latched fault or safety interlock is silently blocking step changes without raising a visible alarm (see CCR-030 for a similar unannounced-fault pattern)
MediumALCMS/PLC command signal wiring or communication link fault preventing the command from reaching the controller
MediumThe requested step is outside a configured minimum/maximum limit and is being rejected by validation logic without a clear operator-facing message
LowerController command-processing task locked up (partial firmware fault) while other functions remain responsive
Required Tools
MultimeterProtocol analyzer or serial monitorCCR event/alarm log toolCCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Do not repeatedly re-send a command as the only troubleshooting step — investigate the root cause, since a masked interlock or logic fault could recur at a critical moment.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the local/remote selector position matches the source the command was actually sent from.
  2. ObservationPull the controller's full event/alarm log to check for a latched interlock or fault silently blocking step changes.
  3. MeasurementVerify the command signal/communication link is actually reaching the controller (correct wiring continuity or communication link activity).
  4. ObservationCheck whether the requested step falls within any configured minimum/maximum limit in the controller.
  5. DecisionSelector position mismatch found → correct operator procedure/switch position. Latched interlock found → resolve the underlying interlock condition per its specific fault topic. Command confirmed reaching the controller with no interlock or limit issue → escalate as a controller command-processing fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the local/remote selection, a latched interlock, the command signal path, a configured limit, or controller command processing.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific blocking condition and verify commands are accepted once cleared.
Test Points
Local/remote selector switch
Controller full event/alarm log
Command signal/communication link
Configured step minimum/maximum limits
Root Cause Verification

Issue step-change commands from both local and remote/ALCMS sources across the full step range and confirm each is accepted and acted upon promptly.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the local/remote selector position and clarify command-source procedures with operators.
  • Resolve the underlying latched interlock condition.
  • Repair the command signal wiring or communication link.
  • Correct the configured step limits if set incorrectly.
  • Reset/reflash the controller if a command-processing lock-up is confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Review the complete event/alarm log periodically, not only currently active alarms, to catch silently latched conditions early.
  • Include a full-range command acceptance test in periodic PM.
  • Document configured step limits clearly in the site commissioning record.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-ALCMS-02 (Lighting Command Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, ALCMS Interface Diagram

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-051 Local Intensity Control Failure

Symptom — Intensity step commands issued from the CCR's local control panel/switch are not acted upon, while remote/ALCMS-issued commands (or vice versa) continue to work normally.

Equipment / System

Local control panel step-selector switch, its wiring to the controller, and the controller's local-mode command interpretation.

Possible Causes
HighLocal selector switch itself failed — worn contacts, broken shaft, or a position not making contact
HighWiring between the local selector switch and the controller's local command input broken or loose
MediumController not actually in local mode despite the local/remote switch appearing to be positioned there — a mode-selection contact fault
MediumA local control panel lock/key switch left in a disabled position
LowerController's local command input circuit (opto-isolator or input card) failed
Required Tools
MultimeterCCR wiring diagramContinuity/probe test leadsInsulated torque screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection of the local control wiring or input card, unless the manufacturer's procedure permits live testing with appropriate precautions.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the local/remote mode switch position and any key/lock switch status at the local control panel.
  2. MeasurementOperate the local step-selector switch through each position and check for correct contact closure/output at the switch itself.
  3. MeasurementCheck continuity of the wiring between the local selector switch and the controller's local command input terminals.
  4. MeasurementVerify the controller is actually registering local mode internally (via HMI status or diagnostic tool), not just switch position.
  5. DecisionSelector switch itself fails to make contact → replace switch. Switch operates correctly but signal doesn't reach the controller → wiring fault. Wiring confirmed intact but controller doesn't register local mode → controller input circuit fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the local selector switch, its wiring, or the controller's local command input circuit.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component through direct testing.
Test Points
Local step-selector switch contacts
Local control wiring at controller terminals
Controller local-mode status/registration
Local control panel key/lock switch
Root Cause Verification

Operate the local selector through every step position and confirm the CCR responds correctly and promptly to each, with the controller correctly registering local mode.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed local selector switch.
  • Repair or replace the local control wiring.
  • Repair the controller's local command input circuit/card.
  • Correct the local control panel key/lock switch position.
Preventive Action
  • Include a full local-control functional test in periodic PM, exercising every step position.
  • Keep the local control panel key/lock switch procedure documented and enforced.
  • Track local selector switch wear and replace preventively based on operating history.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-052 Remote Intensity Control Failure

Symptom — Intensity step commands issued from ALCMS/remote tower control are not acted upon, while local control panel commands continue to work normally.

Equipment / System

ALCMS/PLC communication link, the controller's remote command interface, and remote-mode command interpretation.

Possible Causes
HighALCMS/PLC communication link down or degraded — cable fault, network switch failure, or a fibre/media converter fault on the link to this CCR
HighController not registering remote mode despite the local/remote switch being positioned for remote operation
MediumCommunication protocol mismatch or address/ID misconfiguration after a controller or ALCMS-side change
MediumRemote command input circuit (opto-isolator, communication card) on the controller failed
LowerALCMS-side configuration for this specific CCR removed or altered, so it is no longer being addressed correctly
Required Tools
MultimeterProtocol analyzer or serial monitorNetwork/fibre test equipment (as applicable)CCR configuration toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Loss of remote control removes ATC's ability to adjust runway/approach lighting intensity in real time — treat this as an operationally significant fault and notify air traffic services promptly per local procedure while resolving it.
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection of the communication card.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the local/remote mode switch is correctly positioned for remote operation and that the controller registers remote mode internally.
  2. MeasurementCheck the ALCMS/PLC communication link status — link/activity indicators, cable continuity, or network/fibre diagnostics as applicable.
  3. ObservationVerify the CCR's address/ID and communication protocol configuration matches what the ALCMS expects to see.
  4. MeasurementIf link and configuration appear correct, monitor actual command traffic to confirm whether commands are reaching the controller's communication port at all.
  5. DecisionCommunication link confirmed down → repair cable/network hardware. Link up but address/protocol mismatch found → correct configuration on the CCR or ALCMS side. Link and configuration correct but commands still not registering → controller communication card fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the communication link, the address/protocol configuration, or the controller's communication card.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and verify remote commands are accepted end-to-end.
Test Points
Local/remote mode switch and controller mode status
ALCMS/PLC communication link (cable, network, or fibre)
Controller address/ID and protocol configuration
Controller communication card
Root Cause Verification

Issue step-change commands from ALCMS/remote tower control across the full step range and confirm each is accepted and acted upon promptly, with the correct step reflected back to ALCMS.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the faulty communication cable, network switch, or media converter.
  • Correct the CCR's address/ID or protocol configuration to match the ALCMS.
  • Replace the controller's failed communication card.
  • Restore or correct the ALCMS-side configuration for this CCR.
Preventive Action
  • Include a communication link health check (error rates, link status) in periodic PM.
  • Maintain a documented, current record of every CCR's ALCMS address/protocol configuration.
  • Test remote control functionality end-to-end after any ALCMS or network change, not just locally at the CCR.
Related References

SOP: SOP-ALCMS-02 (Lighting Command Verification), SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, ALCMS Interface Diagram

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-053 Step Indication Incorrect

Symptom — The CCR's HMI, local indicator, or ALCMS status display shows a different intensity step than what is actually being delivered at the output — a display/feedback mismatch rather than a true control fault (verify against CCR-048 which covers a genuine wrong-step delivery).

Equipment / System

Controller step status feedback/display logic, HMI, and any status reporting to ALCMS.

Possible Causes
HighStep feedback signal used for display purposes (separate from the actual control setpoint) failed or reads incorrectly
MediumHMI display firmware fault showing a stale or cached step value rather than the live one
MediumStep status reporting to ALCMS uses a different data point or mapping than the local HMI, and one of the two is misconfigured
LowerA momentary display glitch that clears on its own but was not investigated at the time
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterMultimeterCCR configuration toolProtocol analyzer or serial monitor
Safety Precautions
  • Do not assume the discrepancy is purely cosmetic — always verify actual delivered current independently before ruling out a genuine control fault, since an indication fault can mask a real problem.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. MeasurementIndependently clamp-meter the actual output current for the currently commanded step and confirm it matches the design value for that step (ruling out CCR-048).
  2. ObservationCompare the local HMI step indication, any physical indicator lights, and the ALCMS-reported step status against the confirmed actual output.
  3. ObservationCommand a deliberate step change and observe whether each display updates promptly and correctly.
  4. DecisionActual output confirmed correct for the commanded step but one or more displays disagree → indication/feedback fault, isolate to the specific display path that is wrong. Actual output also incorrect → redirect to CCR-048.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific step feedback signal, the HMI firmware, or the ALCMS status reporting configuration.
  6. Root CauseConfirm the specific faulty indication path through step changes and cross-verification.
Test Points
CCR output terminals (clamp meter, ground truth)
Local HMI step display
Physical step indicator lights (if fitted)
ALCMS-reported step status
Root Cause Verification

Command a full sequence of step changes and confirm the local HMI, physical indicators, and ALCMS status all correctly and promptly reflect the true output current at every step.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the failed step feedback signal/sensor.
  • Update or reset the HMI firmware if a display caching fault is confirmed.
  • Correct the ALCMS status reporting configuration/mapping.
Preventive Action
  • Cross-check local HMI, physical indicators, and ALCMS status against actual clamp-metered output during routine PM.
  • Include display/indication verification as a distinct checklist item, separate from output verification, in commissioning.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-ALCMS-02 (Lighting Command Verification)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-054 Step Relay Failure

Symptom — A specific step relay/contactor within the CCR's step-switching assembly fails mechanically or electrically — confirmed by direct inspection as the root cause underlying one or more of the step-fault symptoms (CCR-041 to CCR-047), documented here as the component-level fault record.

Equipment / System

Step relay/contactor assembly used to switch output transformer taps or current reference points for each intensity step (on relay-switched CCR designs).

Possible Causes
HighRelay coil open or burnt out from repeated switching duty or an overvoltage condition on the coil circuit
HighRelay contacts welded closed, worn, or pitted from repeated switching under load, preventing reliable make/break
MediumMechanical linkage or armature binding due to age, contamination, or corrosion
MediumRelay coil driver circuit on the controller board failed, unable to energize the coil even though the relay itself is healthy
LowerIncorrect replacement relay fitted at a previous repair, with a coil voltage or contact rating mismatch
Required Tools
MultimeterTrue-RMS clamp meterInsulated torque screwdriver setContact cleanerManufacturer relay specification sheet
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before removing or testing any step relay — contacts may be switching high current at line voltage.
  • Do not clean or file welded/pitted contacts as a permanent fix — replace the relay.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm which step(s) are affected by the suspected relay and cross-reference against CCR-041 to CCR-047 for the step-specific symptom.
  2. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, check relay coil resistance/continuity against the manufacturer's specification.
  3. MeasurementInspect relay contacts for welding, pitting, or excessive wear.
  4. MeasurementCheck the coil driver circuit on the controller board for correct output voltage to the relay coil when the step is commanded.
  5. DecisionCoil open or contacts confirmed welded/worn → replace the relay. Relay itself tests healthy but coil driver circuit shows no output → controller board fault, not the relay.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific relay or the controller's coil driver circuit.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failure mode — coil, contacts, or driver circuit.
Test Points
Relay coil resistance/continuity
Relay contact condition
Coil driver circuit output at controller board
Root Cause Verification

After replacement, cycle the affected step relay through multiple commanded operations and confirm reliable, clean make/break switching with the correct output current delivered each time.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed step relay/contactor with the manufacturer-specified part (correct coil voltage and contact rating).
  • Repair the controller's coil driver circuit if confirmed faulty.
  • Clean and inspect the mechanical linkage/armature; replace if binding persists after cleaning.
Preventive Action
  • Track step relay switching counts/duty cycles and replace preventively based on manufacturer MTBF data, rather than waiting for failure.
  • Verify replacement relay specifications match the original before fitting.
  • Include contact resistance testing of step relays in the annual PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-055 Intensity Control Relay Sticking

Symptom — A step relay/contactor is mechanically slow to release or occasionally remains latched in its previous position after a step-change command, causing a delayed, intermittent, or momentarily incorrect step transition rather than a complete failure.

Equipment / System

Step relay/contactor mechanical assembly, armature and contact return spring, ambient/internal cabinet conditions.

Possible Causes
HighContamination, dust, or corrosion buildup on the relay armature or guide surfaces increasing mechanical friction
HighWeakened or fatigued return spring no longer providing reliable release force
MediumExcessive heat in the cabinet softening or degrading relay materials, increasing friction or slowing mechanical response
MediumContact surfaces lightly welded/tacked from repeated switching, releasing only under vibration or a subsequent switching event rather than cleanly
LowerRelay nearing end of rated mechanical life with general wear across all moving parts
Required Tools
MultimeterTrue-RMS clamp meter with loggingContact cleanerThermal imaging cameraManufacturer relay specification sheet
Safety Precautions
  • A sticking relay can momentarily deliver an unintended intensity level during a transition — treat repeated occurrences as an operational concern and prioritise correction.
  • Apply LOTO before physical inspection or cleaning of the relay.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationLog step-change events and the corresponding output current transition to characterise the sticking behaviour — delayed release, intermittent, or occurring only after multiple operations.
  2. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, physically inspect the relay armature and contacts for contamination, corrosion, or surface damage.
  3. MeasurementCheck the return spring condition and free movement of the armature by hand (unit isolated) against the manufacturer's expected resistance.
  4. MeasurementThermal-image the cabinet area around the relay during sustained operation to check for excessive ambient heat contributing to the condition.
  5. DecisionContamination/corrosion found → clean and verify free movement. Return spring confirmed weak → replace the relay. Excessive cabinet heat found with no other relay defect → address cabinet cooling (see Division 05) as the underlying cause.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to relay contamination, a weakened return spring, contact tacking, or excessive ambient heat.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific mechanical cause and verify clean, prompt switching after correction.
Test Points
Relay armature and contact surfaces
Return spring condition
Cabinet ambient temperature near the relay
Step-change transition timing (logged)
Root Cause Verification

Cycle the affected relay through repeated step-change commands after correction and confirm prompt, clean, and consistent release and re-engagement with no delayed or intermittent transitions.

Corrective Action
  • Clean and inspect the relay armature and contact surfaces; verify free mechanical movement.
  • Replace the relay if the return spring or contacts are confirmed degraded.
  • Improve cabinet cooling/ventilation if excessive ambient heat is a contributing factor.
  • Replace the relay if nearing end of rated mechanical life.
Preventive Action
  • Include a mechanical free-movement check of step relays in the annual PM.
  • Track relay age/switching count against manufacturer rated mechanical life.
  • Address cabinet cooling deficiencies proactively rather than only after a relay-sticking event.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-08 (Intensity Step Commissioning), SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, Step Relay Assembly Drawing

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue

04 · CCR Protection & Alarms

15 of 15 topics published
CCR-056 CCR Earth Fault Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises an earth fault (ground fault) alarm and trips output, indicating leakage current from the series circuit or internal wiring to earth has exceeded the protection threshold.

Equipment / System

CCR earth fault protection relay/sensor (core balance CT or internal earth leakage monitor), series circuit loop, internal wiring.

Possible Causes
HighDegraded insulation on the series circuit cable or an isolating transformer allowing leakage current to earth
HighWater ingress at a cable joint, pull box, or fixture allowing a conductive path to earth
MediumDamaged or pinched cable insulation from installation or excavation work
MediumInternal CCR wiring insulation breakdown or moisture in the cabinet
LowerEarth fault relay/sensor itself drifted or miscalibrated, giving a false trip
LowerA minor transient switching surge tripping a tightly set threshold
Required Tools
Insulation resistance tester (5kV megger)Earth fault locator/loop testerTrue-RMS clamp meterMultimeterSeries circuit as-built drawing
Safety Precautions
  • Treat an earth fault trip as a genuine safety event until proven otherwise — do not repeatedly reset without investigation, as it may indicate a live conductor in contact with a person-accessible surface.
  • Apply LOTO before loop testing.
  • Use insulated tools and PPE rated for the loop's potential voltage.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the earth fault alarm/trip and any fault-current magnitude reported by the controller.
  2. MeasurementWith the CCR isolated, megger the full series circuit loop insulation resistance to earth and compare against baseline commissioning values.
  3. MeasurementIf insulation resistance is low, segment-test the loop (pull boxes/junctions) to localise the affected section.
  4. ObservationInspect suspect sections for visible water ingress, cable damage, or fixture/isolating transformer failure.
  5. MeasurementVerify the earth fault relay/sensor calibration and threshold setting against the design spec.
  6. DecisionLow insulation resistance confirmed in a specific segment → genuine earth fault, proceed to repair. Insulation resistance normal across the loop → relay/sensor calibration issue or nuisance trip, investigate threshold setting and sensor health.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific cable segment, connector, isolating transformer, or the earth fault relay/sensor itself.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the precise point of insulation breakdown by physical inspection once localised.
Test Points
Series circuit loop insulation resistance to earth (segment by segment)
Earth fault relay/sensor threshold and calibration
Suspect pull boxes/junctions
Isolating transformer insulation
Root Cause Verification

After repair, re-megger the full loop and confirm insulation resistance meets or exceeds the design minimum; run the CCR through a full load cycle with no repeat trip.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the damaged cable/connector/isolating transformer.
  • Dry and reseal a water-ingress point.
  • Recalibrate or replace the earth fault relay/sensor.
  • Adjust the threshold only within manufacturer-approved limits and with documented justification.
Preventive Action
  • Include loop insulation resistance testing (megger) in the annual PM, trended against baseline.
  • Seal cable joints and pull boxes to industry standard to prevent water ingress.
  • Verify earth fault relay calibration during scheduled maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing), SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822), IS 7785

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-057 CCR Overcurrent Alarm

Symptom — CCR trips on an overcurrent alarm, with output current exceeding the protection threshold before the controller shuts down the bridge.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage, current feedback sensor, overcurrent protection relay/logic.

Possible Causes
HighGenuine short-circuit or low-impedance fault on the series circuit loop causing an actual overcurrent
HighCurrent feedback sensor faulty/miscalibrated, causing the controller to over-drive the bridge trying to reach a falsely-low reading, resulting in true overcurrent
MediumOvercurrent threshold set too tight for the circuit's normal inrush/startup profile
MediumBridge firing circuit fault causing an uncontrolled conduction angle
LowerTransient surge/lightning-induced current spike tripping protection correctly
Required Tools
True-RMS clamp meterOscilloscopeInsulation resistance testerMultimeterCCR configuration/parameter tool
Safety Precautions
  • An overcurrent trip may indicate an active short circuit — do not reset without investigation, as repeated fault-current interruption can damage protection devices and pose a fire risk.
  • Apply LOTO before loop or bridge inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationReview the event log for the exact trip current value, timestamp, and whether the trip occurred at start-up or under steady-state run.
  2. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, megger and continuity-test the series circuit loop to check for a genuine short/low-impedance fault.
  3. MeasurementClamp-meter the actual output current on a controlled restart attempt (if safe) and compare against the HMI-reported value.
  4. MeasurementCheck current feedback sensor output and wiring against expected values.
  5. ObservationReview the overcurrent threshold setting against the manufacturer's recommended value for the installed circuit.
  6. DecisionLow loop insulation/resistance confirmed → genuine short circuit, proceed to segment isolation. Loop tests healthy but sensor/HMI mismatch found → feedback sensor fault. Loop and sensor both healthy → threshold too tight or a genuine transient event.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the series circuit loop, the current feedback sensor, or the protection threshold configuration.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component or configuration error.
Test Points
Series circuit loop insulation resistance and continuity
Current feedback sensor output
Overcurrent threshold parameter
Bridge firing signals
Root Cause Verification

After repair, run the CCR through several start/stop cycles and confirm output current tracks the commanded step with no repeat trip.

Corrective Action
  • Repair the short-circuit fault on the loop.
  • Replace or recalibrate the current feedback sensor.
  • Adjust the overcurrent threshold only within manufacturer limits with documented justification.
  • Repair the firing circuit if confirmed faulty.
Preventive Action
  • Include loop insulation/continuity testing in the PM programme.
  • Verify current feedback sensor calibration annually.
  • Document any threshold changes through change control.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Standards: ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic, CCR Protection Schematic

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-058 CCR Overvoltage Alarm

Symptom — CCR trips on an internal overvoltage protection alarm, with the controller detecting a voltage (input, DC bus, or output) above the protection threshold and shutting down the output.

Equipment / System

CCR internal overvoltage protection relay/monitoring circuit, DC bus/output voltage sensing.

Possible Causes
HighA genuine sustained input overvoltage condition (see CCR-005) reaching the internal protection threshold
HighVoltage sensing circuit fault causing a false high reading
MediumTransient voltage spike/surge event (lightning-induced or switching transient) exceeding the instantaneous threshold
MediumOutput transformer tap set incorrectly, causing developed voltage to exceed the protection ceiling under normal load
LowerOvervoltage threshold configured incorrectly for the installed equipment rating
Required Tools
Multimeter with min/max holdPower quality analyzerOscilloscopeCCR configuration/parameter toolCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Do not repeatedly reset an overvoltage trip without investigation — sustained overvoltage can damage internal components and reduce insulation life.
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationReview the event log for the exact trip voltage, timestamp, and whether it correlates with a known switching or supply event.
  2. MeasurementIndependently measure input voltage at the CCR terminals over a representative period to confirm whether a genuine input overvoltage exists (cross-reference CCR-005).
  3. MeasurementVerify the internal voltage sensing circuit reading against an independent meter at the same point.
  4. ObservationCheck for correlation with known transient events (nearby switching, thunderstorm activity, generator changeover).
  5. MeasurementVerify the overvoltage threshold and output transformer tap setting against design documentation.
  6. DecisionIndependent measurement confirms genuine sustained overvoltage → escalate to upstream supply/generator issue (CCR-005). Independent measurement normal but relay trips → sensing circuit fault or threshold misconfiguration. Isolated transient correlating with a known event → protection operated correctly on a real transient.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the upstream supply, the internal voltage sensing circuit, or the threshold/tap configuration.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through comparative measurement.
Test Points
CCR input terminals (independent meter)
Internal voltage sensing circuit output
Overvoltage threshold parameter
Output transformer tap setting
Root Cause Verification

After correction, monitor voltage over a representative operating period, including any known transient-prone conditions, and confirm no repeat trip.

Corrective Action
  • Address the upstream overvoltage cause per CCR-005.
  • Repair or recalibrate the internal voltage sensing circuit.
  • Correct the transformer tap setting.
  • Adjust the threshold only within manufacturer-approved limits.
Preventive Action
  • Include a voltage sensing accuracy check in periodic PM.
  • Ensure surge protection is installed and maintained per CCR-063.
  • Document threshold settings and any changes through change control.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Standards: IEC 60364, IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Protection Schematic, CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-059 CCR Undervoltage Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises an undervoltage alarm and trips or derates output while running, with input or internal supply voltage falling below the protection threshold during operation rather than at start-up.

Equipment / System

CCR undervoltage protection relay/monitoring circuit, input supply, control power supply.

Possible Causes
HighA genuine sag/dip on the input supply during operation, e.g. from a large coincident load starting elsewhere on the feeder
HighVoltage sensing circuit fault causing a false low reading
MediumLoose or degrading input terminal connection developing resistance and dropping voltage under load
MediumUndervoltage threshold set too tight relative to the site's normal supply variation
LowerGenerator/standby supply voltage sagging during a load transfer or under generator loading
Required Tools
Multimeter with min/max holdPower quality analyzer/voltage loggerClamp meterCCR wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV measurement precautions apply.
  • Do not force-restart repeatedly against an active undervoltage condition, as running at reduced voltage can stress the regulator and connected fixtures.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationReview the event log for the exact trip voltage, duration, and timestamp.
  2. MeasurementLog input voltage independently at the CCR terminals over a representative period, including the timestamp of the trip.
  3. MeasurementCompare against the upstream distribution panel voltage logged at the same time to isolate source versus feeder-side sag.
  4. MeasurementInspect and torque-check input terminal connections for looseness/heating.
  5. ObservationVerify the undervoltage threshold setting against the manufacturer's recommended value and the site's documented supply tolerance.
  6. DecisionSag confirmed at the panel too → upstream supply issue, escalate per CCR-004 methodology. Panel voltage normal but CCR terminal voltage sags → loose connection/feeder-side issue. Independently logged voltage stays normal despite a trip → sensing circuit fault or threshold too tight.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the upstream supply, a loose terminal connection, or the internal sensing/threshold configuration.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through comparative logging.
Test Points
Upstream distribution panel voltage
CCR input terminals (independent logger)
Input terminal connections
Undervoltage threshold parameter
Root Cause Verification

Re-log voltage under full load, including peak-demand periods, after correction and confirm it stays within tolerance with no repeat trip.

Corrective Action
  • Rectify loose/high-resistance connections.
  • Escalate and address a confirmed upstream sag.
  • Repair or recalibrate the sensing circuit.
  • Adjust the threshold only within manufacturer-approved limits with documented justification.
Preventive Action
  • Include a voltage-drop/logging survey in the PM programme.
  • Perform periodic thermal imaging of input terminals.
  • Coordinate with the utility/generator team on known load-shedding or transfer events.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-CCR-10

Standards: IEC 60364, FAA AC 150/5345-10

Diagram: Feeder Cable Route Drawing, CCR Protection Schematic

Case Study: —

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-060 CCR Overtemperature Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises an overtemperature alarm and derates or trips output, with an internal temperature sensor (heatsink, bridge, or cabinet) reporting a value above the protection threshold.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage heatsink, internal temperature sensor(s), cooling system.

Possible Causes
HighCooling fan failure or degraded airflow reducing heat dissipation (see CCR-066)
HighBlocked/dirty ventilation filters or vents restricting airflow
MediumAmbient temperature at the installation location exceeding the CCR's rated operating range
MediumTemperature sensor faulty/miscalibrated, giving a false high reading
LowerBridge device degradation increasing internal power dissipation/heat generation for a given output
LowerOvertemperature threshold set too conservatively relative to the manufacturer's actual rating
Required Tools
Thermal imaging cameraMultimeterSensor calibration referenceCooling system inspection tools
Safety Precautions
  • Do not repeatedly reset an overtemperature trip and continue running — this risks accelerated component degradation or fire.
  • Allow the unit to cool and investigate before restarting.
  • Apply LOTO before internal cooling system inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationReview the event log for the exact trip temperature, sensor location, and timestamp.
  2. ObservationConfirm cooling fan operation and airflow at the intake/exhaust.
  3. MeasurementInspect and clean/replace ventilation filters and check for blocked vents.
  4. MeasurementThermal-image the heatsink/bridge and cabinet during a sustained run (where safe) to confirm the actual temperature distribution.
  5. MeasurementIndependently verify the temperature sensor reading against a calibrated reference where practical.
  6. DecisionFan not running or airflow blocked → cooling system fault (see CCR-066/067). Cooling confirmed healthy but temperature still high → ambient conditions or bridge device degradation. Thermal imaging shows normal temperature but the alarm persists → sensor fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the cooling system, ambient/installation conditions, the bridge devices, or the temperature sensor.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and verify temperature returns to normal operating range after correction.
Test Points
Cooling fan operation
Ventilation filter/vent condition
Heatsink/bridge temperature (thermal image)
Temperature sensor calibration
Root Cause Verification

Run the CCR at full commanded step for a minimum of one hour after correction and confirm temperature remains within the normal operating range with no repeat alarm.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the failed cooling fan.
  • Clean or replace blocked filters/vents.
  • Improve cabinet ventilation/installation conditions if ambient is a factor.
  • Recalibrate or replace the temperature sensor.
  • Replace degraded bridge devices if confirmed as the heat source.
Preventive Action
  • Include cooling fan and filter inspection/cleaning in routine PM.
  • Schedule periodic thermal imaging of the power stage.
  • Verify temperature sensor calibration annually.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance), SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Standards: IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic, Cooling System Layout

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-061 CCR Transformer Temperature Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises a transformer (output/isolation) temperature alarm, with a dedicated winding or oil/air temperature sensor on the output transformer reporting a value above the protection threshold.

Equipment / System

CCR output transformer, embedded winding temperature sensor (RTD/thermocouple/thermostat), transformer cooling (natural or forced air).

Possible Causes
HighTransformer overloaded relative to its rated capacity for the connected circuit length/load
HighTransformer cooling airflow restricted (dust, blocked vents, failed cooling fan where fitted)
MediumTransformer winding insulation degrading, increasing internal losses and heat generation
MediumTemperature sensor/RTD faulty or its wiring to the controller damaged, giving a false reading
LowerAmbient temperature in the transformer compartment exceeding design conditions
LowerTransformer tap set incorrectly, causing it to operate outside its optimal efficiency point and generate excess heat
Required Tools
Thermal imaging cameraInsulation resistance tester (5kV)MultimeterTransformer nameplate/rating referenceRTD/sensor test tool
Safety Precautions
  • A genuinely overheating transformer is a fire risk — do not defer investigation or repeatedly reset the alarm.
  • Apply LOTO before any transformer inspection.
  • Allow adequate cooling time before physical inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationReview the event log for the exact trip temperature, sensor location, and duration of the condition before trip.
  2. MeasurementThermal-image the transformer housing/compartment during a sustained run (where safe) to confirm actual temperature and identify hot spots.
  3. MeasurementWith the unit isolated, verify the transformer tap setting against the documented circuit length/load and megger the winding insulation.
  4. MeasurementCheck the temperature sensor/RTD and its wiring for correct resistance/output against the manufacturer's reference table.
  5. ObservationInspect the transformer compartment for dust accumulation or restricted airflow.
  6. DecisionThermal imaging confirms genuine elevated temperature correlating with load/tap mismatch → transformer overload or tap misconfiguration. Thermal imaging normal but alarm persists → sensor/wiring fault. Insulation resistance below baseline → developing transformer insulation fault, escalate for transformer replacement.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to transformer loading/tap configuration, restricted cooling, degrading insulation, or the sensor circuit.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through direct thermal and insulation testing.
Test Points
Transformer winding temperature sensor output
Transformer housing (thermal image)
Transformer tap terminals
Winding insulation resistance
Root Cause Verification

Run the CCR at full commanded step for a sustained period after correction and confirm transformer temperature stabilizes within the normal operating range with no repeat alarm.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the transformer tap setting for the actual load.
  • Clean/restore transformer compartment airflow.
  • Replace the transformer if insulation degradation is confirmed.
  • Repair or replace the faulty sensor/RTD and wiring.
Preventive Action
  • Include transformer thermal imaging and insulation testing in the annual PM.
  • Verify tap setting whenever circuit configuration changes.
  • Keep the transformer compartment clean and ventilated.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Series Circuit Loop Testing), SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance)

Standards: IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822), IS 12290

Diagram: CCR Power Stage Schematic, Transformer Nameplate/Rating Sheet

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-062 CCR Door Interlock Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises a door interlock alarm — either preventing/tripping a run because a cabinet door is open or the interlock switch is faulty, or, less commonly, falsely indicating an open door while the door is actually closed and latched.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet door interlock switch(es), interlock wiring, controller interlock input.

Possible Causes
HighCabinet door genuinely open or not fully latched
HighInterlock switch misaligned, worn, or physically damaged, failing to make contact even with the door closed
MediumInterlock switch wiring loose, broken, or corroded
MediumDoor hinge/latch mechanism worn, preventing the door from seating correctly against the switch actuator
LowerController interlock input circuit fault, ignoring or misreading a healthy switch signal
Required Tools
MultimeterContinuity testerReplacement interlock switchAlignment/adjustment toolsTorque screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Never bypass or defeat a door interlock to force a start — it exists to prevent access to live high-voltage components.
  • Confirm the actual physical door/switch condition before any electrical testing.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationPhysically inspect the door, latch, and interlock switch alignment with the door closed.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated, check continuity across the interlock switch in both the door-open and door-closed positions.
  3. MeasurementInspect interlock wiring from the switch to the controller for looseness, damage, or corrosion.
  4. ObservationCheck for physical wear on the door hinge/latch preventing correct seating against the switch actuator.
  5. DecisionSwitch fails continuity test when door is closed → switch/alignment fault. Switch tests correctly but the controller still shows the alarm → wiring or controller input fault. Door genuinely not closing/latching → mechanical door/latch fault.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the interlock switch, its wiring, the controller input, or the door/latch mechanism.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component by direct testing and physical inspection.
Test Points
Interlock switch contacts (door open/closed)
Interlock wiring continuity
Controller interlock input
Door latch/hinge alignment
Root Cause Verification

After repair, cycle the door open and closed several times and confirm the interlock reliably and correctly reflects the door state with no false alarms.

Corrective Action
  • Realign or replace the faulty interlock switch.
  • Repair the interlock wiring.
  • Adjust or repair the door hinge/latch mechanism.
  • Repair the controller interlock input if confirmed faulty.
Preventive Action
  • Include a door interlock functional test in the monthly PM.
  • Lubricate and inspect door hinges/latches periodically.
  • Keep a spare interlock switch in site stores.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist), SOP-SAFETY-03 (E-Stop Functional Test)

Standards: IEC 60204-1

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic, Cabinet Layout Drawing

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-063 CCR Surge Protection Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises a surge protection device (SPD) alarm/fault indication, typically showing the SPD has operated or reached end-of-life, or the SPD status monitoring circuit reports a fault.

Equipment / System

CCR input/output surge protection devices (SPDs), SPD status monitoring circuit.

Possible Causes
HighSPD has absorbed a genuine surge event (lightning-induced or switching transient) and reached end-of-life, opening its status contact
HighSPD degraded over time from repeated smaller transients, triggering an end-of-life indication
MediumSPD status monitoring wiring loose or damaged, giving a false fault indication
MediumSPD module not correctly seated/installed after a previous replacement
LowerController SPD status input circuit fault
Required Tools
MultimeterSPD manufacturer test/status referenceReplacement SPD moduleTorque screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • A tripped/failed SPD leaves the equipment without transient protection — treat as a priority repair rather than deferring, particularly ahead of lightning season.
  • Apply LOTO before replacing an SPD module.
  • Verify zero energy before removing an SPD, as some designs retain charge.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationCheck the SPD's visual status indicator (if fitted) for a green/healthy or red/failed condition.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated, verify the SPD status monitoring contact/circuit continuity.
  3. ObservationReview the site's recent lightning/surge activity or switching event history to correlate with the alarm.
  4. MeasurementConfirm the SPD module is correctly seated and its connections are secure.
  5. DecisionSPD visual indicator confirms failed/end-of-life → replace the SPD module. Indicator shows healthy but the controller still alarms → monitoring wiring/controller input fault. Loose/unseated module found → reseat and re-test.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the SPD module itself, its status monitoring wiring, or the controller input circuit.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by direct inspection and testing.
Test Points
SPD visual status indicator
SPD status monitoring contact
SPD module seating/connections
Controller SPD status input
Root Cause Verification

After replacement/repair, confirm the SPD status indicates healthy and the controller alarm clears and does not recur across a monitoring period.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed/end-of-life SPD module with the correct manufacturer-specified type and rating.
  • Repair the status monitoring wiring.
  • Reseat a loose SPD module.
  • Repair the controller SPD status input if confirmed faulty.
Preventive Action
  • Include SPD visual/status inspection in routine PM, particularly before monsoon/lightning season.
  • Maintain SPD replacement spares in site stores.
  • Track SPD replacement history to identify sites prone to repeated surge events.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-05 (Spares Management), SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-064 CCR Internal Fault Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises a generic internal fault alarm during steady-state run (not specifically at start-up), indicating a detected fault condition within the controller or power stage that isn't mapped to one of the more specific named alarms.

Equipment / System

CCR controller and internal monitored subsystems, generic fault detection logic.

Possible Causes
HighA monitored internal parameter (voltage, current, or temperature at an internal test point) briefly excursing outside its expected range during run
HighInternal communication bus fault between controller sub-modules during operation
MediumFirmware fault/exception triggering a generic fault flag without a specific mapped cause
MediumA marginal/intermittent internal component developing a fault under sustained operating stress
LowerElectrical noise/interference affecting internal monitoring circuits
Required Tools
CCR controller diagnostic/service toolMultimeterManufacturer internal fault code referenceOscilloscope
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV/control circuit precautions apply.
  • Do not bypass a generic internal fault alarm — it exists to flag a detected abnormal condition even if not individually named.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the exact internal fault code/message and the time/operating condition at which it occurred.
  2. ObservationCross-reference the fault code against the manufacturer's internal fault code reference to identify the flagged subsystem.
  3. MeasurementTest the specific flagged subsystem per manufacturer guidance.
  4. MeasurementReview the controller's internal diagnostic/communication logs for correlating events.
  5. DecisionConfirmed fault in a specific flagged subsystem → component-level repair/replacement. Fault clears after a power cycle and does not recur → likely a transient/intermittent condition, monitor closely and escalate if it recurs.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific internal module/subsystem flagged by the fault code.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through targeted subsystem testing rather than accepting a generic fault code at face value.
Test Points
As specified by the manufacturer's internal fault code reference for the flagged subsystem
Internal communication bus signals
Root Cause Verification

After remedial action, run the CCR through multiple sustained operating cycles and confirm the fault does not recur.

Corrective Action
  • Replace or repair the specific faulty internal component/module identified.
  • Reflash/update controller firmware if a firmware fault is confirmed.
  • Escalate to the manufacturer for an unresolved or recurring generic fault code.
Preventive Action
  • Keep firmware documentation and fault code references current.
  • Track recurring generic fault codes in the site failure database to catch developing problems early.
  • Include internal diagnostic log review in periodic PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02, SOP-CCR-06 (Repeated Fault Investigation Procedure — cross-reference CCR-015)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-065 CCR Communication Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises a communication alarm indicating loss of, or fault in, its data link to ALCMS/PLC or another monitoring system, while the CCR itself may continue operating locally.

Equipment / System

CCR communication interface (serial/Ethernet/fieldbus), ALCMS/PLC link, associated cabling and network infrastructure.

Possible Causes
HighCommunication cable disconnected, damaged, or degraded between the CCR and ALCMS/PLC
HighALCMS/PLC-side communication port, card, or software fault
MediumIncorrect communication parameters (baud rate, address, protocol settings) after a configuration change
MediumNetwork switch/media converter fault on an Ethernet-based link
LowerElectrical noise/interference on the communication cable, especially if not properly shielded/segregated from power cabling
LowerCCR-side communication interface/card hardware fault
Required Tools
MultimeterProtocol analyzer/serial monitorCable testerNetwork diagnostic tool (for Ethernet links)CCR wiring/network diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Standard LV/control circuit precautions apply.
  • Confirm the CCR's actual local run/output status independently before assuming a communication alarm reflects a broader operational fault.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the CCR is otherwise operating normally locally, to distinguish a communication-only fault from a broader control fault.
  2. MeasurementCheck the physical communication cable/connector at both the CCR and ALCMS/PLC ends for damage or disconnection.
  3. MeasurementVerify communication parameters (address, baud rate, protocol) match on both ends.
  4. ObservationCheck the status of intermediate network equipment (switches, media converters) on the link.
  5. MeasurementWhere possible, monitor the communication link directly for traffic/errors.
  6. DecisionPhysical cable/connector fault found → repair/replace. Parameters mismatched → correct configuration on the appropriate end. Intermediate network equipment faulty → repair/replace. Link tests healthy at the physical/protocol level but the alarm persists → CCR or ALCMS-side interface card fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the communication cable, network equipment, configuration mismatch, or an interface card at either end.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through targeted link testing.
Test Points
CCR communication port/connector
ALCMS/PLC communication port/connector
Intermediate network equipment
Communication parameter configuration on both ends
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm stable, error-free communication over a sustained monitoring period and correct data exchange between the CCR and ALCMS/PLC.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the damaged communication cable/connector.
  • Correct communication parameter configuration.
  • Replace faulty network equipment.
  • Replace a faulty communication interface card.
Preventive Action
  • Include communication link testing in routine PM.
  • Ensure communication cabling is properly shielded and segregated from power cabling.
  • Document and version-control communication configuration settings.

SOP: SOP-ALCMS-02, SOP-CCR-11 (Communication Link Testing)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-066 CCR Fan Failure Alarm

Symptom — CCR raises a cooling fan failure alarm, indicating one or more cooling fans have stopped, are running below expected speed, or their status feedback is not confirming operation.

Equipment / System

CCR internal/cabinet cooling fan(s), fan status feedback circuit (tachometer or airflow sensor).

Possible Causes
HighFan motor failed (bearing seizure, winding failure) and stopped completely
HighFan blocked by debris/dust preventing rotation despite a healthy motor
MediumFan power supply/wiring fault, cutting power to the fan
MediumFan status feedback sensor/wiring faulty, giving a false failure indication despite the fan actually running
LowerFan speed controller (if variable-speed) fault, causing the fan to run below the threshold needed to clear the alarm
Required Tools
MultimeterClamp meterReplacement fan of correct ratingTachometer/anemometerCleaning tools
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before accessing or replacing a fan — fan blades can cause injury and internal components may remain live.
  • Allow the cabinet to cool if overtemperature is also present before extended internal work.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationVisually/audibly confirm whether the fan is actually rotating.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated, check fan motor winding resistance/continuity.
  3. MeasurementVerify supply voltage is present at the fan connector when commanded to run.
  4. MeasurementIf the fan appears to run normally, check the fan status feedback sensor and its wiring for a fault causing a false alarm.
  5. ObservationInspect for physical blockage/debris preventing rotation.
  6. DecisionFan not rotating with confirmed supply present → motor/mechanical fault. No supply reaching the fan → wiring/power supply fault. Fan confirmed running normally but the alarm persists → feedback sensor/wiring fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the fan motor, its power supply/wiring, or the status feedback circuit.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component.
Test Points
Fan power supply/connector
Fan motor winding resistance
Fan status feedback sensor output
Fan mounting/blockage
Root Cause Verification

After replacement/repair, confirm the fan runs reliably and the status feedback correctly clears the alarm across a power-cycle test and a sustained run period.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed fan.
  • Clear a physical blockage.
  • Repair the fan power supply/wiring.
  • Repair or replace the faulty status feedback sensor.
Preventive Action
  • Include fan operation and cleaning in routine PM.
  • Track fan run-hours and replace preventively based on manufacturer MTBF data.
  • Keep spare fans in site stores.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance), SOP-CCR-05 (Spares Management)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-067 CCR Cooling Failure

Symptom — CCR's overall cooling system is confirmed inadequate — internal temperatures trend upward under load despite fans appearing to run, indicating a broader cooling deficiency rather than a single fan failure.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet cooling system as a whole — fans, filters, vents, ducting, and (where fitted) heat exchanger.

Possible Causes
HighVentilation filters/vents heavily blocked with dust/debris, restricting airflow despite functioning fans
HighCabinet installed in a location with inadequate clearance for airflow, or in direct sun/high ambient without adequate mitigation
MediumFan(s) running but undersized/degraded output insufficient for the actual heat load
MediumInternal air recirculation due to a damaged or missing baffle/duct, causing hot exhaust air to be redrawn into the intake
LowerHeat exchanger (on liquid or forced-air designs) fouled or degraded, reducing heat rejection capacity
Required Tools
Thermal imaging cameraAnemometer/airflow meterCleaning toolsClamp meterManufacturer cooling system specification
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection or cleaning.
  • Allow adequate cooling time before extended internal work following a cooling failure event.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm all fans are individually running and check their airflow output with an anemometer.
  2. MeasurementInspect and clean/replace filters and check all vents/ducts for blockage.
  3. MeasurementThermal-image the cabinet interior during a sustained run to identify areas of poor airflow or recirculation.
  4. ObservationCheck cabinet installation clearances and exposure against manufacturer siting requirements.
  5. MeasurementIf fitted, inspect the heat exchanger for fouling or degraded performance.
  6. DecisionFans individually healthy but overall airflow low → blocked filters/vents or ducting fault. Recirculation confirmed by thermal imaging → baffle/duct repair needed. Installation clearance/siting inadequate → site modification required.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to filters/vents, ducting/baffles, fan capacity, siting, or the heat exchanger.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific deficiency through airflow and thermal measurement.
Test Points
Filter/vent condition
Fan airflow output (individually)
Cabinet internal air temperature distribution (thermal image)
Installation clearances
Heat exchanger condition (if fitted)
Root Cause Verification

Run the CCR at full commanded step for a sustained period after correction and confirm internal temperatures stabilize within the normal operating range with adequate margin.

Corrective Action
  • Clean/replace filters and clear blocked vents/ducts.
  • Repair or install baffles to prevent recirculation.
  • Improve cabinet siting/clearance per manufacturer requirements.
  • Clean or repair the heat exchanger.
  • Upgrade fan capacity if confirmed undersized.
Preventive Action
  • Include a comprehensive cooling system inspection (not just fan check) in the PM programme.
  • Review siting during any relocation or nearby construction.
  • Trend internal temperature over time to catch gradual cooling degradation.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-09 (Cooling System Maintenance)

Standards: IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-068 CCR Protection Relay Failure

Symptom — A specific CCR protection relay (earth fault, overcurrent, overvoltage, etc.) is confirmed to have failed — either failing to trip under a genuine fault condition, or tripping/latching with no measurable fault present and not responding correctly to reset or test.

Equipment / System

CCR protection relay(s) — electromechanical or electronic — and their associated sensors/wiring.

Possible Causes
HighInternal relay electronic/mechanical failure — component degradation or a failed output contact
HighRelay firmware/configuration corrupted, causing incorrect trip behaviour
MediumRelay power supply fault, causing erratic or no operation
MediumInput sensor (CT, VT, or transducer) feeding the relay has failed, causing the relay to act on incorrect data
LowerRelay test/reset function itself faulty, masking an otherwise healthy relay
Required Tools
Relay test set (secondary injection where available)MultimeterManufacturer relay test procedureCCR configuration/parameter tool
Safety Precautions
  • A relay that fails to trip under a genuine fault is a serious safety risk — treat any confirmed relay malfunction as high priority.
  • Apply LOTO before relay testing or replacement.
  • Do not rely on a suspect relay to protect personnel during other testing.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationDocument the specific relay function affected and the exact nature of the malfunction (fails to trip, false trip, fails to reset).
  2. MeasurementPerform a manufacturer-specified functional/injection test on the relay to confirm actual trip behaviour against its rated setpoint.
  3. MeasurementVerify the relay's input sensor (CT/VT/transducer) is providing correct, healthy signals.
  4. MeasurementCheck the relay's power supply and configuration/firmware against the commissioned baseline.
  5. DecisionRelay fails a proper functional/injection test → confirmed relay fault, replace. Relay passes functional test but the field symptom persists → input sensor or wiring fault, not the relay itself. Configuration found altered from baseline → correct configuration and re-test.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the relay itself, its input sensor, its power supply, or its configuration.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through direct functional testing rather than assumption.
Test Points
Relay trip output under injected test condition
Relay input sensor (CT/VT/transducer) signal
Relay power supply
Relay configuration/firmware version
Root Cause Verification

After replacement/repair, perform a full functional/injection test confirming correct trip and reset behaviour at the rated setpoint before returning the CCR to service.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed protection relay.
  • Repair the relay power supply.
  • Replace the faulty input sensor.
  • Restore relay configuration to the commissioned baseline.
Preventive Action
  • Include protection relay functional/injection testing in the annual PM — do not rely solely on the absence of trips as confirmation of health.
  • Lock relay configuration after commissioning and log any authorized changes.
  • Maintain relay test records for trending.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Standards: IEC 60255
