Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-069 False CCR Alarm

Symptom — CCR displays an active alarm (of any protection type) with no corresponding real-world fault condition found on thorough investigation — the alarm does not correlate with any measurable abnormal parameter.

Equipment / System

CCR alarm/protection logic broadly — sensors, wiring, and controller logic across all protection functions.

Possible Causes
HighA specific sensor (current, voltage, temperature, etc.) has drifted out of calibration, reporting an incorrect value that crosses the alarm threshold
HighSensor wiring loose, corroded, or picking up electrical noise, producing spurious readings
MediumAlarm threshold set too tight relative to normal operating variation, causing legitimate but nuisance trips
MediumController software/firmware bug misinterpreting a healthy signal as a fault condition
LowerElectromagnetic interference from nearby equipment affecting sensor or signal wiring
Required Tools
Calibrated reference meter/instrument matching the alarmed parameterOscilloscopeMultimeterCCR configuration/parameter toolManufacturer alarm code reference
Safety Precautions
  • Do not simply mask or disable an alarm believed to be false without confirming this through proper investigation — a genuinely intermittent real fault can mimic a false alarm.
  • Apply LOTO before sensor/wiring inspection.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationIdentify the specific alarm raised and the exact parameter/threshold that triggered it, from the event log.
  2. MeasurementIndependently and simultaneously measure the actual parameter (voltage, current, temperature, etc.) using a calibrated reference instrument at the same point the sensor monitors.
  3. MeasurementInspect the relevant sensor wiring for looseness, corrosion, or routing near noise sources.
  4. ObservationReview whether the alarm threshold is appropriately set relative to the site's normal operating variation, per manufacturer guidance.
  5. DecisionIndependent measurement confirms the parameter was genuinely at the alarmed value → not a false alarm, investigate as a real fault per the relevant specific topic. Independent measurement shows the parameter was normal → confirmed false alarm, proceed to isolate sensor/wiring/threshold/firmware cause.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific sensor, its wiring, the alarm threshold configuration, or a controller firmware issue.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through calibrated comparative measurement — never conclude "false alarm" without independent verification.
Test Points
The specific sensor relevant to the alarmed parameter
Sensor wiring at both ends
Alarm threshold configuration
Controller firmware version
Root Cause Verification

After correction, monitor the CCR through a representative operating period and confirm the specific alarm does not recur while genuine fault detection remains intact (verified by controlled test if appropriate).

Corrective Action
  • Recalibrate or replace the drifted sensor.
  • Repair the sensor wiring.
  • Adjust the threshold only within manufacturer-approved limits with documented justification.
  • Update controller firmware if a software bug is confirmed by the manufacturer.
Preventive Action
  • Include sensor calibration checks across all protection functions in the annual PM.
  • Document threshold settings and require change control for any adjustment.
  • Investigate every alarm occurrence — do not develop a habit of dismissing alarms as "probably false."
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-070 Repeated CCR Protection Trip

Symptom — The CCR trips repeatedly on the same or varying protection alarms over multiple operating cycles, rather than a single isolated trip event, indicating either an unresolved underlying fault or a genuinely intermittent condition.

Equipment / System

CCR, all protection subsystems — investigation spans the full protection and alarm chain.

Possible Causes
HighAn underlying cause from a specific protection topic (CCR-056 through CCR-069) that has only been reset, not actually resolved
HighA genuinely intermittent fault — loose connection or marginal component — that passes isolated testing between trips
MediumA protection threshold set too tight for the equipment's normal operating envelope, causing repeated nuisance trips under otherwise healthy conditions
MediumA developing/degrading component (transformer, bridge device, sensor) that fails progressively under load, triggering different alarms at different times
LowerOperator repeatedly resetting and restarting without allowing proper investigation between trips
Required Tools
MultimeterData logger for trend/repeated-event analysisCCR event log export toolRelay test set
Safety Precautions
  • Repeated forced resets against an unresolved protection trip can cause component damage or create a genuine safety hazard — do not simply keep resetting and retrying without investigation.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationExport and review the CCR event/alarm log across all recent trips to determine whether the same specific alarm recurs each time or different alarms occur.
  2. DecisionSame specific alarm repeats → treat as that topic's fault not yet fully resolved; re-open the relevant investigation with more rigorous root cause verification. Different alarms occur at different times → suspect a common underlying cause (e.g. a marginal power supply or cooling deficiency) affecting multiple protection functions, or a genuinely intermittent condition per Division 22 methodology.
  3. MeasurementWhere an intermittent connection is suspected, perform a wiggle test — with power isolated — on suspect connectors/terminals while monitoring continuity.
  4. MeasurementReview whether protection thresholds are set appropriately relative to the equipment's normal operating envelope, per manufacturer guidance.
  5. Root CauseConfirm root cause with a sustained multi-cycle test under representative load conditions rather than a single successful run.
Test Points
As per the specific recurring alarm(s) identified in the event log
Root Cause Verification

Require a minimum of five consecutive successful full-load operating cycles, including under realistic field conditions, before closing out.

Corrective Action
  • Apply the specific recurring alarm's corrective action, with emphasis on thorough root cause verification rather than a quick reset.
  • Address a common underlying cause if multiple alarms trace back to one root issue.
Preventive Action
  • Make event log review a standing part of any repeated-trip investigation.
  • Track recurring alarm patterns in the site failure database.
  • Review protection threshold settings periodically against actual operating data.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Repeated Fault Investigation Procedure)

Rev 0 — Initial issue

05 · CCR Cooling & Internal Components

10 of 10 topics published
CCR-071 CCR Cooling Fan Not Working

Symptom — One or more internal cooling fans in the CCR cabinet fail to run when the unit is powered and under load, with no airflow detected at the fan outlet despite the fan being commanded on (continuously or via thermostatic control).

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet cooling fan(s), fan power supply/wiring, fan thermostat or controller-driven fan relay, heat sink and power electronics compartment.

Possible Causes
HighFan motor winding failure or seized bearing, preventing rotation even with supply present
HighBlown fan fuse or tripped fan circuit protection isolating fan supply
MediumFailed fan relay, thermostat switch, or controller output driving the fan
MediumBroken or disconnected fan power wiring/connector
LowerFan blade mechanically jammed by a foreign object or debris despite the motor being intact
Required Tools
True-RMS digital multimeterClamp meterInsulated screwdriver setFan power wiring diagramTachometer (optional)
Safety Precautions
  • Isolate and LOTO the CCR before opening the cabinet or reaching near the fan blade guard.
  • Allow the heat sink and power electronics to cool before close inspection, as surfaces may remain hot after shutdown.
  • Do not bypass fan protection or run the CCR at full load with cooling disabled to "test" — this risks thermal damage to the power stage.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationVisually and audibly confirm which fan(s) are not running while the unit is powered and commanded to cool.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated and verified dead, check the fan circuit fuse/breaker for continuity.
  3. MeasurementRestore power under controlled conditions and measure voltage at the fan connector terminals when the fan is commanded on.
  4. DecisionCorrect voltage present at the fan terminals but fan does not spin → fan motor/bearing fault. No voltage at the fan terminals → upstream relay, thermostat, wiring, or fuse fault.
  5. MeasurementIf voltage is absent, trace back through the fan relay/thermostat/controller output to locate the point where the command signal or supply is lost.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific fan motor, fan fuse, relay/thermostat, or wiring segment.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the failed component by isolated bench or in-circuit testing before replacement.
Test Points
Fan connector supply voltage
Fan circuit fuse/breaker continuity
Fan relay/thermostat output
Fan motor winding resistance
Root Cause Verification

After replacement/repair, confirm the fan runs continuously (or cycles correctly under thermostatic control) through a full load cycle, and verify airflow is present at the outlet.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed fan motor assembly.
  • Replace the blown fan fuse with the correct rating and type — do not upsize.
  • Replace the faulty relay, thermostat, or repair the controller output circuit.
  • Repair or replace damaged fan wiring/connector.
  • Clear any mechanical obstruction from the fan blade.
Preventive Action
  • Include a functional fan check (visual/audible run and airflow) in the routine PM schedule.
  • Track fan run-hours and replace preventively based on manufacturer service life.
  • Keep the cabinet interior clean to reduce the risk of debris jamming the fan.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-072 CCR Fan Running Continuously

Symptom — The CCR cooling fan(s) run continuously at full speed regardless of load or internal temperature, including at start-up and low intensity steps when cooling demand should be minimal.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet cooling fan(s), thermostat/temperature sensor, fan controller logic or relay.

Possible Causes
HighFan thermostat or temperature sensor stuck closed/failed, reporting a permanently high temperature
MediumFan relay contacts welded/stuck in the energized position
MediumController configured or defaulted to continuous-fan mode rather than thermostatic control
LowerGenuine elevated internal temperature due to a separate cooling deficiency (blocked filter/vents), causing the thermostat to correctly hold the fan on
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterCalibrated reference temperature probeCCR configuration/parameter toolFan wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before inspecting the thermostat, relay, or wiring inside the cabinet.
  • Do not disable the fan or force it off to "test" without first ruling out a genuine overtemperature condition.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the fan runs continuously across a range of load/intensity conditions, not only under genuinely high ambient or internal temperature.
  2. MeasurementIndependently measure internal cabinet/heat sink temperature with a calibrated reference probe and compare against the thermostat's reported/trip value.
  3. DecisionIndependent measurement confirms genuinely elevated temperature → investigate as a cooling deficiency (see CCR-074/075/076/077). Independent measurement shows normal temperature → thermostat/sensor, relay, or configuration fault.
  4. MeasurementIf temperature is normal, check thermostat/sensor continuity and calibration against manufacturer reference values.
  5. MeasurementCheck fan relay contacts for welding by removing the control signal and confirming the fan de-energizes.
  6. ObservationReview the controller configuration/parameter settings for fan operating mode (thermostatic vs continuous).
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the thermostat/sensor, the relay, or an incorrect configuration setting.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed or misconfigured component.
Test Points
Internal cabinet/heat sink temperature (reference measurement)
Thermostat/sensor continuity and setpoint
Fan relay contact state with signal removed
Fan operating mode configuration parameter
Root Cause Verification

After correction, confirm the fan cycles appropriately with internal temperature across at least one full representative operating period, including low-load conditions.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed thermostat/temperature sensor.
  • Replace the fan relay if contacts are welded or degraded.
  • Correct the controller configuration to the manufacturer-specified fan control mode.
  • If a genuine cooling deficiency is found, address the underlying blockage/ventilation fault.
Preventive Action
  • Include thermostat/sensor calibration checks in the annual PM.
  • Document fan control configuration and include it in commissioning/handover records.
  • Monitor fan run-hours to flag abnormal continuous operation trends early.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Diagram: CCR Cooling Fan Wiring Diagram

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-073 CCR Fan Starting Intermittently

Symptom — The CCR cooling fan starts and stops erratically, cycles on and off rapidly, or only runs intermittently rather than starting reliably and running continuously/thermostatically as designed.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet cooling fan, fan motor, thermostat/sensor, relay, and associated wiring/connectors.

Possible Causes
HighLoose or corroded fan power connector/terminal causing an intermittent circuit
HighDegrading fan motor bearing or winding causing intermittent starting under load
MediumMarginal or fluttering thermostat/relay contact repeatedly making and breaking near its setpoint
MediumFan capacitor (for capacitor-start motors) degrading, causing inconsistent starts
LowerVibration-induced intermittent connection at a poorly secured wiring run
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterData logger for trend/repeated-event analysisInsulated screwdriver setFan wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before performing any wiggle test or connector inspection with power isolated.
  • Do not attempt to diagnose intermittent faults by touching live fan wiring while energized.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationLog the pattern of fan starts/stops over a representative period to characterise the intermittency (random vs. load-related vs. temperature-related).
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated, perform a wiggle test on the fan power connector and wiring while monitoring continuity.
  3. MeasurementInspect and clean/tighten the fan connector and terminals, checking for corrosion or looseness.
  4. MeasurementCheck the thermostat/relay contact behaviour near its setpoint for contact flutter.
  5. MeasurementIf fitted, check the fan run/start capacitor's capacitance against its rated value.
  6. DecisionWiggle test reveals an intermittent connection → wiring/connector fault. Connector and wiring sound but fan still starts intermittently → motor bearing/winding or capacitor degradation.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific connector, wiring segment, thermostat/relay, or fan motor/capacitor.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the intermittent fault by reproducing it under controlled conditions where possible.
Test Points
Fan power connector/terminals (wiggle test)
Thermostat/relay contact behaviour at setpoint
Fan start/run capacitor (if fitted)
Fan motor winding resistance
Root Cause Verification

After repair, monitor fan operation through a sustained multi-cycle period and confirm consistent, reliable starting with no recurrence of intermittency.

Corrective Action
  • Clean, tighten, or replace the fan connector/terminals.
  • Repair or re-secure fan wiring found to be loose or vibration-damaged.
  • Replace the fan motor or start/run capacitor if degraded.
  • Replace the thermostat/relay if contact flutter is confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Include connector/terminal tightness checks in the fan inspection PM.
  • Secure fan wiring against vibration during maintenance.
  • Track intermittent-fault occurrences in the site failure database to catch developing patterns early.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Repeated Fault Investigation Procedure), SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-074 CCR Heat Sink Overheating

Symptom — The heat sink for the CCR power stage (thyristor/IGBT bridge) reaches an abnormally high temperature under normal load, triggering a thermal alarm or reducing output, even though ambient cabinet conditions appear otherwise normal.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage heat sink, thermal sensor, cooling fan and airflow path directly over the heat sink.

Possible Causes
HighHeat sink fins clogged with dust/debris, reducing surface area available for heat dissipation
HighCooling fan airflow not reaching the heat sink due to blockage or fan fault upstream
MediumDegraded thermal interface (paste/pad) between the power device and heat sink, increasing thermal resistance
MediumPower device (thyristor/IGBT) itself degrading and dissipating more heat than normal for the same load
LowerThermal sensor drifted, reporting a falsely high temperature
Required Tools
Infrared thermometer/thermal cameraTrue-RMS clamp meterCalibrated reference temperature probeCCR configuration/parameter tool
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO and allow the heat sink to cool before physical inspection or cleaning.
  • Do not touch the heat sink or power devices during or immediately after operation — surfaces can cause burns.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the alarm/trip temperature and load conditions at the time of the event from the event log.
  2. MeasurementWith the unit isolated and cooled, visually inspect the heat sink fins for dust/debris accumulation.
  3. MeasurementConfirm cooling fan airflow is reaching the heat sink directly (see CCR-071/072/073/076/077 if fan or blockage is suspected).
  4. MeasurementUnder controlled load, use an infrared thermometer/thermal camera to compare temperature across the heat sink and at the power device mounting point.
  5. MeasurementIndependently verify the thermal sensor reading against the reference measurement.
  6. DecisionHeat sink clean and airflow confirmed but power device mounting point runs hot → thermal interface or power device fault. Heat sink dirty/blocked → cleaning required. Sensor reading disagrees with reference → sensor fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to heat sink fouling, airflow restriction, thermal interface degradation, power device fault, or sensor fault.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by resolving it and re-measuring under representative load.
Test Points
Heat sink fin surface temperature (thermal imaging)
Power device mounting point temperature
Airflow at the heat sink
Thermal sensor reading vs. reference
Root Cause Verification

After correction, run the CCR at full load and confirm heat sink temperature remains within manufacturer limits over a sustained operating period with no repeat alarm.

Corrective Action
  • Clean the heat sink fins of dust/debris using appropriate methods (compressed air, brush) with power isolated.
  • Resolve any upstream airflow restriction or fan fault.
  • Reapply thermal interface material at the power device mounting.
  • Replace the degraded power device (thyristor/IGBT) if confirmed faulty.
  • Recalibrate or replace the thermal sensor.
Preventive Action
  • Include heat sink cleaning in the scheduled PM, at a frequency matched to the site's dust environment.
  • Trend heat sink temperature under comparable load conditions to catch gradual degradation early.
  • Verify thermal sensor calibration during scheduled maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection), SOP-CCR-10 (Protection Relay Calibration)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-075 CCR Cabinet Overheating

Symptom — Overall internal cabinet temperature runs abnormally high, triggering a general cabinet overtemperature alarm, even though individual components (heat sink, fan) may test normally in isolation.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet enclosure, cabinet temperature sensor, ventilation path, and all internal heat-generating components collectively.

Possible Causes
HighCombined restricted ventilation/filter blockage reducing overall airflow through the cabinet
HighElevated ambient temperature at the equipment shelter/room beyond the CCR's rated operating envelope
MediumMultiple internal components each running slightly hot, cumulatively raising cabinet temperature
MediumCabinet door/panel left open or improperly sealed, disrupting the designed airflow path
LowerCabinet temperature sensor miscalibrated or poorly located, reading unrepresentatively high
Required Tools
Calibrated reference temperature probeInfrared thermometer/thermal cameraAnemometer (airflow measurement)CCR configuration/parameter tool
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before internal inspection.
  • Allow the cabinet to cool before extended internal work to avoid heat-related injury.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the cabinet overtemperature alarm value and correlate with ambient shelter/room temperature and recent load history.
  2. MeasurementIndependently measure ambient temperature at the equipment shelter/room and compare against the CCR's rated operating range.
  3. MeasurementConfirm all cabinet doors/panels are correctly closed and sealed per design, and inspect for airflow bypass paths.
  4. MeasurementCheck ventilation/filter condition and airflow rate through the cabinet (see CCR-076/077 if blockage suspected).
  5. MeasurementWith individual components tested normal, use thermal imaging to identify any localized hotspot contributing to overall rise.
  6. DecisionAmbient temperature at/above rated limit → environmental cause, review shelter cooling/ventilation. Ventilation/filter restricted → blockage fault. Individual components normal, no external cause found → sensor/location fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to environmental conditions, ventilation restriction, door/panel sealing, or the cabinet temperature sensor.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the primary contributing factor(s) through resolution and re-measurement.
Test Points
Ambient shelter/room temperature
Cabinet internal airflow rate
Door/panel seal integrity
Cabinet temperature sensor reading vs. reference
Root Cause Verification

After correction, monitor cabinet temperature across a full daily/load cycle, including peak ambient conditions, and confirm it remains within the manufacturer's rated envelope.

Corrective Action
  • Resolve ventilation/filter restriction (clean or replace filters, clear blocked vents).
  • Improve equipment shelter cooling/ventilation if ambient temperature exceeds the rated envelope.
  • Repair or replace door/panel seals to restore the designed airflow path.
  • Recalibrate or relocate the cabinet temperature sensor if confirmed unrepresentative.
Preventive Action
  • Include shelter ambient temperature checks alongside CCR PM.
  • Trend cabinet temperature against ambient and load to catch gradual degradation.
  • Confirm door/panel seals during scheduled maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-076 CCR Ventilation Blockage

Symptom — Airflow through the CCR cabinet's ventilation openings (intake/exhaust louvres, vents, or ducting) is restricted or absent, reducing overall cooling effectiveness despite the fan running correctly.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet ventilation openings, louvres, vent grilles, and any associated ducting.

Possible Causes
HighExternal vent/louvre blocked by debris, vegetation, snow, or nesting material
HighInternal ductwork or vent path obstructed by dust build-up or a dislodged component
MediumVent grille physically damaged or incorrectly reinstalled after prior maintenance, restricting the opening
MediumEquipment shelter/cabinet positioned or modified such that the vent path is partially obstructed by nearby equipment or structure
LowerFan operating correctly but rotated/ducted in the wrong orientation after a prior fan replacement
Required Tools
Anemometer (airflow measurement)Flashlight/inspection mirrorInsulated screwdriver setCCR cabinet ventilation diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before physically inspecting or clearing any ventilation path near the fan or power electronics.
  • Be alert for pests or nesting material when clearing external vents.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the fan is running correctly (see CCR-071) to isolate the fault to the ventilation path rather than the fan itself.
  2. MeasurementMeasure airflow at the intake and exhaust vents with an anemometer and compare against the manufacturer's rated airflow.
  3. ObservationVisually inspect external vents/louvres for debris, vegetation, snow, or nesting material.
  4. ObservationVisually inspect internal ducting/vent path for dust build-up or a dislodged/misaligned component.
  5. DecisionLow airflow with a visible external obstruction → clear the blockage. Low airflow with no visible external obstruction → inspect internal duct path and grille orientation/fitment.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific external vent, internal duct section, or grille.
  7. Root CauseConfirm restored airflow meets rated value once the obstruction is cleared.
Test Points
Intake vent airflow rate
Exhaust vent airflow rate
External louvre condition
Internal duct path condition
Root Cause Verification

After clearing the blockage, re-measure airflow at intake and exhaust and confirm it meets the manufacturer's rated value; monitor cabinet/heat sink temperature through a full load cycle to confirm effective cooling is restored.

Corrective Action
  • Clear debris, vegetation, snow, or nesting material from external vents/louvres.
  • Clean or clear internal ductwork/vent path.
  • Repair or correctly reinstall a damaged or misaligned vent grille.
  • Relocate or modify obstructing nearby equipment/structure where feasible.
Preventive Action
  • Include external vent inspection and clearing in the routine PM, especially before seasons prone to debris or nesting.
  • Install or maintain vent screens to reduce debris/pest ingress without restricting airflow.
  • Verify airflow rate periodically as part of the cooling system PM.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-077 CCR Filter Blockage

Symptom — The CCR's intake air filter (where fitted) is significantly clogged, reducing airflow into the cabinet and contributing to elevated internal temperature, despite the fan and ventilation openings being otherwise functional.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet intake air filter/filter media, filter housing/frame.

Possible Causes
HighFilter media saturated with dust/particulate beyond its rated service interval
MediumFilter installed with incorrect orientation or an incorrect/non-standard replacement filter restricting airflow
MediumUnusually high ambient dust/particulate environment accelerating filter loading beyond the normal PM interval
LowerFilter frame/housing damaged or poorly seated, allowing bypass airflow that reduces effective filtration without necessarily reducing total airflow
Required Tools
Anemometer (airflow measurement)Flashlight/inspection mirrorReplacement filter media (correct manufacturer type)
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before opening the filter housing or accessing the intake path.
  • Use appropriate respiratory PPE when handling heavily loaded filters, particularly in high-dust environments.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationVisually inspect the filter media for visible dust loading/discolouration and compare against a clean reference filter.
  2. MeasurementMeasure intake airflow with the filter in place and compare against the manufacturer's rated airflow for a clean filter.
  3. ObservationConfirm the filter is the correct manufacturer-specified type and is correctly oriented and seated in its housing.
  4. MeasurementWith the filter removed, re-measure airflow to confirm whether the filter itself is the primary restriction.
  5. DecisionAirflow improves significantly with the filter removed → filter loading confirmed as the primary restriction. Airflow remains low with the filter removed → investigate ventilation path or fan (CCR-071/076).
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to filter loading, incorrect filter type/fitment, or a damaged housing/seal.
  7. Root CauseConfirm restored airflow meets rated value once the filter is replaced and correctly seated.
Test Points
Intake airflow with filter installed
Intake airflow with filter removed
Filter media visual condition
Filter type/orientation vs. manufacturer specification
Root Cause Verification

After replacement, re-measure intake airflow and confirm it meets the manufacturer's rated value; monitor cabinet/heat sink temperature through a full load cycle to confirm effective cooling is restored.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the filter media with the correct manufacturer-specified type.
  • Correct the filter orientation/fitment or repair the housing seal.
  • Adjust the filter replacement interval to match the site's actual dust environment where it exceeds the standard PM assumption.
Preventive Action
  • Include filter inspection and replacement in the routine PM at a frequency matched to the site's dust environment.
  • Stock the correct manufacturer-specified filter type to avoid substitution with an incorrect part.
  • Log filter replacement dates to track loading trends over time.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-078 CCR Internal Dust Accumulation

Symptom — Significant dust/particulate build-up is found on internal components (PCBs, terminals, heat sink, contactors) during inspection, raising the risk of overheating, tracking/insulation faults, or intermittent contact issues, even where no active alarm is currently present.

Equipment / System

CCR cabinet interior generally — control board, terminals, contactors, heat sink, and other internal surfaces.

Possible Causes
HighFilter blockage or degraded filtration allowing unfiltered air and particulate into the cabinet over time (see CCR-077)
HighCabinet seals (door, cable entries, panel joints) degraded or improperly closed, allowing dust ingress bypassing the filtered path
MediumHigh ambient dust/particulate environment at the site exceeding the cabinet's rated ingress protection under normal operating conditions
MediumExtended interval since last internal cleaning relative to the site's dust environment
LowerDust generated internally by a degrading component (e.g. arcing contactor, overheating insulation)
Required Tools
Flashlight/inspection mirrorAnti-static compressed air / ESD-safe vacuumInsulation resistance tester (500V/1000V)PPE (respiratory, eye protection)
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before opening the cabinet for cleaning or inspection.
  • Use anti-static/ESD-safe cleaning methods to avoid damaging sensitive control board components.
  • Use appropriate respiratory and eye PPE when cleaning heavily loaded interiors.
  • Do not use standard (non-ESD-safe) compressed air or ungrounded vacuum equipment directly on control boards.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationDocument the extent and location of dust accumulation during inspection, noting any components with unusually heavy build-up.
  2. MeasurementCheck the intake filter and cabinet seals (door, cable entries, panel joints) for degradation or improper closure allowing unfiltered ingress.
  3. MeasurementWhere dust is present near current-carrying terminals or the control board, perform an insulation resistance check to rule out tracking risk.
  4. ObservationInspect for any localized source of internally generated dust/debris, such as an arcing contactor or degrading insulation.
  5. DecisionIngress traced to filter/seal degradation → address the ingress path (see CCR-077 or reseal). No clear ingress path found and dust localized near one component → investigate that component as a possible internal source.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific ingress path or internally generated source.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the accumulation rate is consistent with the identified cause by comparing against the last recorded cleaning/inspection interval.
Test Points
Cabinet seal integrity (door, cable entries, panel joints)
Filter condition
Insulation resistance near affected terminals/board
Suspected internal dust source component
Root Cause Verification

After cleaning and addressing the ingress path, re-inspect at the next scheduled interval and confirm the accumulation rate has reduced to expected levels for the site's dust environment.

Corrective Action
  • Clean internal components using anti-static/ESD-safe methods appropriate to each component type.
  • Repair or replace degraded cabinet seals.
  • Address the filter condition per CCR-077 if filtration is the ingress path.
  • Replace or repair any internally degrading component identified as a dust source.
Preventive Action
  • Set an internal cleaning interval matched to the site's actual dust environment, not a generic default.
  • Include cabinet seal inspection in the routine PM.
  • Photograph internal condition at each PM visit to trend accumulation over time.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-079 CCR Control Board Failure

Symptom — The CCR control board (PLC/controller logic board) exhibits erratic behaviour, fails to boot, loses configuration, or stops responding entirely, with symptoms not attributable to a single sensor, relay, or power stage fault.

Equipment / System

CCR control/controller board (PLC or dedicated logic board), its power supply feed, and associated I/O terminals.

Possible Causes
HighControl board component failure (e.g. degraded capacitor, damaged I/O driver) from age, heat, or a transient surge event
HighControl board power supply feed out of tolerance, causing unstable board operation
MediumCorrupted firmware/configuration from an incomplete update or unexpected power loss during a write cycle
MediumMoisture or dust contamination on the board causing intermittent shorts or leakage paths
LowerA connected field device or wiring fault back-feeding an out-of-range signal into a board input, damaging that input
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterOscilloscopeManufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolFirmware/configuration backup mediaESD-safe handling equipment
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before removing or handling the control board.
  • Use proper ESD precautions (wrist strap, ESD mat) when handling the board to avoid further damage.
  • Confirm board power is fully discharged before removal, per manufacturer procedure.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationDocument the exact symptom (fails to boot, erratic behaviour, lost configuration, unresponsive) and any error/status LEDs or codes.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated and verified dead, inspect the board visually for obvious damage, discolouration, bulging capacitors, or contamination.
  3. MeasurementRestore power under controlled conditions and measure the board's incoming power supply voltage against the manufacturer's tolerance.
  4. DecisionBoard power supply out of tolerance → investigate the upstream power supply (see CCR-006 series) rather than the board itself. Board power supply within tolerance but board still faulty → board-level hardware or firmware fault.
  5. MeasurementWhere possible, attempt to reload firmware/configuration from a known-good backup per manufacturer procedure.
  6. DecisionBoard recovers after firmware/configuration reload → corrupted firmware/configuration was the cause. Board does not recover → hardware fault, proceed to board replacement.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the control board hardware, its power supply feed, or corrupted firmware/configuration.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failure mode before replacement or reconfiguration is finalised.
Test Points
Control board incoming power supply voltage
Board status/error LEDs or codes
Firmware/configuration integrity
Board I/O terminals for signs of overvoltage damage
Root Cause Verification

After replacement or firmware/configuration restoration, confirm the CCR boots correctly, retains configuration through a power cycle, and operates through a full representative load cycle with no recurrence.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed control board with a like-for-like spare.
  • Reload firmware/configuration from a verified backup, or reconfigure per manufacturer defaults if no backup exists.
  • Correct the upstream control power supply if found out of tolerance.
  • Clean and re-protect the board enclosure if contamination is confirmed as a contributing factor.
Preventive Action
  • Maintain a current, verified firmware/configuration backup for each CCR controller (cross-reference CCR-001).
  • Include a control board power supply voltage check in the PM schedule.
  • Protect the board compartment from moisture/dust ingress per CCR-078 findings.
  • Keep a spare control board on site or readily available given its criticality to CCR operation.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist), SOP-CCR-11 (CCR Cooling System Inspection)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-080 CCR Power Electronics Failure

Symptom — A power electronics component in the CCR bridge (thyristor, IGBT, diode, or associated snubber/gate drive circuitry) fails, resulting in loss of output, abnormal waveform, a protection trip, or visible component damage.

Equipment / System

CCR power stage bridge — thyristor/IGBT modules, diodes, snubber circuits, and gate/base drive electronics.

Possible Causes
HighA specific power device (thyristor/IGBT/diode) has failed short or open, from age, thermal stress, or a transient overvoltage event
HighGate/base drive circuit fault preventing correct firing/switching of an otherwise healthy device
MediumSnubber circuit component (resistor/capacitor) failed, exposing the power device to excessive switching stress
MediumSustained overheating (see CCR-074) accelerating power device degradation
LowerA transient surge or lightning-induced event damaging one or more devices despite surge protection
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeter (with diode/semiconductor test function)OscilloscopeInsulation resistance testerManufacturer power stage test procedureESD-safe handling equipment
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO and verify all capacitors in the power stage are fully discharged before touching any bridge component — stored energy can persist after isolation.
  • Treat all power stage terminals as live until proven de-energized with a tested meter.
  • Follow the two-person rule for HV isolation per site electrical safety procedure.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationRecord the exact fault symptom (loss of output, abnormal waveform, protection trip, visible damage) and any associated alarm code from the event log.
  2. ObservationWith power fully isolated and verified dead, visually inspect the bridge for signs of visible damage — scorching, cracked casing, blown fuses.
  3. MeasurementTest each power device (thyristor/IGBT/diode) individually using the multimeter's semiconductor test function or manufacturer-specified in-circuit/out-of-circuit test method.
  4. MeasurementInspect and test snubber circuit components (resistor/capacitor) associated with any failed device.
  5. MeasurementCheck the gate/base drive signal to each device with an oscilloscope, where a device tests electrically healthy but does not switch correctly.
  6. DecisionA specific device tests failed (shorted/open) → device replacement required. All devices test healthy but switching is abnormal → gate/base drive circuit fault.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific failed power device, snubber component, or drive circuit fault.
  8. Root CauseConfirm whether the failure was an isolated component failure or the result of an underlying cause (overheating, surge event, drive fault) that must also be addressed to prevent repeat failure.
Test Points
Individual power device semiconductor test (in-circuit/out-of-circuit)
Snubber circuit component values
Gate/base drive signal at each device
Bridge output waveform
Root Cause Verification

After replacement/repair, run the CCR through a full start-up and load-step cycle while monitoring output waveform and device temperatures, confirming stable operation with no recurrence.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the failed power device with a manufacturer-specified like-for-like part.
  • Replace failed snubber circuit components.
  • Repair or replace the gate/base drive circuit if confirmed faulty.
  • Address any underlying overheating or surge-related root cause to prevent repeat failure.
Preventive Action
  • Include power stage thermal monitoring and device inspection in the PM schedule.
  • Verify surge protection devices are present, correctly rated, and periodically tested.
  • Maintain a spare power device inventory given the criticality of the bridge to CCR operation.
  • Address cooling deficiencies promptly (CCR-074/075) to avoid accelerating power device degradation.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-02 (CCR Output Verification), SOP-CCR-04 (CCR Isolation & LOTO Procedure)

Standards: IEC 61820-3-2 (supersedes IEC 61822)

Rev 0 — Initial issue

06 · CCR Monitoring & Communication

15 of 15 topics published
CCR-081 CCR Display Blank

Symptom — The CCR front panel HMI/display shows nothing at all — no backlight, no text, no indicator lamps — even though the unit appears otherwise powered and, in some cases, is still regulating output current normally.

Equipment / System

CCR front panel HMI/display module, its power feed, and the data link between the display and the main controller.

Possible Causes
HighDisplay module power supply feed failed or disconnected, independent of the main controller
HighDisplay module itself failed (backlight, driver, or panel hardware)
MediumRibbon cable/data connector between the display and controller loose, damaged, or disconnected
MediumMain controller has failed or is not booting, so no data is being sent to the display (see CCR-079)
LowerDisplay brightness/contrast setting inadvertently set to minimum, appearing blank rather than genuinely powered off
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterCCR wiring/HMI diagramInsulated screwdriver setManufacturer diagnostic tool
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before opening the cabinet to access display wiring or connectors.
  • Confirm the CCR's actual run state independently (e.g. output current) before assuming the unit itself is off, since a blank display does not necessarily mean the CCR is not running.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm whether the CCR is otherwise operating normally (output current present) despite the blank display, to separate a display-only fault from a full unit fault.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated and verified dead, check continuity/condition of the display's power feed fuse or supply wiring.
  3. MeasurementRestore power under controlled conditions and measure voltage at the display module's power input terminals.
  4. DecisionCorrect voltage present at the display but screen stays blank → display module hardware fault. No voltage at the display → upstream power feed, fuse, or wiring fault.
  5. MeasurementInspect and reseat the ribbon cable/data connector between display and controller.
  6. ObservationIf the display briefly shows content at power-up before going blank, check brightness/contrast configuration via the controller's parameter tool.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the display module, its power feed, the data connector, or a brightness/contrast configuration issue.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component by isolated testing before replacement.
Test Points
Display module power input voltage
Display power feed fuse continuity
Display-to-controller data connector/ribbon cable
Display brightness/contrast configuration
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm the display shows correct content immediately at power-up and remains stable through a full operating cycle.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or restore the display's power feed/fuse.
  • Replace the failed display module.
  • Reseat or replace the damaged ribbon cable/data connector.
  • Correct the brightness/contrast configuration.
Preventive Action
  • Include a display functional check in the routine PM.
  • Keep a spare display module on site given its role in local diagnostics.
  • Document default brightness/contrast settings in the site configuration record.
Related References

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-082 CCR Display Incorrect

Symptom — The CCR front panel HMI/display is powered and legible but shows incorrect, garbled, or nonsensical content — wrong characters, corrupted graphics, or values that do not correspond to actual CCR operation.

Equipment / System

CCR front panel HMI/display module and its data/firmware link to the main controller.

Possible Causes
HighDisplay firmware corrupted or mismatched with the controller firmware version
HighDisplay driver/graphics hardware degrading, producing corrupted characters or graphics
MediumData link between display and controller experiencing errors, garbling transmitted content
MediumUnderlying controller fault feeding genuinely incorrect data to an otherwise healthy display (see CCR-079, CCR-090/091/092)
LowerIncorrect language/localisation or display configuration setting selected
Required Tools
Manufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolFirmware/configuration backup mediaTrue-RMS multimeterOscilloscope
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before accessing internal wiring or connectors.
  • Do not act on displayed values for safety-critical decisions until the display's accuracy is confirmed — verify with independent measurement first.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationDocument exactly what is shown incorrectly — garbled characters/graphics, or plausible-looking but wrong values — and under what conditions it occurs.
  2. MeasurementIndependently verify actual CCR operating parameters (current, status, step) with reference instruments and compare against what the display shows.
  3. DecisionDisplayed values disagree with independently measured actual values → underlying controller/sensor data fault, investigate per the relevant specific topic (CCR-090/091/092). Displayed content is garbled/corrupted rather than simply wrong → display or data link hardware/firmware fault.
  4. MeasurementWhere garbling is suspected, check the display firmware version against the controller firmware version for compatibility.
  5. MeasurementInspect the data link/ribbon cable between display and controller for damage or a marginal connection.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to display firmware, display hardware, the data link, or an underlying controller data fault.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by resolving it and re-verifying display content.
Test Points
Display firmware version vs. controller firmware version
Data link/ribbon cable condition
Independently measured actual operating parameters vs. displayed values
Display language/localisation configuration
Root Cause Verification

After correction, confirm the display shows accurate, stable content matching independently verified operating parameters through a full representative operating period.

Corrective Action
  • Update or reflash display firmware to the correct, compatible version.
  • Replace the display module if hardware degradation is confirmed.
  • Repair or replace the data link/ribbon cable.
  • Correct display language/localisation configuration.
  • If the underlying cause is a controller/sensor data fault, address that fault per the relevant topic.
Preventive Action
  • Keep display and controller firmware versions aligned per manufacturer compatibility guidance.
  • Include display content verification against reference measurement in the PM.
  • Maintain a firmware version log for each CCR unit.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-083 CCR Display Flickering

Symptom — The CCR front panel HMI/display flickers, dims and brightens erratically, or intermittently blanks and returns while otherwise showing correct content, rather than remaining stable.

Equipment / System

CCR front panel HMI/display module, its power feed, and the data link to the main controller.

Possible Causes
HighLoose or marginal display power connector causing an intermittent supply
HighDisplay backlight driver degrading, producing visible flicker
MediumMarginal data link/ribbon cable connection causing intermittent refresh issues
MediumDisplay power feed voltage fluctuating due to an upstream control power supply issue
LowerElectromagnetic interference from nearby switching equipment affecting the display driver
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterOscilloscopeData logger for trend/repeated-event analysisInsulated screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before performing a wiggle test or connector inspection with power isolated.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationLog the flicker pattern over a representative period — constant, load-related, or random — to characterise the fault.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated, perform a wiggle test on the display power connector and data ribbon cable while monitoring continuity.
  3. MeasurementUnder controlled power-on conditions, measure the display's supply voltage stability with an oscilloscope, watching for dips or noise coinciding with flicker.
  4. DecisionWiggle test reveals an intermittent connection → connector/wiring fault. Supply voltage shows genuine instability → upstream control power supply fault. Connections and supply both stable → backlight driver degradation or EMI.
  5. MeasurementIf EMI is suspected, check display cable routing and separation from high-current/switching wiring per manufacturer guidance.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the display connector/wiring, the control power supply, the backlight driver, or an EMI/routing issue.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by reproducing and resolving it under controlled conditions.
Test Points
Display power connector and data ribbon cable (wiggle test)
Display supply voltage stability (oscilloscope)
Control power supply output
Display cable routing relative to switching wiring
Root Cause Verification

After repair, monitor the display through a sustained multi-cycle operating period and confirm stable, flicker-free operation with no recurrence.

Corrective Action
  • Clean, tighten, or replace the display power connector or data cable.
  • Repair or replace the upstream control power supply if found unstable.
  • Replace the display module if the backlight driver is confirmed degraded.
  • Re-route display cabling away from high-current/switching wiring if EMI is confirmed.
Preventive Action
  • Include connector/cable tightness checks in the display PM.
  • Verify control power supply stability during scheduled maintenance.
  • Follow manufacturer cable routing/separation guidance during installation and maintenance.
Related References

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-084 CCR Keypad Not Working

Symptom — The CCR front panel keypad/pushbuttons do not respond, or only some keys respond, when pressed — local navigation, parameter entry, or local start/stop commands cannot be issued via the keypad.

Equipment / System

CCR front panel keypad/pushbutton assembly and its connection to the controller.

Possible Causes
HighKeypad membrane/switch assembly worn or physically damaged, especially on frequently used keys
HighKeypad connector/ribbon cable to the controller loose, corroded, or disconnected
MediumController input scanning for the keypad has failed or locked up while the rest of the controller functions normally
MediumMoisture or contamination inside the keypad membrane causing keys to stick or fail to register
LowerA local keypad lockout/lock function has been enabled, intentionally or inadvertently, in the configuration
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterManufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolInsulated screwdriver setContact cleaner (manufacturer-approved)
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before opening the panel to access keypad wiring/connectors.
  • Use only manufacturer-approved cleaning products on the keypad membrane to avoid damaging the seal.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationTest each key individually and record which keys respond and which do not, to distinguish a single-key fault from a total keypad failure.
  2. ObservationCheck the controller configuration for an active keypad lockout/lock function.
  3. MeasurementWith power isolated, inspect and reseat the keypad connector/ribbon cable.
  4. MeasurementWhere possible, use the controller's diagnostic tool to verify whether individual key presses are being received by the controller at all.
  5. DecisionNo keys register at the controller → connector/wiring or controller input fault. Some keys register and others do not → localized membrane/switch wear on the non-responding keys. Keys register but no action occurs → controller logic or lockout configuration.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific worn key(s), the connector/cable, the controller input scanning, or a lockout configuration.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific failed component or configuration setting.
Test Points
Individual key response (physical and at controller diagnostic level)
Keypad connector/ribbon cable
Keypad lockout/lock configuration setting
Controller key-scan input function
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm every key responds correctly and issues the expected local command through a full functional check.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the worn or damaged keypad membrane/switch assembly.
  • Clean, reseat, or replace the keypad connector/ribbon cable.
  • Disable an inadvertently enabled keypad lockout.
  • Address the controller input scanning fault per manufacturer procedure, up to controller replacement if required (see CCR-079).
Preventive Action
  • Include a full keypad functional check in the routine PM.
  • Keep a spare keypad assembly on site given its role in local operation.
  • Document any intentional keypad lockout configuration in the site record to avoid confusion during future troubleshooting.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-085 CCR Local Control Failure

Symptom — Commands issued from the CCR's local control position (front panel keypad/switches in local mode) fail to take effect — start, stop, or step-change commands are accepted by the panel but the CCR does not respond, or local mode cannot be selected at all.

Equipment / System

CCR local/remote selector switch, local control input path, and controller logic governing local mode operation.

Possible Causes
HighLocal/remote selector switch faulty or not making proper contact, so the controller does not register local mode as selected
HighLocal control command wiring or input terminal fault between the keypad/switches and the controller
MediumController logic fault or configuration error preventing local commands from being actioned even when correctly received
MediumA latched interlock or protection condition silently blocking command execution (see CCR-001, CCR-070)
LowerKeypad itself faulty, distinct from the local control logic (see CCR-084)
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterManufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolCCR control schematicInsulated screwdriver set
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before accessing selector switch wiring or control terminals.
  • Confirm no interlock/protection condition is being silently overridden before repeated local command attempts.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the local/remote selector switch position and verify the controller's displayed/reported mode matches the physical switch position.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated and verified dead, check continuity of the selector switch and its wiring to the controller input.
  3. MeasurementRestore power under controlled conditions and verify the controller input terminal state changes correctly when the selector switch is toggled.
  4. DecisionController-reported mode does not match the physical switch position → selector switch or wiring fault. Mode matches but commands are still not actioned → controller logic, configuration, or a latched interlock/protection condition.
  5. ObservationReview the controller's event/alarm log for any latched interlock or protection condition blocking command execution.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the selector switch, its wiring, controller logic/configuration, or a latched protection condition.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause and rule out a keypad-only fault per CCR-084.
Test Points
Local/remote selector switch continuity and position feedback
Controller-reported operating mode
Controller event/alarm log for latched conditions
Local command input terminal state
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm local start, stop, and step-change commands each take effect correctly through a full functional check.

Corrective Action
  • Replace the faulty local/remote selector switch.
  • Repair the local control command wiring or terminal.
  • Correct the controller configuration or logic fault per manufacturer procedure.
  • Clear the latched interlock/protection condition only after confirming and resolving its underlying cause.
Preventive Action
  • Include local/remote selector switch functional testing in the routine PM.
  • Verify local control functions during every scheduled maintenance visit.
  • Document local mode configuration and interlock logic in the site SOP.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist), SOP-CCR-04 (CCR Isolation & LOTO Procedure)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-086 CCR Remote Control Failure

Symptom — Commands issued from the remote control system (ALCMS/tower/PLC) fail to take effect at the CCR — the CCR does not start, stop, or change step in response to remote commands, or remote mode cannot be selected.

Equipment / System

CCR local/remote selector switch, remote control input interface, communication link to ALCMS/PLC, and controller logic governing remote mode operation.

Possible Causes
HighLocal/remote selector switch not correctly set to remote, or faulty (see CCR-085 for switch-level diagnosis)
HighCommunication link between the CCR and ALCMS/PLC down or degraded, preventing remote commands from reaching the controller (see CCR-087/088/089)
MediumRemote command mapping/configuration mismatch between the ALCMS/PLC and the CCR controller
MediumA latched interlock or protection condition blocking command execution regardless of source
LowerRemote command issued from the wrong ALCMS/PLC point or workstation due to a configuration/addressing error upstream
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterManufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolCommunication link test equipment (per protocol)CCR control schematic
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before accessing selector switch or communication wiring.
  • Coordinate with the ALCMS/tower control room before issuing test commands, to avoid confusion with live operational traffic.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the local/remote selector switch is correctly set to remote and the controller reports remote mode selected.
  2. ObservationConfirm whether the communication link to ALCMS/PLC is up and healthy (see CCR-087/088/089) as a first branch point.
  3. DecisionCommunication link is down → investigate as a communication fault per the relevant specific topic. Communication link is healthy → investigate command mapping, configuration, or a latched condition.
  4. MeasurementWith the link confirmed healthy, issue a test command from ALCMS/PLC (coordinated with the control room) and monitor whether it is received at the CCR controller's input/register.
  5. ObservationReview command point mapping/addressing configuration between ALCMS/PLC and the CCR to rule out a mismatch.
  6. ObservationReview the controller's event/alarm log for a latched interlock or protection condition blocking command execution.
  7. Fault LocationIsolate to the selector switch, the communication link, command mapping/configuration, or a latched protection condition.
  8. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause through resolution and a successful coordinated remote command test.
Test Points
Local/remote selector switch position and controller-reported mode
Communication link status
Remote command receipt at the CCR controller input/register
Command point mapping/addressing configuration
Root Cause Verification

After repair, coordinate with ALCMS/tower control room and confirm remote start, stop, and step-change commands each take effect correctly through a full functional check.

Corrective Action
  • Correct the local/remote selector switch position or replace it if faulty.
  • Resolve the underlying communication link fault per the relevant specific topic.
  • Correct command point mapping/addressing configuration.
  • Clear the latched interlock/protection condition only after confirming and resolving its underlying cause.
Preventive Action
  • Include remote command functional testing (coordinated with the control room) in the routine PM.
  • Maintain a documented, version-controlled command point mapping record between ALCMS/PLC and each CCR.
  • Verify communication link health as a standing part of remote control troubleshooting.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-01 (CCR Daily Start-Up Checklist), SOP-CCR-12 (CCR–ALCMS Communication Verification)

Diagram: CCR Control Schematic

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-087 CCR PLC Communication Failure

Symptom — Communication between the CCR controller and its associated PLC is down or failing entirely — no data exchange, a communication fault/alarm is raised, or the PLC shows the CCR as offline/unreachable.

Equipment / System

CCR controller communication port, PLC communication port, and the physical/network link between them.

Possible Causes
HighPhysical communication cable/connector damaged, disconnected, or incorrectly terminated
HighCommunication port failure at either the CCR controller or the PLC (hardware fault)
MediumCommunication protocol/parameter mismatch (baud rate, address, protocol type) between the CCR and PLC
MediumPLC program/logic fault or the PLC itself offline/faulted, independent of the CCR
LowerElectromagnetic interference or improper cable routing/shielding degrading signal integrity on the link
Required Tools
Communication link test equipment (per protocol — e.g. RS-485/Modbus tester)True-RMS multimeterManufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolCommunication wiring diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before physically inspecting or reterminating communication wiring.
  • Coordinate with other stakeholders relying on the PLC before taking the link offline for testing.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm the exact nature of the failure — no communication ever established, or communication that was previously working has stopped — and check both the CCR and PLC for their respective fault indications.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated where required, physically inspect the communication cable, connectors, and termination for damage or looseness.
  3. MeasurementVerify communication protocol parameters (baud rate, address, protocol type) are correctly and identically configured at both the CCR controller and the PLC.
  4. MeasurementUsing appropriate test equipment for the protocol, verify signal presence and integrity on the communication link.
  5. DecisionNo signal present on the link → cable/connector/port hardware fault. Signal present but no valid communication → protocol/parameter mismatch. Signal and parameters correct but PLC itself faulted → PLC-side investigation, independent of the CCR.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the communication cable/connector, a port hardware fault at either end, a protocol/parameter mismatch, or a PLC-side fault.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by restoring communication and verifying stable data exchange.
Test Points
Communication cable/connector condition and termination
Protocol parameters at CCR controller vs. PLC
Signal presence/integrity on the link
CCR and PLC fault/status indications
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm stable communication with no dropouts through a sustained monitoring period, and verify data exchanged matches expected values at both ends.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the damaged communication cable/connector.
  • Replace the failed communication port hardware at the CCR controller or PLC.
  • Correct protocol/parameter configuration to match at both ends.
  • Escalate to the PLC-responsible party if the fault is confirmed PLC-side.
  • Improve cable routing/shielding if EMI is confirmed as a contributing factor.
Preventive Action
  • Include communication link integrity checks in the routine PM.
  • Document and version-control communication protocol configuration at both ends.
  • Follow manufacturer cable routing/shielding guidance during installation and maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-12 (CCR–ALCMS Communication Verification)

Diagram: CCR Communication Architecture Diagram

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-088 CCR ALCMS Communication Failure

Symptom — Communication between the CCR and the Airfield Lighting Control and Monitoring System (ALCMS) is down or failing entirely — the ALCMS shows the CCR as offline/unreachable, or no status/command data is being exchanged.

Equipment / System

CCR controller communication interface, ALCMS gateway/server-side interface, and the network/link between them (which may route via an intermediate PLC).

Possible Causes
HighNetwork/link fault between the CCR site and the ALCMS — cable, fibre, switch, or network equipment failure
HighCCR-side communication interface/gateway hardware fault
MediumALCMS-side configuration error — incorrect point address, IP address, or device profile for this CCR
MediumAn intermediate PLC or RTU in the communication path has failed or lost its own link (see CCR-087)
LowerALCMS server/application-level fault affecting this CCR's data point specifically, while the underlying network is healthy
Required Tools
Communication link test equipment (per protocol)Network cable testerManufacturer/ALCMS diagnostic toolCommunication architecture diagram
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before physically inspecting communication wiring at the CCR.
  • Coordinate with the ALCMS/control room administrator before taking any action that could affect other monitored equipment on the same network segment.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationConfirm at the ALCMS whether only this CCR is offline/unreachable, or whether multiple devices on the same network segment are affected.
  2. DecisionMultiple devices affected → likely a shared network/link fault, investigate network infrastructure rather than this CCR specifically. Only this CCR affected → investigate this CCR's link, interface, or ALCMS configuration.
  3. MeasurementCheck the CCR-side communication interface/gateway for correct power, status LEDs, and physical link integrity.
  4. MeasurementIf an intermediate PLC/RTU is in the path, verify its communication status independently (see CCR-087).
  5. ObservationVerify the ALCMS-side configuration (point address, IP address, device profile) matches the CCR's actual configuration.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the network/link, the CCR-side interface hardware, an intermediate PLC/RTU, or an ALCMS-side configuration error.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by restoring communication and verifying the CCR reappears correctly in the ALCMS.
Test Points
CCR-side communication interface/gateway status
Network/link integrity between CCR site and ALCMS
Intermediate PLC/RTU communication status (if applicable)
ALCMS-side point/device configuration
Root Cause Verification

After repair, confirm the CCR shows correctly online in the ALCMS with accurate status/command exchange through a sustained monitoring period.

Corrective Action
  • Repair or replace the faulty network/link infrastructure.
  • Replace the failed CCR-side communication interface/gateway.
  • Correct the ALCMS-side point/device configuration.
  • Resolve the intermediate PLC/RTU fault per CCR-087 if applicable.
Preventive Action
  • Include CCR-to-ALCMS communication verification in the routine PM.
  • Maintain a current network topology and point-mapping document for the ALCMS system.
  • Monitor network infrastructure health independently of individual CCR status to catch shared faults early.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-12 (CCR–ALCMS Communication Verification)

Standards: —

Diagram: CCR Communication Architecture Diagram

Case Study: Division 25 — Field Case Study Troubleshooting (cross-reference where applicable)

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-089 CCR Communication Intermittent

Symptom — Communication between the CCR and PLC/ALCMS drops out and recovers repeatedly rather than failing completely or remaining stable, producing intermittent "offline" indications, data gaps, or repeated reconnection events.

Equipment / System

CCR controller communication interface, communication cable/link, and the PLC/ALCMS-side interface.

Possible Causes
HighLoose or marginal communication connector/termination causing an intermittent physical connection
HighMarginal network/link quality — degraded cable, failing switch port, or a link operating near its error-rate limit
MediumElectromagnetic interference intermittently corrupting communication traffic
MediumCommunication timeout/retry parameters set too tight for actual network latency, causing false dropout indications
LowerA shared network resource intermittently overloaded by other traffic, causing periodic congestion
Required Tools
Communication link test equipment (per protocol)Data logger for trend/repeated-event analysisNetwork cable testerTrue-RMS multimeter
Safety Precautions
  • Apply LOTO before performing a wiggle test on communication wiring with power isolated.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationLog the pattern of communication dropouts over a representative period — timing, duration, and any correlation with load, weather, or other network activity.
  2. MeasurementWith power isolated, perform a wiggle test on the communication connector/termination while monitoring the link.
  3. MeasurementTest the communication cable/link for error rate, attenuation, or intermittent continuity using appropriate protocol test equipment.
  4. ObservationReview communication timeout/retry parameter settings against actual network latency and manufacturer recommendations.
  5. DecisionWiggle test reveals an intermittent connection → connector/termination fault. Cable/link tests show a genuine quality issue → cable/infrastructure fault. Connection and cable both sound → EMI, timeout parameter, or network congestion.
  6. Fault LocationIsolate to the connector/termination, the cable/link, EMI, timeout configuration, or network congestion.
  7. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by reproducing and resolving it under monitored conditions.
Test Points
Communication connector/termination (wiggle test)
Cable/link error rate and continuity
Communication timeout/retry configuration
Network traffic/congestion at the shared segment
Root Cause Verification

After repair, monitor communication continuously through a sustained multi-day period and confirm no recurrence of intermittent dropouts.

Corrective Action
  • Clean, tighten, or replace the communication connector/termination.
  • Replace the degraded communication cable or resolve the failing network infrastructure component.
  • Improve cable routing/shielding if EMI is confirmed.
  • Adjust timeout/retry parameters only within manufacturer-recommended limits.
  • Address network congestion at the shared segment if confirmed as a contributing factor.
Preventive Action
  • Include communication connector/termination checks in the routine PM.
  • Trend communication link quality/error rate over time to catch gradual degradation early.
  • Document timeout/retry parameter settings and require change control for adjustment.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-06 (Repeated Fault Investigation Procedure), SOP-CCR-12 (CCR–ALCMS Communication Verification)

Diagram: CCR Communication Architecture Diagram

Rev 0 — Initial issue
CCR-090 CCR Wrong Status Indication

Symptom — The CCR's reported operating status (run/standby/fault, or local/remote mode) shown on the local display and/or at the PLC/ALCMS does not match the CCR's actual physical state.

Equipment / System

CCR controller status logic, status indication outputs (local display and remote data points), and associated sensors/feedback contacts.

Possible Causes
HighStatus feedback contact/sensor (e.g. contactor auxiliary contact) worn, misaligned, or failed, reporting an incorrect physical state
HighController status logic fault or corrupted internal state, independent of the underlying physical condition
MediumCommunication data mapping error causing the correct internal status to be displayed/transmitted incorrectly at the display or PLC/ALCMS
MediumA genuine but very brief/transient state change not being captured due to a slow status update/polling rate
LowerLocal display and remote (PLC/ALCMS) status disagree with each other, indicating the fault is isolated to one indication path rather than the controller's internal state
Required Tools
True-RMS multimeterManufacturer diagnostic/configuration toolCommunication link test equipment (per protocol)CCR control schematic
Safety Precautions
  • Treat status indication as unverified until confirmed by direct physical/electrical observation — do not make operational decisions based on unverified status alone.
  • Apply LOTO before physically inspecting feedback contacts or sensor wiring.
Diagnostic Procedure
  1. ObservationDirectly observe the CCR's actual physical state (output present/absent, contactor position, etc.) and compare against what is shown on the local display and separately at the PLC/ALCMS.
  2. DecisionLocal display and remote status agree with each other but both disagree with actual physical state → likely a controller-level status logic or feedback sensor fault. Local display and remote status disagree with each other → likely isolated to the communication/data mapping path for one of the two.
  3. MeasurementCheck the relevant status feedback contact/sensor (e.g. contactor auxiliary contact) for correct mechanical alignment and electrical continuity.
  4. MeasurementWhere the local/remote indications disagree with each other, verify the data mapping/point configuration between the controller and the PLC/ALCMS.
  5. Fault LocationIsolate to the specific feedback contact/sensor, the controller status logic, or a communication/data mapping error.
  6. Root CauseConfirm the specific cause by resolving it and re-verifying that displayed/transmitted status matches actual physical state across several state changes.
Test Points
Actual physical CCR state (direct observation)
Local display status vs. actual state
Remote (PLC/ALCMS) status vs. actual state
Status feedback contact/sensor condition
Root Cause Verification

After correction, cycle the CCR through several state changes (start/stop, mode changes) and confirm the local display and remote status both correctly and promptly reflect the actual physical state each time.

Corrective Action
  • Repair, realign, or replace the failed status feedback contact/sensor.
  • Correct the controller status logic fault, up to controller replacement if required (see CCR-079).
  • Correct the data mapping/point configuration between the controller and PLC/ALCMS.
  • Adjust the status update/polling rate only within manufacturer-recommended limits if a slow rate is confirmed as contributing.
Preventive Action
  • Include a status indication verification (comparing actual state to displayed/transmitted status) in the routine PM.
  • Document status point mapping and require change control for any adjustment.
  • Periodically verify feedback contact/sensor condition during scheduled maintenance.
Related References

SOP: SOP-CCR-12 (CCR–ALCMS Communication Verification)
